reviews.author: Roman Hien
reviews.text: 1:99 Shorts is a collection of eleven inspirational short stories by Hong Kong performing arts elites who were invited by the Hong Kong Film Workers Association in 2003. In 2003, when the whole people were deeply troubled by SARS, everyone was in a panic, and their lives suffered the most terrifying threat. The Hong Kong government invested 5.5 million to shoot these 11 short stories, which aims to encourage Hong Kong people not to forget to Dream on, even in adversity, regain their confidence, and strengthen themselves under adversity.

Not too surprising considering the exterior motives behind this anthology, and there are a couple of worthwhile entries, but overall it's probably best to lower your expectations when watching this.

reviews.text: UPA's first feature-length film - and the first cel-animated feature made in the United States by anybody other than Disney in 18 years - is an admirable leap in ambition, but by 1959, what remained of the studio was not remotely equipped to deal with that ambition, which is possibly why so much of the talent had to be poached from elsewhere, including newly ex-Disney director Jack Kinney as director and newly ex-Warner animator Abe Levitow as animator director. It was a box-office failure that hastened the demise of UPA and brought a formal end to the studio's relationship with distributor Columbia, and I really don't think that we need to stand in judgment of the audiences from 1959 that…

reviews.author: Michael Shawn
reviews.text: It was a great choice to use Mr. Magoo sparingly in a feature based on a popular fairy tale (or folkloric tale, if you prefer), since a little of his shtick goes a long way. But they found exactly the right balance because this was surprisingly outstanding. The simple animation is charming and wildly colorful, the character designs look retro-cool, the voice characterizations are fittingly hilarious or heroic, and the music is perfectly suited to this particular adaptation. The Wicked Wazir stands out as the most entertaining aspect of the film with his menagerie of sewer pets and his repeatedly bungled attempts at stealing the lamp (plus he's voiced by Hans Conried), but I also much appreciated Aladdin and his…

reviews.author: Lowbacca
reviews.text: I... don't think I have anything against Mister Magoo, per se, but I do feel like Mister Magoo only has one real joke and I feel like that can only go on for a reel or so. It seems that they felt this was the case as well, because they've mostly just tried to embed Magoo as a running gag character in the story of Aladdin by making him Aladdin's uncle. Magoo, wisely, isn't the real central point of the story, but he sure does cause things to happen around Aladdin. So storywise, this movie just can't figure out how to make any of this work.

reviews.author: Sean
reviews.text: A typical romp with UPA, visually at least. It's a very nice looking film with the style and animation you want from UPA. The plot is more or less what you expect from One Thousand and One Nights, which is to say the plot of some form of Aladdin. The characters of the princess and Aladdin are fine, though pretty bland. The stand out characters here are Mr. Magoo, being pulled from the UPA shorts, plays pretty well especially in the small doses they use him in. The other being The wicked wazir, played with such personality by Hans Conried. Both of them, along with the art and animation, make this a fine watch, though admittedly, if you're not invested…

reviews.author: Colby
reviews.text: I’m not sure why this tries to be both a Mr. Magoo film and an Aladdin one; it isn’t really effective in either attempt and at only 75 minutes the writers certainly bit off more than they could chew. Mr. Magoo is not a very slapstick character, either, and so it only works when he cheats death through his nearsightedness. We don’t get much of that, as I’ve already mentioned they have to spend much of the 75 minutes in a straightforward Aladdin retelling. There’s also no attempt to Magoo the rest of the cast (yes, I’m using Magoo as a verb). Every character is drawn in a realistic style — Wacky Racers or Scooby-Doo type. Then there’s Mr. Magoo,…

reviews.author: momalley
reviews.text: I watched this to add 1959 (i.e. the year of Sleeping Beauty) to my "Counterprogramming Disney" list. It is the only American animated feature released that year that wasn't produced by Disney, though as is often the case in American animation, it basically comes back around to Disney in the end anyway, because it's directed by Jack Kinney, a former Disney animator who has director credits on a whole host of early Disney films, including Dumbo and Pinocchio and produced by Stephen Bosustow, another former Disney animator, who went on to co-found what would eventually become UPA, a rival animation studio to Disney--basically the same ol' story of Disney resistance that happens again and again with everyone from Don Bluth…

reviews.author: Fitzgerald Sanchez
reviews.text: This is more or less essentially the same story structure as the color Popeye short Aladdin and his Wonderful Lamp minus the stereotypical stuff of the time. In its place was of course the abstractly iconic style of UPA which made up for the decently solid and stylized experience. Hans Conried and Jim Backus plus some others like Alan Reed and Daws Butler helped to make this great too. Sure, it came out before the 1992 Disney classic of Aladdin like a few other adaptations of the 1001 Nights story, and yet it managed to be pretty fun and enticing playing it (mostly) fairly straight from beginning to end.

reviews.author: Jordan Miller
reviews.text: This was probably the most obscure old Aladdin I watched, and yet it was actually one of the best ones. There's not much I appreciate more than seeing a quasi-serious plot being turned into a comedy; it worked for Taming of the Shrew and it works for these Aladdins, too.

reviews.author: Tim West
reviews.text: I've never been much of a fan of Mr Magoo - he's both offensive and dull - so I wasn't expecting much of a Magoo-in-Aladdin film, but this was actually quite fun. The jokes are still mostly irritating or don't land, but the art and design are beautiful. I loved all the towering repeating impossible palaces, with their skewed perspective and mosaic tilework. The seascapes at the end are particularly gorgeous, too. And the design of the Wazir's animal friends is a lot of fun. Everything's quite jolly and enjoyable. I was expecting a 1950s movie set in the Middle East to be hella racist, but it's actually fine, mining its comedy from the usual ridiculous characters and Magoo's dull absurdities rather than anything culturally specific. Not sure why it's named for the 1001 Nights when the tale's exclusively Aladdin. The genie's great, also.

reviews.text: I was surprised I hadn't heard the story of Georg Elser before. He was a Christian - a carpenter, no less! - and a non-party-aligned Communist who, in 1939, planted a bomb intended to kill Adolf Hitler. And he would have done it, too, had Hitler not departed the conference he was speaking at a little bit early - the thirteen minutes of the film's English title. (In Germany it's called Elser, suggesting he's more famous in his home country)

reviews.text: WEGEN NEBEL!We watched this at an event that dealt with resistance fighters from World War II, who *would have* changed the world—the whole thing arranged by the mother of my best friend, which is why we were both allowed to serve drinks to the guests there :)An actor from our theater also portrayed Georg Elser, who was in the foreground at the event, and several people and experts were invited to inform about other resistance fighters…The film was a great conclusion of the evening, not intrusive but very realistic, informative and paired with a good cast. It’s the familiar mix of happy memories and sickening torture scenes that we’ve seen before and that always make these films so memorable and paining. Films like these are there to help us to remember, which is important considering many of us tend to forget.

reviews.text: A strange mashup of Jules Verne stories 20,000 Leagues and The Mysterious Island. Editing is disastrous, as if shots are randomly stitched together and gaps filled with excessive intertitles. Some ridiculous blackface doesn't help. Audiences must have been impressed by underwater scenes though. They're nothing special now, mostly viewing coral reefs in monochrome. I couldn't help but read those intertitles in David Attenborough's voice. Scenes of the submarine and ship on the water surface look great, with characters donning century old diving gear. Overall, interesting as a historical work but not an enjoyable film.

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: I have two reviews to write about this. One is extremely horny, about Lee Marvin’s BDE, and the sexual tension between him and Randolph Scott. The other is more analytical, about Budd Boetticher‘s flawless pacing, the absolute genius of the wagon scene, and how much better Scott was for this role than any of the proposed alternatives. Both of my reviews converge, though, on that scene in the crowded wagon, during the storm, in which both of the men who aren’t Annie Greer’s husband see nothing but her; in which there are two layers of protection between her and Masters, with Stride the most intimate, and her husband further away; in which she knows from the very start that Masters is dangerous, because she’s a woman and can feel the threat to her that men around her blithely overlook.

reviews.author: The Film Foundation
reviews.text: In 1956, director Budd Boetticher, then 40 years old, would make his first film with Randolph Scott, then 58 years old. SEVEN MEN FROM NOW was the first of seven Westerns that the two would make together as director and leading man. The film was made for John Wayne's production company, Batjac, but when Wayne died in 1979 and the Batjac film library found itself in transition, the film more or less went missing.

reviews.author: Cormac 👑
reviews.text: Normalise movies being sub-90 minutes again, I beg. One picture in and I can already tell Budd Boetticher is one of the more economical storytellers there is or was, and my tired, worn-out 2021 brain thanks him for his service. There’s an art to saying so much with so little, and Hell, I feel like I’ve just been through film school and back in the length of these 78 minutes. That, before you know it, feels like half.

reviews.author: HKFanatic
reviews.text: The challenge is how to write about this film without using the word 'economical.' Too tough, this is only about 78 minutes long and each moment is gripping as we witness Randolph Scott's solemn quest to bring seven bank robbers to justice. Meanwhile, Lee Marvin, as is often the case, radiates a sense of danger that almost feels too raw, too feral for Fifties Hollywood. The framing of each shot tells a story of its own, with the frame of the wagon itself used to great effect, and the WarnerColor looks positively lush.

Loved this one, instant all timer.

reviews.text: I have to say, this is one of Gaspar Noe’s more fascinating works. This is a 17 minute short about a guy explaining how he got AIDS, what it is doing to him, and what he has been doing since he got AIDS. The reason I say this is fascinating is because this short is so Gaspar Noe while not being much like Gaspar Noe at all. It is truly astonishing how Noe manages to put his signature nihilism in literally everything he does. I say that as a complement for managing to be able to look at everything your own way and communicate that to the viewer. This short definitely goes into nihilism and Noe’s views of humanity, which…

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: We are creatures of climate. Not only the one we exist amidst, but that which warms and cools and rests and rages within. Some storms leave behind a kind of turmoil that is never forgotten, no matter how much gets rebuilt, and despite best efforts to move on, particles of a dark, typhonic past have a tendency to outlast our conscious regard thereof. In these storms most intemperate, wherein bright, effulgent fires rage like scorned gods on high, we pray for the ashes left behind to be carried up and oceanward by the zephyrs of time, but those most bemoaned by such events hold onto extinguished embers as evidence of their old, inclement selves. We may try and sometimes succeed in forgetting, but the sun and the sea, with their eternal recall, will always one day reclaim what they are owed.

reviews.author: Gregor Kreyca
reviews.text: A three hour long Japanese investigation-procedural crime/drama from the mid 1960’s isn’t exactly an easy undertaking. And indeed, Tomu Uchida’s A Fugitive from the Past proofed to be quite challenging at times. It tested my attention-span on more than one occasion, during its lengthy runtime. There’s no getting around it, it’s a long movie and it feels long. But it’s also wonderfully shot, acted and directed and manages to tell a gripping at times moving story about choices, consequences, guilt and redemption. It is talky, very talky at times but the analytical police procedural is very well done and the movie also manages to give the viewer inside into world of a post-war japan.

reviews.author: Abhishek
reviews.text: Seemingly reminiscent of both in a discrete way- having the thrilling, disquisitive police-procedural elements of Kurosawa's "High and Low" and those cynical and expressively critical choices akin to Ōshima's "Death By Hanging" at times, Uchida's film fitly purveys a comprehensive, allegorical tale of human condition bespeaking the socio-political specters of hurtful past and destined atonement. Accompanied by a haunting score and noir-infused narrative, keeping that subtle sense of gritty realism, this morally complex story shines in its depiction of societal vulnerability and desperation- all in all, an incisive manifestation of moral culpability and expiation reflecting both- post-war devastation and the collective passivity and feebleness issuing from it.

reviews.author: jeliben
reviews.text: A three hour crime epic from Japan that uses the police procedural format as a jumping-off point, but goes far beyond such narrow trappings to explore post-war privation and wide-ranging systemic rot. This shares some DNA with High and Low especially in its diptych structure, but it differs mainly by being wider in scope, its use of more experimental techniques like negative film stock during moments of violence (harrowing—one murder scene is among the saddest I’ve seen recently), and for plumbing deeper emotional depths. It is a tragedy all around, closer to a Dostoevskian adaptation of Tourneur’s Out of the Past. reviews.author: JamesLNeibaur
reviews.text: When Stan Laurel and Oliver Hardy left their longtime home at the Hal Roach studios and joined the prestigious 20th Century Fox, there were a lot of changes. First, the studio did not quite know what to do with Laurel and Hardy, they just knew the duo was popular enough to be profitable. Laurel and Hardy, veterans who dated back to the silent era, had not really augmented their style much, and were still performing in a manner that fit beautifully in the 1920s, and comfortably in the 1930s. But as we entered the 1940s, comedy became more brash and verbal (Bob Hope, Abbott and Costello). Laurel and Hardy didn’t quite fit that style.

reviews.author: Hallie 💃
reviews.text: This sure would be better if there were any English subtitles for it. Unfortunately I had to really struggle to take an auto-generated French transcript and run it through a translator but even then it wasn't enough. I had a skim through the almost-incomprehensible text and I get the jist of what Noé was doing. But even the idea of having to read subtitles for an audiovisual hypnotic short is hardly going to give the correct experience. It's a shame because something like this could be some good dumb fun, but unfortunately due to language barriers it's worse than inaccessible to me. The Lynch inspirations come across clearly though and I guess that's something I can at least pick up on, as well as there being a more comedic approach to his existential dialogue which appears in his serious work.

The novel television special style is made much more strange and sinister by these manipulative effects, the editing going into the same hypnotic register as the characters’ speech.

reviews.author: sarah
reviews.text: It’s hard to consider any A Star is Born film without drawing comparisons to the others, but the 1937 original (a loose remake in itself) sets up such a strong groundwork for this story—it’s unsurprising that we have four versions now, all with their own stars and contemporary twists. My favorite will always be George Cukor’s 1954 version, but this one, a Janet Gaynor and Fredric March vehicle, is incredibly special. There’s still terrible heartbreak, but the overall film is a lot more playful and condensed. Vicki Lester’s eventual successful career is not actually shown in great detail, and we only really see the aftermath of her tremendous success. Overall, this film didn’t impact me as much as the 1954 version, but I still had a great time watching it. (And now I'm really curious to see where the 2018 one will be placed in my ranking.)

reviews.text: Cukor in many ways is the key Hollywood Director: emerging from Pre-Code to star studded comedies to some noir to Serious Dramas to what is arguably the climatic high of his career, this larger than life color musical that celebrates the system of Hollywood while lamenting its darker sides at the same time (no Hollywood picture is a Hollywood picture without a paradox at the center). Despite being an “epic,” this is a pretty simple picture: one star rises, the other falls, and while only three hours long (I watched the version with the Ken Burns-esque still photo montages) it feels like you’ve lived years with these people. Cukor’s staging is seemingly simple—less expressively dynamic than the black and white…

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: Stunningly ahead of its time from the opening sequence, which was ostensibly shot on location at a real Hollywood gala (or it feels like it was, anyway), to its ending, which is more heart-breakingly ambiguous than anything else being churned out by the studios at this time. Most Hollywood films about the movie industry have a thick layer of artifice caked on them, but not this, which never for a moment feels anything less than real - and it's all the more terrifying for it ("I don't want to see your face!").

reviews.text: Very slight 67 minute movie with an intriguingly oddball premise that's just entertaining enough. A Supreme Court Justice (played by Frank Morgan) decides to go on a fishing vacation and ends up right smack in the middle of this small town race for mayor. There's a small tiny upstart mayoral candidate named Adams (his slogan is "A New Broom Sweeps the Town Clean") who's running against the well established incumbent mayor who will apparently try anything to hold onto his position. Adams ends up in a melee at one point and ends up being arrested and thrown in a jail cell and the mayor specifically orders the police to keep him in there for as long as they possible can…

reviews.author: hellohildy
reviews.text: A comedy I can rely on for gentle entertainment whenever needed - this charming little film features a terrific lead performance by Frank Morgan. As a incognito, vacationing Supreme Court justice, he gets drawn into small town politics and after lots of various fun set pieces and interactions with a variety of great supporting actors, he gets to make a very patriotic speech about holding leadership to account. He says that in allowing politicians to be corrupt and to run things for their benefit instead of the public, that public is failing in its duties as citizens, and intimates that allowing that kind of power makes fascism possible. This was 1943 after all.

Not saying who he is, they go to court and Grant grudgingly pays the fine. However, he sees there that there are several people involved in other petty crimes, emphasis on petty. One man affected is Bill Adams (Richard Carlson), who wants to run for mayor. Together, along with Grant's secretary Lucy (Jean Rogers), they work to fight corruption with their own brand…

The trick is that they don't know who they're dealing with. Taking an interest in a young lawyer and mayoral candidate's career just makes the court room and political arena more appealing than the river bank. reviews.author: Stephen M
reviews.text: A Japanese prison break movie that’s notable for several reasons. First, it provided a breakout role for Ken Takakura, who went on to be a big Japanese star. Second it was wildly popular with the public, leading to 17 (!) sequels between 1965 and 1972. Third, it’s seen as an early example of the yakuza genre. It draws a lot from Hollywood prison movies, including The Defiant Ones with two escaped prisoners handcuffed together. But it has a distinctly Japanese flavor. Not a great film by any stretch but it has its memorable moments.

reviews.author: Kaishakunin
reviews.text: 網走番外地 Abashiri Prison is not the kind of movie Teruo Ishii is known for. Nothing gory, no over the top sleaze, no unethical violence or sexual assault here; it’s a classical prison flick, reminiscent of The Defiant Ones and of Cool Hand Luke, with deep and interesting characters, shot in a classy b/w cinematography, and set in the gorgeously snowy Hokkaido landscape. The cast is quite impressive too; familiar faces of Japanese cinema Ken Takakura, Kunie Tanaka and Testsurō Tamba all deliver subtle and sweet performances. It’s a pretty good film, the first of a long series and the Eureka Blu-ray presentation is stunning, I can’t recommend it enough.

reviews.text: Neil Armstrong, a man better remembered for being first than he is for being funny, once said that his greatest regret was that “my work required an enormous amount of my time, and a lot of travel.” It’s a bittersweet line from a taciturn giant who always tended to find the right words; an admission of deep sadness coated inside the candied shell of a solid quip. But while no one expects an Armstrong quote to make them laugh, some people — especially filmmakers — only seem to hear the pain underneath the astronaut’s punchline.

reviews.text: After Death gets off to a decent start (in a crappy sort of way) but unfortunately the rest of the film doesn't live up to it. This was released as a second sequel to Lucio Fulci's classic zombie film but doesn't share much in common other than zombies and an island setting. To be fair, there's a handful of good ideas on display on here and the film obviously takes influence from Lamberto Bava's Demons and Lucio Fulci's The Beyond but the plot is never able to capitalise on these elements and instead spends most of the runtime procrastinating with dull characters. On the plus side, there's some decent gore effects and it is mostly entertaining for the duration. As Italian zombie films go: there are worse ones than this (and better ones)

reviews.author: SupremeLemon (지존레몬)
reviews.text: The captivating beauty of these images of sand lies in the construction of their granular representation through cogent articulations of elemental and primordial qualities, manifested in relation to the wind that moves them and the light that falls upon them. They emerge as specific conditions of visibility within which the image subsists only insofar as it relinquishes anecdote and assurance. It may, indeed, be nothing more than grains shifting, scattering, accumulating; the wind inscribes without writing; light grazes the surface of the emulsion as though searching for a foothold. If the desert has long been inscribed in myth as void, origin, and site of liberation--an extreme landscape where humanity confronts its own negation, where annihilation coexists with the promise of…

reviews.author: Gerry
reviews.text: One of the most stunning textural experiments I’ve ever seen, striking a perfect balance between cohesive structure and the impromptu feeling of something that was captured. It begins with inscrutable speckled images, where it’s impossible to tell what exactly you’re seeing between the sand in the wind and the grain from the 16mm photography, before moving into more visually digestible images of lines of sand carried across the desert floor, to macro images of individual particles, and to wider shots of the landscapes, before coming full circle into the beginning’s visual abstractions. A beautiful blend of control and chaos, exhibiting how light and filmic texture interact with the most elemental parts of the natural world, and one of the most perfect experimental films ever made.

reviews.text: It’s tempting to think of “An Elephant Sitting Still” as a suicide note written with blood in a dirty patch of hard snow. Hard to sit through and impossible to forget, this torpid four-hour anti-drama is suffused with the sort of hopelessness that cinema only sees every once in a long while (Werner Herzog’s “Stroszek” and Béla Tarr’s “The Turin Horse” come to mind), and the man who made it — a former student of Tarr’s — killed himself before the world premiere of his monolithic first (and last) feature. His name was Hu Bo, and he was 29 years old.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: The world is a wasteland. An Elephant Sitting Still is a major work of 2018, a treatise on the despair of living. This story of intersecting characters slowly tightens itself around four nihilistic lost souls. They talk of how anyone can waste their time on meaningless things, of how no one truly knows about existence, about how life is fundamentally about agony. There's a repeated idea that everyone is the same. All the leads blame others, thinking they are faultless and bad decisions belong to those who shaped the characters. They all accept a brutal honesty, both in universe and through the storytelling's uncompromising nature. This is a film about being useless to the world, of people who don't know what…

reviews.text: Watching An Elephant Sitting Still is like watching director Hu Bo tearing open his and his people's own wounds and showing them to the world in close-up. It's ugly and depressing, but you just can't move your eyes away for its almost four-hour runtime. There's not one single shot that doesn't ooze pain and nihilism, saves for the last scene, where a rare glimpse of hope comes at last.

reviews.text: One major event happened between the releases of Analyze This and Analyze That and it's 9/11. I'm working on a theory where a butterfly effect occurred on De Niro and Crystal, two iconic New Yorkers, where their acting careers took a nosedive in the aftermath of that day. Before 9/11, Bob and Bill were ironclad movie stars. After 9/11, De Niro did Showtime, Analyze That, Godsend, Shark Tale, Meet the Fockers and on and on he kept watering down his legacy. It's like there was a curse. Analyze That was so toxically bad that Billy Crystal essentially retired from acting. This is a rough draft theory that needs further analyzing, but I'm flabbergasted by the idea of it.

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: Angel Baby wants to be both a sleazy exploitation flick and a righteous movie about honest religious faith. It's an uneasy combination, made particularly so by the fact that about half the cast (Burt Reynolds, Joan Blondell at times, and Mercedes McCambridge) are acting in the former, while everyone else is sedately making the latter, particularly George Hamilton and Salome Jens (as preachers Paul Strand and Angel Baby), who appear to be making a nice romance about two good kids who super love God.

reviews.author: RanchoTuVu
reviews.text: Lurid southern evangelism and faith healing. It might be George Hamilton's best film. The entire cast does exceedingly well. Salome Jens as "Angel Baby", a faith healer, will reach out and touch your soul even today. Mercedes McCambridge exceeds in intensity and weirdness what she accomplished in "Johnny Guitar". When Salome Jens emerges on stage as Delilah as Hamilton is delivering a sermon on lust, it becomes one of the the greatest moments in cinematic history. Seriously. McCambridge's eyes practically leave her head when Salome brushes her skimpily dressed body against that of McCambridge's "husband" the young, handsome George Hamilton. Released by Allied Artists in 1961 the mix of sex and spiritual awakening was the template for Russ Meyers and others to expand on. It really is a masterpiece.

Although Gantry is a much more powerful film and anchored by the great performance of Burt Lancaster, "Angel Baby" is quite good on its own.

reviews.text: First hour is kind of rough, with lots of cliché characterization and ugly desaturated, handheld camera work (with no clear indication why it's been shot this way until the last like 30m), but this hugely picks up around the time it goes full The Blood on Satan's Claw supernatural cult horror an hour in and then for some ungodly reason caps the whole thing off with 30m of "what if Witchfinder General was a torture porn movie?" Unsure whether this is Actually Good or not but the bizarre whiplash of witnessing Evans' paranoid, untethered photography and penchant for bonkers gruesomeness infect a 70s British folk horror locale in that finale was enough to get my lizard brain going and forget all the times actors opened their mouths in this. Gotta be some value in that, right?

reviews.author: Thomas
reviews.text: Alexander Kluge´s Golden Lion winning sophomore feature film “Artists Under the Big Top: Perplexed” is even more abstract, experimental, meta, and challenging than his debut film “Yesterday Girl”. It´s a collage film the blends the fictional storyline about a young circus owner who dreams of a new kind of circus with archive footage, newsreels, and quotations from philosophers. The movie explores the conflict between idealism and commercialism as well as the systemic resistance to change and progress, which can be seen as a representation of Kluge´s own frustrations with the German film industry he tried to modernize. “Artists Under the Big Top: Perplexed” is inaccessible and kind of exhausting to watch but it´s also filled with unconventional filmmaking, intriguing symbolism, and striking images. Alexander Kluge deserves more recognition as an innovative pioneer of New German Cinema.

reviews.author: ZubinShy
reviews.text: A really admirable and epiphanic effort of filmmaking, especially montage. Documentary footage of Adolf Hitler at an art exhibition is underscored with a Spanish version of the Beatles’ “Yesterday”. Alexander Kluge is juxtaposing sounds and images in a way that was deemed unthinkable before. Using the same handheld semi-documentary cinema vérité style as his debut feature “Abschied von gestern”, switching between colour and black-and-white film, freely interspersing fictional scenes with documentary material, interviews, newspaper clippings, still images and intertitles. Kluge detaches the soundtrack from the visible images presented, and thus, what is heard is seldomly congruent with what is projected, and yet, they inevitably correlate.

I'm assuming here that I'm not dancing around spoiler territory given the film's title and poster. Uwe Boll doesn't soften anything in the script either by feigning a Robin Hood angle where the victims of the sub-prime mortgage and credit crises are aided. Nor do any wheels of change begin turning. No regulation, no championing of reform by politicians, no rays of hope for the little guy.

reviews.text: Anche qui, il buon Sergio Corbucci ci riprova con un nuovo “giallo napoletano” dopo “La Mazzetta” e gli viene anche meglio del primo. Lo snodo narrativo è un po’ più fluido ma ha qua e là dei buchi e talvolta è poco bilanciato l’aspetto giallo con la commedia (Renato Pozzetto, pur facendomi ridere, mi sembra troppo fuori parte visti i toni). Per il resto il film lo ricordi soltanto per i bravissimi caratteristi napoletani, un bravo Mastroianni (che mi ha ricordato tanto Chaplin) e, per l’ultima volta sulle scene, il meraviglioso Peppino De Filippo (che se anche acciaccato e invecchiato, ha dei tempi comici fenomenali). Per il resto il film va ad intermittenza, a volte funziona e a volte no … peccato, se fosse stato più centrato sarebbe stato un ottimo giallo!

Das reicht aber nur so gerade, um die Spielschulden seines Vaters zu begleichen. Bei seinem nächsten Gig, einem Ständchen vor einem Haus, passiert ein Mord. Anstatt dass er sich endlich aus der WG und Sippenhaft mit seinem Vater befreit, versucht er diesen und weitere Morde aufzuklären.Ausgerechnet der Spezialist für Brutales und Komödien legt hier einen reichlich lahmen Giallo vor, dessen Sprachwitz hinkt wie einige der Beteiligten. Diesen Gaul hätten auch Danneberg, Hess und Co. nicht reanimieren können.

Mastroianni est en mode idiot nerveux (un peu à la Jack Lemmon) pis Ornella Muti est Ornella Muti pas mal dedans. C’est un peu épais et le pacing est très flasque mais c’est aussi pas mal le fun; y’a une scène de char qui se termine avec un gars qui fait caca dans son pantalon ET une scène où Marcello fait de la coke en s’en beurrant plein dans la face, donc pas dans les Mastroianni les plus classy, mettons. Bonus: la musique est une bouillabaisse incompréhensible de Riz Ortolani qui rote dans un vocoder.

reviews.author: PacificNil
reviews.text: "Leichen muss man feiern, wie sie fallen" sollte wohl das einleiten, was Anfang der Siebziger erfolgreich mit dem Italowestern geschah: Eine Transformation ins Komödiengenre. Sergio Corbucci, der zuvor zahlreiche ernsthafte Italowestern drehte, drehte in den Siebzigern zwar bereits Komödien, jedoch nur wenige und vor allem wenig wegweisende Westernkomödien - "Stetson" (1975) ist darüber hinaus ziemlich nervig. Sein Ausflug ins Giallogenre in heiterer Form besitzt herausragende Zutaten, insbesondere die Schauspieler sind erste Liga, darüber hinaus sind sie auch passend besetzt, z. B. Natala Tulli als Mafiaschläger. Dazu gibt es einen intelligenten Umgang mit Vorbildern, insbesondere Argento, und einige überzeugende Setpieces. Den Genuss trübt, dass der Film auch die wirre Dramaturgie vieler Gialli auf die Spitze treibt; bei knapp 2 Stunden Laufzeit wäre etwas mehr Spannung und fokussierte Erzählweise angenehmer gewesen. Der Film spielt übrigens in der Weihnachtszeit und sollte der Stimmung, die er verbreitet, auch in dieser Zeit gesehen werden.

reviews.author: Josiah Morgan
reviews.text: One of the best and most complex opening shots I've ever seen gives way to an immensely complex film rooted in subversion of classicist tradition. Almost everything we see is mirrored or interrupted by horizontal lines - Blier's people are framed between doorways and through windows and in images cruelly oriented to destruct our established visual points of reference. The machinations of his camera are always transparent, revealing awareness of not only space but intimate understanding of the characters - and narratively this film is lovely, with no metaphor - simply finding people in relation to their quarters, their surroundings, the empty streets and inconsistent reds.

reviews.author: DavidS60
reviews.text: In Being Canadian, Robert Cohen sets off on an epic road trip from Nova Scotia to British Columbia in search of what it means to be a Canadian. The documentary confirms that Canadians are polite, apologetic, resistant to but also strangely accepting of periodically frigid temperatures, and like to look down their collective nose at Americans while simultaneously feeling a bit overshadowed and insecure about the neighbours to the south, especially in light of the events of the past year. As a Canadian, it was nice to see the beautiful landscapes and enjoy some of the self-deprecating humor, but the movie felt a bit aimless and much of it felt heavily contrived. While those who are unfamiliar with Canadian culture may learn a thing or two, Canadians themselves will simply shrug at the end and think ‘yeah, that aboot sums it up, eh?'

Yes, it’s THAT similar. Inanimate objects flying across rooms. A child taken by a hidden force and trapped in another dimension within the house. An unorthodox “believer” that assists in retrieving that child. Hell, the little girl falls just short of being Carol Ann (it’s just Carol).

reviews.author: WraithApe
reviews.text: Beyond Darkness, part 5 of the incredibly confusing La Casa series. If my understanding is correct, The Evil Dead and TED II were released in Italy as La Casa and La Casa 2 respectively, then La Casas 3-7 were made as sequels, even though they have nothing to do with Raimi's films. La Casa 6 is also known as House II and La Casa 7 House III, but none of their predecessors are related to the original House as far as I can tell. A clusterfuck of releasing that only the Italians can understand - my mind's gone already. Not having seen any of the previous installments in the La Casa series, I don't know how much continuity there is…

This film is apparently the fifth entry in the La Casa series. We begin with an execution of a witch and then follow the priest and his family as they move into a new home which is haunted by the witch...or something. The pacing is really all over the place. It switches tone and focus often, which is really quite jarring and means that it's difficult to ever get a real handle on the story; so it often drags. The score is completely over…

Santiago, BEYOND THE CALL OF DUTY is set during the waning days of the Vietnam War. While it delivers Concorde’s requisite amounts of action and violence in depicting the inhumanity of war, it also occasionally tries to show a serious side. Haphazardly pieced together using unrelated footage from other Corman productions — you may notice actor Todd Field, for instance, from EYE OF THE EAGLE 2 — BEYOND THE CALL OF DUTY takes its time getting to its story, which doesn’t begin to emerge until almost 20 minutes into the picture.

But the biggest sin of Big Top Pee-Wee is that it doesn't seem to understand the character of Pee-Wee Herman. By giving him a story that involves (oddly) infidelity, you've made a man out of a man-child. A strong take in similarity to the famous build of French New Wave stylings, the theming constantly takes in a natural application of Cinéma vérité (even though this direct film dives into a lot of fantasied imagination directly) but also with a thematic blend of the youth challenging that of the status quo. Within British New Wave especially, there is the embodiment of the "Angry Young Men" movement of ideation, speaking to subcategory of youth at the time that was…

reviews.author: Rizki
reviews.text: Billy Liar belongs to the British New Wave that established the “angry young man” as the figurehead of a new cinematic movement rooted in working-class reality. Actors such as Albert Finney, Tom Courtenay, and Laurence Harvey embodied rebellious figures from a lost generation — too young for the war, too old for the baby-boom revolution — rejecting the dictates of the old guard and raising their own voices amid a world of conventions built around marriage, steady jobs, and children, with the pub as the only possible escape.

reviews.author: Will Steele
reviews.text: If ever there was a film to epitomise me, it would be this. Written decades ago and only witnessed near 60 years after its release, Billy feels as close to me as I’ve ever seen on screen. For me, Billy Liar resonates like some endless echo exclaimed down the cavernous walls of time. Billy is a dreamer, incapable of action, bound by place and people yet unbound in vivid, immaterial imagination. In essence, he is the fallible man. William Fisher is a man undone by ambition. Life is wide and full of random opportunity, yet seizing them can seem all too illusive. I strive not to be bound by my inhibitions, yet time and time again I am. The train departs taking with it prospect, but often it is our destiny to fold. I am Billy and there is some beauty in that, I think.

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Billy Liar is a light-hearted look at the life of a young man struggling to make his dreams a reality. Based on the 1959 Keith Waterhouse novel and directed by John Schlesinger, it stars Tom Courtenay - who had previously understudied for Albert Finney in the West End theatre adaptation - as Billy and Julie Christie as Liz, one of his three girlfriends. The film follows the story of Billy Fisher, a young man living in the fictional town of Stradhoughton in Yorkshire, who dreams of escaping his mundane life and becoming a successful writer. However, he is unable to make a decision on which of his three girlfriends he should marry, and his indecision leads to a series of…

reviews.author: Hutch
reviews.text: Fantasy brought to its knees by a lack of courage. I know that feeling all too well. This is a terrific film anchored by the great Tom Courtenay as Billy Fisher. He’s a young man who avoids the monotony of his Yorkshire working class life by inventing an imaginary world and spending large chunks of his days in it. The rest of the time he spends unsuccessfully spinning plates, balancing three girlfriends, a move to London, a history of petty fraud and a grim home life. His fantasies keep him afloat - his realities sink him.

reviews.text: Black and Blue represents what is easily director Deon Taylor's best work as a filmmaker to date, crafting a surprisingly competent, even often enjoyable, cop thriller with strong performances (especially from Naomie Harris, Tyrese Gibson, and Frank Grillo) and well-put together action sequences. That being said, it's rather disappointing that this is only competent when it could've been so much more given the subject matter; I think Taylor and writer Peter A. Dowling would've been better off had this just been a straightforward action film because their attempts at social commentary, while certainly timely and deeply admirable, are handled too clumsily and simplistically to make a real impact. As far as films like this go, you can certainly do worse.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Teruo Ishhi directing a hardboiled B thriller with a wonderful seedy atmosphere. A journalist investigating a prostitution ring wakes up next to a strangled dead woman and off he goes to a consppiracy laced high constrast B&W travelogue through a high detailed underworld. Ishii is great at nasty small bits of action and keeping the menace high. It s both packed with incident and very economical. Life feels so cheap even romantic gestures come out as minimal and desperate. Ishii's action is brutal, stylized and often includes one or two extra good touches to enrich it. I'm sure if a company like Arrow put this out in one of those "Japanese B crime" boxd set its cult reputation would build fast.

reviews.author: nagoya
reviews.text: Nice adventure, a blend of noir and pop cinema, populated by girls, pimps, transvestites and criminals. Teruo Ishii's brilliant direction keeps the narration at brisk pace and the big band soundtrack underlines with great excitement the most important scenes. The only micro-flaw I noticed is a certain naïveté of the tone not very well suited to the underworld in which the film is set, but probably this has to do more with the fact that I am watching the film near 60 years after it was made than with the real intentions of the filmakers. Recommended a watch in the dark to enjoy the b&w cinematography at its best. P.S. Thanks to Mike for recommending this peculiar piece of cool entertainment some months ago.

Shigeru Amachi is outstanding as in other films. The entire series (haven't found "Shirosen himitsu chitai" yet) is based on both of these actors' skill & presence which didn't bother them the slightest. reviews.text: This film does not feel like it should be this underwatched. It feels like it should be spoken of in the same breath as your favorite noir films. The main difference between it and classic Hollywood noir is that it doesn't flinch from showing all the dirty bits--drug use, nudity, and violence are all prominently featured. While not outright pornographic or transgressive, it's still a surprising level of risque for 1960.

reviews.text: I've mentioned it in other reviews, but I think it's essential for me to reiterate that Teruo Ishii laid the foundation from which the popular Pinky Violence films would later build off. Blind Woman's Curse stands out as his most influential work in that regard. It's a measured piece of filmmaking from the king of cult cinema and continues his streak of phenomenal opening and final acts. If you're a fan of the Female Prisoner Scorpion series, or even Lady Snowblood, you should prioritize checking this out. Meiko Kaji is as good as ever, and Hoki Tokuda leaves quite the impression too. It simply doesn't get too much better than watching two badass women demolish a bunch of sleazy men, all while learning to respect each other and settle their differences along the way.

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: As George Romero first discovered — and hordes of other filmmakers have since refined — zombies are a fun and effective vehicle for addressing the most intractable anxieties of the modern world; even bone-deep social ills have a funny way of seeming more digestible when explored through a story about people rabidly eating each other’s entrails. A scattershot but clear-eyed bit of midnight madness that renders colonialism as a literal plague, Jeff Barnaby’s “Blood Quantum” may bite off more human flesh than it can chew, but this hopeful modern howl against the indignities suffered by Canada’s indigenous population (the Mi’gMaq in particular) is still a credit to its genre. It may not be a great zombie movie, but it’s a uniquely powerful reminder of why zombie movies are great.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: The questions that arise when engaging in genre cinema are about which rules to follow and which rules to break. Which subgenres, which homages, which responses, which new grounds to explore? Entering into genre cinema with the intention of asserting a political identity, a cultural identity, a national identity, adds further questions - what will be said if I break this rule? What does it mean for the political or cultural content if I reference this other film? What are the implications of combining these?

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Written, directed and edited by Jeff Barnaby, Blood Quantum is filled with body fluids, intestines and advantageous expressions on colonialism. It's a well-made zombie horror which, despite an irritating inclination to deliver too much expository dialogue, features some kinetically staged set-pieces. The zombie genre has repeatedly carried varying degrees of social criticisms, and the transcendental portrayal here of a too-often distorted image of native Americans is particularly pleasing.

reviews.text: Can't help but feel kneecapped a little bit by how obviously it's not just homaging Raimi's (and Jackson’s) manic splatter comedy sensibility but straight-up plagiarizing it to less effective ends. The shaky claustrophobic POV camerawork, the dismemberment aftermath twitching gag, the big push-in and "groovy!" into the lens... There is however a lot of residual passionate amateur charm to the fact that Evil Dead inspired someone to go out and make a no-budget, one-man crew knockoff with even fewer resources than him. This dude is credited as director, writer, cinematographer, editor, make-up artist, dual-role star, etc...

It's pretty one note, but what we do get is an enjoyable tribute to Sam Raimi's film - certain aspects are lifted wholesale, including camera angles, set pieces and…

reviews.author: RensDad666
reviews.text: Talk about a labor of fked up, effects driven, Evil Dead coded, splatter comedy love. Bloody Muscle Body Builder in Hell, quite unashamedly marketed as “The Japanese Evil Dead”, is a film that wouldn’t exist if not for the gigantic ambition and massively committed heart of Shinichi Fukuzawa. Taking decades to film with the little time and resources he could find, BMBBIH embodies the same raw visual spirit of Sam Raimi’s DIY splatter-punk masterpiece, and manages to do so with even less commercial movie-making means. But, I’d be lying if I said it didn’t match the amount of heart and soul pouring out of its production.

reviews.text: Argentinian film about a man pushing sixty still trying to make himself useful in his family and society. In return for a good deed, he is given a fighting dog, and from here the film becomes what it is - a buddy/road movie, but of a kind you've never seen. Strangely, you get great performances from the old man AND the dog. I’ve never seen a dog act so well in a movie before … if he was even acting, I don’t know what to call it (let’s just say he was much more believable than the title character in the Scooby Doo movie). What I liked is that the film never took a single clichéd route. A very pleasant watch.

However, the inheritance comes with some stipulations. He (she) is given a large sum of money, which must be spent within a certain period of time, and the heir must be completely broke again when the deadline arrives. However, the film could have benefited from more precise rules for Brewster's spending spree. reviews.author: Chance H.
reviews.text: First things first, Brimstone is batshit crazy. I mean, seriously - there is no possible way to anticipate the events that unfold just by reading the vague synopsis. I really haven't experienced a story this dark and disturbing in a while, but fortunately for me, it's my kind of crazy. Guy Pearce gives one of the most sinister performances in recent memory and Dakota Fanning excels in using her striking features, eyes in particular, to maximum effect. Told non-chronologically in four chapters (titled Revelation, Exodus, Genesis, and Retribution), Brimstone is a deviant film with deviant characters that spits on the typical three-act structure and is sure to polarize anyone willing to give it a go. Thankfully, I ended up on the side that really enjoyed it. So far, Brimstone is one of my favorite films of 2017. Highly recommended - especially if you're in the mood for something visually stunning, thematically distasteful, and refreshingly different!

reviews.author: VippleStein
reviews.text: Most of the reviews I'm reading about this surreal comedy seem to interpret the blasé reactions and strange motivations of the characters as satire on modern (c. 1980) dehumanization and alienation. There is even a short speech from one of them about the concrete city being dehumanizing and having no soul. (In which case that's a bit on the nose.) And maybe it was intended that way, but I think possibly Blier was shooting for something larger here, more metaphysical, more nihilistic. All of the Blier films I've seen (this one, Going Places, & Menage) could be labelled as "anti-social comedies", but I'm not sure this one is actually "social" at all.

reviews.text: Constantin Film was a German distributor and production company. Bullets Don't Argue was made right alongside A Fistful of Dollars as one of their first efforts, and the two films share some of the same crew, including one Ennio Morricone composing the score. reviews.text: Fairly uninteresting spaghetti western -- although with some appropriately cartoonish sequences -- made before the genre was doing all that much. Fun moment in this where, surrounded by desert sand, Rod Cameron is blowing cigar smoke up his prisoner Ángel Aranda's blanket to try and scare away a rattle snake that's somewhere up his body. It's a little (or a lot) gay and the film does gather steam from there. Horst Frank's melodramatic death scene is fun too, as is the ghost town and the scorpions in the dried up well, and a goofy mine cart play. Mimmo Palmara's bare chest and pantomime laugh before he realises he's been stabbed is one for the ages.

reviews.text: Rundskop revolves around Jacky, a dodgy, hypermasculine farmer who takes part in illegal trading of hormones, and the murder of a police officer which, in a way, is connected to Jacky's business. But what this movie should've been is a full-on character study. The aforementioned 'murder' subplot, with its narratively unappealing character dynamics, regular disentanglements from the main plot (which create new minor plotlines without closure) and the writer's favourite 'coincidences' (with which he tries to depict 'fate' but actually highlights 'lazy writing'), drags the whole movie and prevents the viewer from observing what s/he really wants to - Matthias Schoenaerts's Jacky. Totally unrecognisable, the Belgian actor delivers a jaw-dropping, intensely physical performance which, for the first time in a…

reviews.text: I was unaware that there was a hormone mafia underworld, but I suppose that if there's a world for anything, that someone will find an "UNDER" world for it too. This is a pretty interesting film that shows the physical and mental drain that comes with being an enforcer in organized crime. Some good acting especially from Matthias Schoenaerts. There's a bunch of brutal violence and the trauma that Jacky suffers as a child is heart wrenching. It's not a movie I will recommend for the faint of heart, but it's a powerful and horrifying drama.

So the whole crime aspect doesn't translate well unless you're familiar with Flanders and Wallonia... something about switching out tires to cover up a murder. A bit distracting but that’s ok - it’s just the device that drives the real story, which is something else entirely. Tragic and dark, literally, using the Se7en color palette. Proved to the world that Matthias Schoenaerts can act (like a bull, in this case)

reviews.text: If you've seen The Iron Giant, The Water Horse, How to Train Your Dragon, ET: The Extraterrestrial, or any other variation on the "kid befriends beast" premise, you've seen this movie pretty much beat-for-beat. But yet, Bumblebee works. And bizarrely, the movie doesn't work *despite* its familiarity and cliches and simple plot-structure; it works *because* of it. The only word you can use to describe a film like this is "charming", because that's what it is. Hailee Steinfeld is charming, Bumblebee is charming, the 80s are charming, and the humor is charming. It's just a pleasant, heartfelt, sweet movie, even if it's not revolutionary. Not everything has to be. Nuff said.

Structured in two mostly mirrored parts (a docufiction edit played against a short fiction version of the same series of events - in this respect the experience reminded me of Trent Harris's THE BEAVER TRILOGY) Campos uses this conceit to confront ideas around the sculpting of identity, voyeurism, peer moulding of sexuality, whether relationships (physical or online) can truly be considered merely transactional and much more. But the content is as discomforting to watch as anything he's made since,…

reviews.author: Drew Edelstein
reviews.text: Learning about early cinema is truly a blessing and a curse. For instance, I knew nothing of the Italian Superspectacles, excessively budgeted and exuberantly crafted works of cinema that pushed the medium forwards by challenging the conventional methods of production; these movies were bonafide prestige pictures, and could only be seen in "real theaters," as the dumpy commodities that nickelodeons tended to be were incompatible with the heightened ticket price films this expensive to produce demanded. Audiences were eating up this wave of spectacle, however, and the industry began a ground-up rebranding of cinema as a serious art, instead of a disposable form of entertainment for the masses. Between this and the prior year's Quo Vadis?, films sporting reel counts…

reviews.author: Will Sloan
reviews.text: The original Caged Heat (1974) was the directorial debut of Jonathan Demme, but this in-name-only sequel sees the director's chair filled by an equally esteemed craftsman, Cirio H. Santiago (Vampire Hookers). The Filipino auteur was no doubt working through the national trauma of the Marcos regime as he handled this story of a dictator's daughter and mistress (two separate people, to be clear) finding themselves in a brutal island prison after a CIA-backed assassination hoax. Santiago goes through all the women-in-prison paces: lashings, mudfights, forced stripteases, the works. While the daughter believes in fighting for her country, only the American capitalist mistress understands that everything is transactional. In the latter role, Jewel Shepard gives a hammy bad-girl performance, which must have been her way of carving out a little fun and staying sane during the ordeal.

Santiago threw together this nominal sequel to Jonathan Demme's debut feature, one of the more enduring WiP movies, long after he'd become a successful mainstream filmmaker. But aside from the setting it doesn't have much to do with the original at all. Instead it's mostly a fairly standard WiP movie, delivering most of the expected ingredients, though is more on the tamer side for these types of films. There is a bit of political intrigue as well but it's hardly a priority. I was quite surprised that this was just on YouTube but the weathered VHS rip I saw actually gave it a certain charm in making the film look more like a classic era exploitation movie than a product of the 90s.

reviews.author: Rafael "Mister Movie" Jovine
reviews.text: A film that seems almost forgotten even though its legacy persists to this day. Although it is likely that films of this nature, with multiple characters and plotlines that converge in one place, have been done before none were exploited as much by this point. Films like Friday and Barbershop, to name just a few, clearly share its inspiration. It would be remiss of me not to talk about the super hit song, "Car Wash", which spun off from this movie and still in many ways remains a classic. The most bizarre thing, however, is the fact that Schumacher (yes Joel Schumacher) was the screenwriter of this movie.

reviews.author: chavel
reviews.text: Carnal Knowledge might have been the first film to really deal with sex addiction, and the first film to use the word c*u*n*t* in cinema. It also contains one of Jack Nicholson’s three best performances (I’m sure you’ve seen “Cuckoo’s Nest” and “Chinatown” by now). Nicholson ages twenty years in the movie, from his college years to middle age, the whole time keeping female conquests on something of a scorecard. The mid-section deals with what is likely the longest lasting relationship of his adult life (Ann-Margret is the sex kitten who yearns to be treated as something more). One shouting match exchange suggests Nicholson’s immaturity level as he eschews tenderness to instead bully, and his final scene suggests a pathetic attempt to go from limp to aroused. An important film, I think the best one from Mike Nichols (“The Graduate”) who directed from playwright/cartoonist Jules Feiffer’s script. Art Garfunkel, clumsy with women, is the best friend.

reviews.author: Edgar Cochran ✝️🍋
reviews.text: Noé's entry into the face of cinema is more of an exercise in style to work in his aggressive delivery of his ideas rather than a purely experimental film, like it has been labeled to. Maybe those segments which make the film seem "incoherent" or "experimental" as a whole refer mainly to the cinematic influences, like the opening sequence nodding at Franju's Blood of the Beasts (1949) and Blood Feast (1963) by Gordon Lewis. Despite its style over substance, the style correlates with the film's bleak and pessimistic statements about the selfishness of the world, with certain technical stunts possibly suggesting that the film is actually a mockery at certain segments of modern society, and a dark comedy.

The humor sprinkled screenplay carries raw heartfelt emotions as well that strike the right chord. Pleasant visuals and soulful music enhance its wanderlust charm. reviews.text: Welles is perhaps the greatest amateur in cinema, having never learned to "properly" direct because of the artistic success of Citizen Kane. His camera placements are always off in some way: actors are pushed too close in, the angle much too slanted, the sight lines mismatched. Characters jump off screen and then back into place without reason, and spatial relations are constantly shifting with motivation. Actors deliver Shakespearean dialogue much too pointedly, as if they were still on the stage any no sense for the camera. There's too much love paid to the bombastic sets and some of the cuts take away from poignant moments in which the camera should simply rest. Shots are either filled with too much information…

The film's TMDb summary ("...As Noel begins to spiral downwards, alienating co-workers and customers in the process, it turns out this same community of people may be the only ones capable of saving Noel from self-destruction.") certainly doesn't help matters. It proves illustrative, though, given that it's in direct opposition to Poekel's minimalist approach, which privileges small, glancing detail over underlined emotional beats. The emotional weight remains resolutely in the margins, which only makes the rare moments of unguarded emotion (e.g. Noel walking home after the first delivery) more potent. What elevates the film is how resolutely it clings to Noel's (Audley)…

reviews.author: Lucinda
reviews.text: Christmas, Again. Even the title makes me feel sad. But there's more emotional truth in this film than a hundred other feel-good Christmas movies. The ultra-specificity of the setting and characters here (writer-director Charles Poekel worked as a Christmas-tree seller himself for several years and based this screenplay on his own experiences) bring the story to life in a way that’s completely captivating. Kentucker Audley's understated performance feels heartbreakingly real, and everything's lit by blinking jewel-coloured fairy lights. I cried (and now I'm crying again). Could be my new favourite melancholy Christmas movie.

reviews.author: Kurdt
reviews.text: Michael Haneke, the king of coldness, strikes again. His films are so often an intensely uncomfortable experience despite the fact that he usually keeps his audience distant from central characters. Code Unknown is no different, except this time the viewers themselves are practically a character entrenched in the film itself. Despite being an opaque film that’s hard to decipher, Haneke seems to be speaking directly to the audience more than ever. He did this with Funny Games and its commentary on movie violence, but here moral issues are addressed. There’s many scenes with conflict, and Haneke seems to be simply asking his viewer “how would you react?”

reviews.author: Ben Reiss
reviews.text: In the late 90’s early 2000s these types of “hyperlink movies” were everywhere. The young Americans were making Magnolia, Pulp Fiction, and Traffic. Crash (not the good one) won an academy award. In Mexico Iñárritu made Amores Perros, then 21 Grams, and then Babel, each time iterating on themes of connectivity. In 2013 the Wachowski sisters put a stamp on the trend with their woefully under appreciated Cloud Atlas. The trend provided an opportunity for ambitious filmmakers to tell huge stories about a world that thanks to the internet is now being connected in ways that it never was before. Somewhere in there Michael Haneke managed to sneak in his own rendition on the trend.

reviews.text: "Coma" is a 1978 thriller directed by Michael Crichton. Although the film has some science fiction tonal build to it, a natural companioned style to anything Crichton, it also holds a reality-based grasp to it as well, something that Crichton does amazingly well in the execution of balance. There is something to be said about how amazingly Crichton is with an auteur-based build that distinctly focuses on the technicality of things. For example, this, a thriller circumnavigating direct surgical procedures and medical practices almost at times seems to have the performance and dialogue building of seeing the actual thing. To the untrained eye (as obviously I am no surgeon who can tell direct specifics), much of the films specifics has…

reviews.author: anna nomaly
reviews.text: Both a medical drama and a slow-burn paranoia thriller in the classic ‘70s tradition, Coma succeeds due to how earnestly Crichton tackles the material. It would be easy to make this subject overly dry or ludicrously silly, but he avoids both pitfalls by centering real-world social stakes and giving viewers a strong emotional entry point via the central romantic relationship. Douglas’ casting shows great skill; although he’d been in few movies at this time, his preternaturally untrustworthy presence effortlessly ratchets up the tension.

reviews.text: Michael Crichton’s 1978 thriller was a lean, mean, truly unsettling affair about a medical student who uncovers a plot to render patients into comas so that their bodies can be harvested. Here, the premise is unnecessarily bloated in its running time as Lauren Ambrose starts investigating why patients are not waking up from routine operations. The big name cast proves distracting as most of them have nothing to do (Geena Davis’ character for example serves little to no purpose) while Ellen Burstyn’s turn as a gatekeeper at a mysterious medical facility is strictly out of pantomime. Do not resuscitate.

reviews.author: hellohildy
reviews.text: Not a bad B pic from 1939. This is RKO’s slightly chickenshit swing at the Nazis, who they never overtly reference. At this time the US isn’t in the war, and the government isn’t anxious to throw the underprepared US military into the fray. Hollywood, as well as a portion of the population, were growing concerned by all they were reading in the papers, seeing in the newsreels and hearing on the radio. The first major film to deal with the Nazis was Warner Brothers’ “Confessions of a Nazi Spy” in 1939. MGM produced “The Mortal Storm” and Samuel Goldwyn produced “Foreign Correspondent” in 1940. “Conspiracy” can’t stand to that kind of competition, but as a B thriller is was fun.

reviews.text: Val Kilmer is surprisingly watchable as a war vet and PTSD sufferer in this southern border town actioner in the vein of First Blood or the Walking Tall remake, only made with a fraction of the budget and craft. It’s firmly in the former Bruce Wayne’s late-aughts paycheck phase, a junky Friday-night DTV pick from Movie Gallery. With limited resources for elaborate set pieces, Jason Goes to Hell director Adam Marcus channels his baser horror instincts in the schlocky final act, letting a rage-fueled Kilmer loose in a run of stealthy, savage revenge encounters that feel as much Jason Voorhees as John Rambo: throwing knives, stakes, shears, bullets, and even some nail gun action.

reviews.author: Matt Winfield 🇨🇦
reviews.text: Man, seeing Jack Nicholson blubbering to the point of tears when he talks about how much Roger Corman meant to his early career, such a heartwarming and raw moment. And that's pretty much what this doc is all about. A stream of talking heads from the “Corman Film School” – a who's who of now big names in Hollywood giving appreciation to the career, the opportunities, and the lasting impact Roger had on the history on cinema.

reviews.author: Dennis Vehlen
reviews.text: Felt like this was due for another rewatch in paying tribute to Roger Corman's incredible legacy. Still one of my favourite film maker documentaries and one that I think is a great introduction to Corman and a wonderful appreciation of his work and impact with so many of his former students and collaborators singing his praises. Larry Karaszewski posted the other day that "Modern American cinema starts with Roger Corman" and you can't add much to that. I definitely shed a few tears watching this again (plus Jack Nicholson being unusually emotional when talking about the way he owes everything to Roger always gets to me).

reviews.author: Kenneth Clark
reviews.text: Sydney Finkelstein wrote an incredible book, Superbosses, which argues there exists an upper echelon of leaders who are exceptionally skilled at identifying, developing, and launching others. These leaders create a kind of “talent incubator” around themselves, and many of their peers, employees, or protégés go on to become leaders and innovators in their own right. And in some instances even outshine the “superboss” who gave them the tools. It’s an incredible book that will truly change the way you interact with people both professionally and socially and invite them to have symbiotic relationships when it comes to success.

reviews.author: Gregor Kreyca
reviews.text: Here’s the fucking thing, I love this man! I don’t think there is any other single person who has done more for the (American) independent film then Roger Corman. From the movies he directed, produced, distributed to the immense and versatile talent a discovered and fostered before and behind the camera. Roger Corman’s mark on Cinema in general is undeniable and forever lasting. I can’t even imagine what the 60’s, 70’s and 80’s would have been without him. He has given me many of the best and treasured movie-moment of my childhood and live in general. And to this day I am (re)discovering his work. And my appreciation and admiration for his craft, work ethic and artistic achievements is ever-growing.…

reviews.author: noir1946
reviews.text: This is one of the best documentaries I’ve seen about a filmmaker in terms of providing a clear and entertaining view of him as a person and an artist, though describing Roger Corman, the master of the low-budget film, as an artist might be stretching a point. Through film clips and interviews with the actors with whom he has worked, directors who got their starts with Corman, and directors whose work has been influenced by him, Alex Stapleton’s film gives us insight into a pioneering filmmaker and an innovative period in American film.

It received much less fanfare than his other famous stories titled A Christmas Carol and A Tale of Two Cities. Dickens died in 1870. Disney copied his cricket character and story while putting his own twist and name on the product and got his own copyright exactly 1 year after the copyright of Dickens' original Cricket Crocket elapsed which was good for 70 years…

reviews.text: At one point during the film, the supposedly happy family man and bumbling private eye, Bobby Grady, is slouched in the driver's seat of his car while on a stakeout. In his hands, he is holding a John Fowles' book, "The French Lieutenant's Woman". In this post-modern novel, the narrator interrupts the story to present to the protagonist three possible endings: stay faithful to his wife and live unhappily ever after; have an affair with all the disruptions that ensue but ultimately wind up happy; or have an affair and everything just goes to shit.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Kathleen Turner seems to have a lot of fun with this ridiculous role. Ken Russell's films are always envelope-pushing in terms of taste, and they often leave their themes out in the open. This one is no different, as it explores with bluntness sexual repression and liberation. The big idea seems to boil down to the fact that the former is bad and the latter is good, but there's a little room for nuance here as Bobby's wife is depicted as, at least, human. Indeed, there's a hint here that some middle ground is needed, but that gets short shrift as a false priest is stabbed with a metal dildo.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: Zhang Yimou is a master of colour. His films are bright and vibrant, utilising many shades to produce endless sequences of beautiful, if shallow, imagery. Zhang Yimou is also a master of scale, able to use an enormous number of extras to provide epic action and expansive storytelling. When there's a core purpose to his works, these skills allow Zhang Yimou to make a masterpiece like Hero. When he's compromised by pandering to the mainstream, he ends up with mediocre fare like The Great Wall. Yet perhaps the most intriguing films by Zhang Yimou are the ones caught in the middle such as House of Flying Daggers and Curse of the Golden Flower, films which are safe in their storytelling…

reviews.text: "Curucu, Beast of the Amazon" is a 1956 jungle creature film directed by Curt Sidomark. It resides heavily within the B-movie monster movie narrative, essentially being a film assembled of loose narrative and stock footage to satisfy creature double features. It's connectively bad in design but doesn't really make any apologies for doing so as you should've known that walking into things. For that reason, the film should be enjoyed in a marathon formation, or with company, as it's the same kind of bare bones effort that we strangely would embrace from a Ted V. Mikels film 10-15 years later but obviously mixed with that atomic age creature flair.

reviews.author: Nick FW
reviews.text: The film that'll likely come to mind initially when watching Curucu is Creature from the Black Lagoon. While that one deservedly remains the iconic classic of the two, this one has a number of things it excels at in comparison. The exotic Brazilian locations add a tidal wave of authenticity to the proceedings, and the vibrant color photography (a rarity during the 1950s monster movie boom) captures them in all their beauty. I found the two leads/love interests pretty fun to watch, too, in that they're both stubborn and arrogant jerks; nice that they found each other. And there's also a fairly good twist leading into the last act I didn't see coming, but makes all the sense in the world.

reviews.author: anna nomaly
reviews.text: The pancake poster is awful and irrelevant, almost certainly a reason why this film was never taken more seriously. As family dramedies go, it’s pretty terrific, wearing its melancholy heart on its sleeve to great emotional effect and generating major laughs from true-to-life, refreshingly wholesome comic observations. Hedges’ screenplay wheels through setups and payoffs like nobody’s business, and it’s disarmingly frank about how much Dan’s grieving process has negatively affected nearly every other aspect of his life. Honesty is paramount. Even when the short-lived saga of Ruthie Draper threatens to become too mean, it’s illustrating truth: otherwise loving families can turn callous and shitty at the drop of a hat, and toxic masculinity can rear its ugly head just as easily. Carell and Binoche are lovely here. It’s tough to think of a less likely screen pairing, but their fumbling, charged chemistry is off the charts.

Richard Todd is a straightlaced colonial policeman who uncovers a diamond smuggling operation at…

reviews.author: Dennis Vehlen
reviews.text: The first Edgar Wallace movie to be shot in color is one produced by Harry Alan Towers and Constantin Films rather than Rialto who started with the popular Wallace pictures a few years earlier and it's sadly also one of the least entertaining ones. The African locations are pretty and the cast is promising but the direction is lifeless and the mystery ultimately stays dull. Richard Todd is not very interesting as Sanders but German actress Marianne Koch and Danish beauty Vivi Bach have their moments in the female parts (with a bunch of hilarious 60s reactions of outrage of a woman being a doctor). This also has the laziest scene ever of a man getting killed by a stock footage crocodile that doesn't seem to be even remotely close to where he is. I wanted to like this more, but it really just makes you miss the fun and energetic Wallace films of Harald Reinl or Alfred Vohrer.

It started out rather promising, with nice on-location photography and some solid performances, including Richard Todd as an upright peeler in a British colonial outpost and Bill Brewer as a slippery profitier with his hands in numerous cookie jars. Unfortunately, it then takes on the energy of a 'whodunnit' TV show, complete with chase scenes and a damsel in distress. Not bad, mind you, just nothing to go out of your way for. I'd say that WINDOMS WAY (1957), with Peter Finch, is a superior Colonial potboiler.

reviews.text: Death Force is fluid and vibrant, delivering all of the lone samurai vs. gangsters action you could want, especially given that two of the gangsters attempted to murder the samurai before they were gangsters and before the samurai was a samurai and became a samurai as a result of the gangsters slitting his throat and pushing him overboard whereupon he wound up on a Pacific Island inhabited by two Japanese soldiers still fighting WWII in 1978 who save his life, teach him how to be a samurai and put him on the road to vengeance against the gangsters back in L.A. The colors are lurid, the decapitations are righteous, but Death Force still plays more like an extended series of interlocking character studies than an exploitation piece. Cirio Santiago went all out with Death Force, making what could be the most 1970's film ever by making all of the 1970's films all at once.

reviews.author: Travis Lytle
reviews.text: For all of its low-budget limitations and exploitative sensibilities, Paul Bartel's "Death Race 2000" is a very smart film. Superficially, the film is about a cross-country road race in a dystopic United States of the future where contestants are awarded points for dispatching pedestrians while the nation watches glued to TV sets. Under the surface, the story reveals a neat satire dealing with government, entertainment, and media. "Death Race 2000" presupposes an obsession with reality TV decades before that obsession infected mass media.

reviews.text: Revenge like ripples in a pond. Lee Van Cleef always a badass but maybe never this cool, (almost) always one step ahead of everyone else. I love that the men who were thieves, rapists, and murderers become business owners and politicians (viva l'Italia!). I love the shocking burst of non-diegetic music when the piano player hits the key to signal the start of the first showdown. I love the nondescript settings that take on a supernatural quality when a dust storm starts up right at the climactic gun battle. I love this movie. Bumped up a half star from last year for finally getting to see it on a big screen. Even bowdlerized, the wordless opening section that ends with a stylized montage of John Phillip Law firing guns remains a powerful and economic set-up for the very tight, clever revenge arc that follows.

With a cold open/flashback structure there's always a danger of sucking some of the suspense out of a story by revealing up front how it ends. At 76-minutes, this is rarely an issue with Decoy. It bristles with nastiness both from Jean Gillie as one of the most fatale of the femme fatales and from Sheldon Leonard as a surprisingly thuggish police sergeant (with the ridiculous moniker Joseph "Jo-jo" Portugal). The basic conceit is that every male character, regardless of what side of the law they are on, wants to sleep with Gillie's character. Watch her for a few minutes, and you'll get it.

A imagem do cinema é produzida no imediato e assim também é Ato Final.
