reviews.author: allain♡
reviews.text: Beneath Death’s somber veil lies tenderness the world seldom speaks of. The strong scent of formaldehyde. Hair gently combed. Thickly applied makeup. Garments ironed with reverence. Each are but serene gestures of love for a life that once bloomed, breathed, lived, walked amongst us. To care for the dead is a sacred calling; taboo to most, offers glory to none, yet still a labor that eventually touches every single soul in time. And though the Grim Reaper may arrive without warning, I find comfort in the promise of a warm departure: one that does not mimic the coldness or rigidity of my still body, but instead holds the warmth of memories and presence of those I once cherished, as they look upon me, one last time.

reviews.text: Fritz Lang, as a teenager, once confronted Death in a hallucinatory visitation, and that became the psychic blueprint of his entire work. You feel that teenage delirium pulsing through every frame, that strange mixture he later described as “horror, but not panic,” as though the film were attempting to stabilize a lifelong love affair with the void. Layered on top of that is the trauma of a young Austrian soldier who had stared at mortality in its most industrialized form during the First World War, who returned from the trenches half-blind and completely changed. It’s no wonder this became the first truly personal statement of his career: a film born not out of aesthetic ambition alone, but out of intimate…

reviews.author: san
reviews.text: From a visual perspective, it’s stunning, impactful, and striking. Fritz Lang is certainly a force to be reckoned with, and this film alone can easily defend that claim. It’s without a doubt ambitious and innovative, but when it comes to the plot there are disconcerting efforts. In particular, it’s the anthology of the three romantic tragedies that drag the film from a stable level of coherence. They are exotic and bizarre, and while this level of fantasy can further show the strong direction from Lang, it unfortunately results in a lot of unnecessary scenes that tear the film’s identity. That’s not to say those scenes were unenjoyable, but it definitely made me struggle to connect with the story as I fumbled to justify their purpose.

reviews.author: Samantha
reviews.text: We can be so quick to denounce art of a sexual nature. It’s oddly hypnotic and satisfying to see the juxtapositions in this anthology – the work of fine artists and extreme filmmakers, all tackling the subject head on. It’s at times farcical, uncomfortable, intimate, and odd. None of the approaches are quite the same, and I imagine no one viewer would resonate with each one. It’s difficult to comprehensively “enjoy” something so varied and unflinching. Yet it compellingly presents the intersection of human sexuality, pornography, and art – a junction not often enough crossed in any meaningful way, and for that I appreciate it. I’d love to see more feature-length ventures into this territory.

reviews.text: I recently watched Detroit 9000 (1973) on Tubi. The storyline unfolds in Detroit during a period of civil unrest between African Americans and white police officers. When a Black fundraiser is robbed by white criminals, the threat of riots and the city tearing apart looms. In response, the police department assigns their best white and black officers to work together and bring the culprits to justice.

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: Grimy but well-plotted Detroit crime story about two cops put on a potentially politically disastrous case. This is my favorite kind of movie, or anyway one of them, with pungent wit and some well-tuned ambiguity, plus a glut of explosive violence that trips between exciting and tough-to-watch. Speaking of ambiguity, the whole thing is surprisingly organic regarding the late-film plot twist, but then kind of hammers the point home a couple too many times, which almost spoils the effect but doesn't really. If the story and characters aren't enough to keep you glued to the screen (you prick), stay tuned for an appearance late in the film from Senator Ted Cruz as Mr. Larson.

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: Devil Doll is awesome. Director Lindsay Shonteff does a ton with very little, creating a genuinely unsettling, sentient ventriloquist's dummy through nothing more than slowly shifting eyes, small, shuffling feet, and a handful of brief shots of it from behind. In addition, it regularly gestures toward the most lurid elements of mind control, while also keeping the evil!hypnotist (Bryant Haliday as The Great Vorelli) off screen enough to keep us interested in him and his schemes, something reinforced by the amount of time we have to spend with Mark English (William Sylvester), the supremely bland, very American reporter who is our main character.

The reality is that there is something far more devious afoot, with the Hugo quite possibly being a soul trapped within the dummy's body.

reviews.author: Andy Summers 🤠
reviews.text: Arthur Penn's Bonnie and Clyde from the late sixties managed to capture the imagination of critics and audiences alike as it sauntered onto the screen back in 1967, heralding a new era for filmmakers willing to show more sex and violence onscreen without risk of the censors derailing cinema's progression. It was nominated for ten Academy Awards, winning just the two, but it was a watershed moment in late sixties cinema. It also helped reignite an interest in real-life 1930's gangsters, and John Milius had an idea to emulate Penn's film with his own account of bank-robber John Dillinger's time in the spotlight.

Both Dillinger and Purvis were clearly a pair of narcissists seeking public adoration; the only difference was their means of achieving it. reviews.text: A surprisingly decent film, especially worth watching for F. Murray Abraham's syphilitically demented portrayal of Al Capone. It did, however, leave me with one outstanding question: has Martin Sheen done anything of consequence since "Apocalypse Now"? I mean, fair dues to the guy, Coppola's Vietnam masterpiece and "Badlands" are enough on their own to justify legendary status (and let's chuck in pervy "The Little Girl who Lives Down the Lane" while we're at it). But it seems for the last so many decades the only time his name comes up is in connection to some Christian movie or to forgettable films by his innumerable spawn. I hope I'm wrong and that there's a classic 80s Martin Sheen movie out there waiting for me to stumble upon it. He's fine "Dillinger & Capone", but it's Abraham you'll remember.

reviews.text: Belongs to the same cinematic lineage as White Noise and Safe—films in which modern capitalism pushes its beneficiaries to the brink of breakdown in mysterious, almost inexplicable ways. Marco Ferreri deserves credit for tackling post-modern, post-industrial ennui through the language of absolute mundanity. And for a filmmaker who claimed not to believe in the political power of cinema, this body of work stands as a living contradiction to his own words.

As he gets his steak ready he dismantles the gun, preparing the parts in olive oil to clean and grease the rusty mechanisms. After dinner he settles down to watch home movies projected onto his wall, fantasising himself into his memories.

reviews.text: Document of the Dead is a documentary covering George Romero's ...of the Dead films mainly the making of Dawn of the Dead. This is a concept that was ahead of it's time in 1981 as some film students were granted access to create a project on the making of a film. It features interview clips with Tom Savini, Susan Tyrrell, Ken Foree, David Emge, Christine Forrest, Scott H. Reiniger, Michael Gornick, Richard P. Rubinstein and the man George Romero himself. I really like the shots in which questions are being asked from the interviewer as the crew walks around the Monroeville Mall. Nostalgia level 100.

In retrospect, it might be the thing that made me want to work with or edit film for a living, something that has yet to happen in any sort of form. I guess there's still time.

reviews.text: Watched the newly updated version which goes beyond Dawn and Day. It's always great to Romero, Savini and their talented group on location and attempting those practical effects. This doc made an impression on me when I was in film school because of its reflections on the editing skills of Romero. Ironically, editing is one the doc's biggest flaws, especially when we move past George's prime and into the muddled digital age. Romero isn't unkind when he's asked about the newest generation of filmmakers who are shamelessly bringing back the dead in film after film. Nevertheless, he does express mild dissatisfaction at Hollywood's ruthless exploitation of the genre that he fathered at a time when independents were thriving. The producers of The Walking Dead should be thanking Romero every single chance they get.

reviews.text: Murphy and Snipes are great. Lots of LOL moments and the premiere scene was moving for me. I'm a big fan of the original films so this was especially fun for me as a genre film geek. But being close to the originals also made it harder for me to accept the many artistic liberties taken. Although the film is about the making of Dolemite (1975), most of the iconic scenes that we see being shot in the film are from the two sequels... The Human Tornado (1976) and Disco Godfather (1979). But I don't think writers Scott Alexander and Larry Karaszewski ever intended for this to be a 100% accurate bio pic... like their other works Ed Wood, The People vs. Larry Flynt, etc.... these films are more about the passion and triumphs of their subjects than historical accuracy.

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: It’s safe to assume that Eddie Murphy has always worshipped at the altar of “Dolemite” mastermind Rudy Ray Moore, as the lewd, brash, and infectiously self-possessed blaxploitation icon blazed the trail that Murphy later followed to his own fame. At the very least, Moore’s foul-mouthed comedy records (e.g. “Eat Out More Often”) and his total disregard for white audiences helped light the way forward. But Murphy, who was a Hollywood-minted star by the time he was 25, probably never thought he would relate to Moore’s hardscrabble career quite as much as he has in recent years. Once you get paid $15 million to star in “Beverly Hills Cop III,” you can only have so much in common with a pioneer…

reviews.text: The writers of the wonderful Ed Wood make a welcome return to their winning formula of a director using his infinite ambition and limited talent to convince everyone around him to help make his dream of making a movie a reality. Dolemite Is My Name isn’t as poignant as Ed Wood — Rudy Ray Moore’s story was a lot happier than Ed Wood’s, and he didn’t work with a dying Bela Lugosi on top of that — but it’s got way more big laughs, with a terrific Eddie Murphy performance at its center, and a hilarious Wesley Snipes in a key supporting role. While I’m sure this is better in a theater, DIMN a perfect Netflix movie: Not too taxing, endearingly sweet, consistently funny, and extremely rewatchable.

reviews.text: My ongoing quest to watch every Cold War film has taken a detour to the rubbish tip lately, but that's what being comprehensive does for you. If anything, they come off as pathetic and deeply disturbed. Watching them justify killing civilians and calling them traitors doesn’t create empathy. reviews.text: The main point of interest in this adaptation is, of course, John Barrymore's Hyde. He's assembled out of stage makeup, matted hair, gnarled fingernails, wild eyes, and hunched posture. He's brought to life through stage-derived silent acting: the mugging, flailing, and histrionic gestures within wide shots of labs and music halls. It's an enormous performance; attention-grabbing, at least, though that's partly to the film's detriment, since nothing else onscreen can match it. Mamoulian's adaptation remains the gold standard.

reviews.text: The second of three adaptations of The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, and while overshadowed by the more famous outing with John Barrymore, this hard-to-find version has merits that make it a unique experience. It’s one of the only times I’ve seen the story told in the present day. Normally, it’s a period piece in London, but we get some modern touches that are appreciated. Hyde leads the police on a chase through the city and on rooftops and even burns down a building. There’s footage of a real fire and firefighters trying to contain it. The plain and naturalistic cinematography gives the movie a grounded style atypical of the period and the story normally. Sheldon Lewis is pretty good as Hyde, who might get more screen time than Jekyll. Has that ever happened in a feature-length adaptation before?

reviews.author: John Charles
reviews.text: If you've seen a couple of Cirio Santiago's MAD MAX knockoffs, you know whether you will like the rest. Talk about a directorial stamp; it would be hard to tell these films apart if you didn't recognize the imported stars (a very relaxed David Carradine earns some easy money here). Tons of explosions and bullet hits, minimal dialogue, cardboard characters, terrible music and audio (this one is in Ultra Stereo, but still sounds like crap)...DUNE WARRIORS is more of the same and I remember renting it back in '91 and thinking, "How can there still be a domestic market for these things?" This isn't really any better all these years later, though Code Red's Blu-Ray (which runs about 17 minutes longer than the previous U.S. release) looks great.

reviews.author: Eli Hayes
reviews.text: No surprise that Hooper's directorial debut is a borderline non-narrative, impressionistic portrait of America with plenty of political subtext disguised as an aggressively edited and deeply psychedelic sensory experience(/overload). Some of the most idiosyncratic utilizations of POV-filmmaking you'll ever come across and the use of space here (which would define Hooper's later career-successes) is extraordinary, allowing a very lo-fi narrative to become something larger and more affecting through its thoughtful and playful concentration on environments, locations, edifices, etc., bookmarked with sequences capturing such a deep sense of realism that it feels like you're watching a cultural landmark of a fiction-feature wrapped in archives of late-1960s Austin, Texas.

reviews.text: Muddled Taiwanese junk starring Ho Tsung Tao (Bruce Li), again on a bloody path of violent retribution. Why, you ask? Double crossed deals over ownership of a gold mine. Besides the obligatory murdered father, that is. The father to a martial expert has a shorter lifespan than a mayfly in these pictures. Chiang Tao turns up in his usual antagonist role, and it's fights front to finish. Except, nobody has a lick of prowess and director Han Bao Chang got this birdbrained notion that he should film the actors executing each move slowly, so that he could speed up the film in post-production. Needless to mention, this was an epic fucking failure, with the finished action sequences chaotically fluctuating from tortoise to Benny Hill and back, sometimes every few frames. The stolen spaghetti western music doesn't help matters one bit. Great for movie night urinary incontinence-inducing laughter, but otherwise, completely worthless.

reviews.author: Jack Russo
reviews.text: Blinded by gold and mired in mud. A definitive demonstration of martial arts mediocrity and lesser still an act of Bruceploitation; an attempt at pushing Li past the lingering image of Lee towards his own screen presence, an ambition immediately humbled by a fractured print which preserves little of the climax aside from Li getting his ass kicked. Features an unwieldly array of awkward medium shot brawling too close for clarity and too distant for character, occasionally undercranked into absurd whiffle bat violence delivered with little impact aside from the dirt which stains the white attire. The stolen Morricone score that whistles between the action hints at a more dramatic grandeur within the conspiratorial gold mining narrative, though this never eventuates; the specifics cannot speak louder than the sound of fists.

reviews.text: Eva is an interesting piece of media that shows Gaspar's lack of experience at the time and it feels like a practice exercise on his dazzling filmography. But despite his obvious errors, the short manages to be devastating. Gaspar takes sexuality and identity and merges it with the unforgiving loneliness that comes with the lack of acceptence, and with that stubborn struggle that doesn't allow us to look beyond our own reflection. This unstable sensation blurs the perception of who we really are, or who we want to reach, but this dreamy moment quickly turns into a nightmarish labyrinth that unless solved will get us trapped into being lonely and empty for as long as we decide to play with these unsettling circumstances...

reviews.author: kian hosseini
reviews.text: "Eversmile, New Jersey" is a lackluster film that left me disappointed and unengaged. With a weak plot and lack of character development, it felt more like a subpar TV movie than a feature film. Even with a runtime of just 90 minutes, I found the experience to be tedious and unenjoyable. The sole redeeming aspect of the film is the presence of the esteemed Daniel Day-Lewis, who, despite his talent, delivers one of his most underwhelming performances. His character's constant repetition of the line "I'm a dentist!" became tiresome and contributed to the overall monotony of the film. While Day-Lewis is renowned for his selective approach to roles, I find myself questioning how this film found its way into his otherwise impressive filmography. In short, "Eversmile, New Jersey" proved to be a forgettable and unsatisfying viewing experience.

Whereas The Yellow Cab Man treated Skelton as a first-rate, progressive comedian, using innovative sets and glimpses of surrealism to aid the comedy, this nostalgic bore affords him very few memorable lines. Fortunately, the talented Sally Forrest is on hand as the love interest, and in one set piece she delivers a particularly erotic dance brilliantly choreographed…

reviews.text: Around the same time prolific Philippines director Cirio H. Santiago was making countless post-apocalyptic action movies cheaply for Roger Corman’s Concorde Pictures, he began also making military-themed action movies for the drive-in crowds and home video. His first Vietnam War film is notable as a big break for actor Robert Patrick, who co-starred in several Santiago movies (wearing the same Johnny Reb cap in most of them) before breaking big as the unstoppable T-1000 robot in TERMINATOR 2: JUDGMENT DAY.

reviews.text: Director Cirio H. Santiago is know for his post apocalyptic and namsploitation flicks. Eye of the Eagle falls into the latter category. If you're looking for a serious Vietnam flick this will definitely disappoint you, BUT if you're looking for a cheesy so-bad-its-good 80's b-movie action this is for you. Roger Corman produced this Filipino production so that should tell you something. The action stays constant as an elite fighting force carries out missions of involving multiple fire fights. Plot isn't really important as long as the bad guys die. Its fun to see a (not that great) performance by a young Robert Patrick 5 years before he'd gain worldwide fame by playing the T-1000 in Terminator 2.

Santiago didn’t even spring for glass in the windows, thinking we’d never notice the squares of white cardboard. reviews.text: This contains an exceptional example of, for lack of a better way to describe it, visual wordplay, wherein Felix tricks a man into taking him to Hollywood by exploiting what some (fools) might call a flaw in the animation--its lack of detail--by turning his black inkblot body into the same shape as a travel bag. In any medium where more of a transformation were required, this joke would distract you from itself with the transformation. By simple virtue of the fact that Felix is just black-on-white with almost no definition to his body, he is able to replicate the bag without more than animation showing his body shape change. His tail emphasizing its role as the handle at the end is the icing on the cake; it's remarkably funny.

reviews.author: Gregor Kreyca
reviews.text: Oh boy, last night I started something. Recently I purchased a 34 movie strong Edgar Wallace Box-set. That one should keep me occupied for a while. The Fellowship of the Frog was the first Wallace Krimi and very fortunately, we are off to a decent start. Crime, pulp, snappy one-liners, some action, a little sex (at least for the late 50’s) and pretty decent atmosphere is what this first Edgar Wallace adaptation has to offer. And I dig it! It’s all rather simply constructed and a bit hokey but also well-shot and cast and (most importantly) very entertaining.

reviews.author: threepenny
reviews.text: He robs safes in an elaborate outfit that sort of makes him look like a frog. He has his men tattooed with a frog. He leaves frog stamps at the scene of the crime. Gotta respect a man who stays on-brand. He's also got an abandoned factory lair filled with traps, and an obsession with one particular girl. The chief inspector (Siegfried Lowitz) is baffled, as is the rich amateur detective (Joachim Fuchsberger) and his goofy sidekick butler (Eddie Arent), with whom he practices judo. I am also completely baffled, as there are as many suspects as cast members: a taciturn father with secret doors in his house, a blind man who isn't blind, incompetent police, competent gangsters, a youngster…

reviews.author: seb
reviews.text: Further diving into the world of Krimis with one of its more convoluted entries. Whereas the story might have its logical flaws from time to time and some of the action sequences are more than a little wonky, Der Frosch mit der Maske makes up for it with its sheer brutality (a sheer unthinkability even in the late 50s) and a few incredibly charming performances. In fact, the character of Richard Gordon, played by the late great Joachim Fuchsberger feels like a slight predecessor to Cary Grant's character in Charade which would obviously release a few years later. Der Frosch mit der Maske is effective and produces a greatly entertaining 90 minutes if one can look past the goofy-looking frog mask.

reviews.author: Travis Lytle
reviews.text: Unable to make up its mind whether it wants to be a look at a corrupt system, a story of the brotherhood of thieves, or a pulpy prison yarn, "Felon" lands as a merely mediocre combination of all of the above. Starring Stephen Dorff, Harold Perrineau, and Val Kilmer, the drama follows Dorff's titular, if accidental, prisoner, as he maneuvers through every prison-film story beat known to cinema. There is grit and attitude to spare, and the story comes together at the end. The path to that end, however, rings as flatly as the work as a whole.

reviews.text: I don't know, man. I fucking love this movie. I've been a fan of Stephen Dorff ever since I was a kid and saw him in Blade. It's gritty and invasive, it puts you right into hell with its protagonist and that's why it works. Prison movies are typically emotional, stripping a character of their innocence is the easiest way to get you emotionally invested and this excels at that. Now I just gotta rewatch Shot Caller.

reviews.text: This is one hell of a confusing film! We start off with a credit sequence showcasing a naked woman swordfighting. From there, we move into a revenge plot focusing on a drugs cartel that employs women to smuggle drugs in their vaginas, mixed with another plot revolving around a killer using a method dubbed "crotch-gouge"! This is really quite an exploitative effort; rather more dark than a lot of the Pinky Violence films. The plot moves very quickly and is really difficult to keep up with. There's so many different characters and things going on. Most of the interest comes from the style and director Teruo Ishii puts on a good show in that respect. The final third in particular has some very interesting scenes - including a dance number and another naked swordfight. It's fine but it all feels very lightweight. There are better genre films than this one out there!

Eventually the dog whimpers and runs off, totally owned. If I was that dog I would have went and jumped off a cliff, because, man, it's all over. It's a moment that manages to ridiculously one-up anything Chuck Norris or Sly Stallone tried to pull off.

reviews.author: Marty McKee
reviews.text: Sadly, star Martin Kove does not play a character named Firehawk in FIREHAWK, yet another war movie directed by prolific Filipino filmmaker Cirio H. Santiago for American release by Roger Corman’s Concorde/New Horizons. Written by Rob Kerchner (story only) and Jeff Yonis (who included a plum role for himself as a cherry named Hobbs), FIREHAWK is a step above the usual Santiago fare, which tend to be sloppy or incoherent. This one delivers meat and potatoes for action fans, but also offers a thoughtful plot and well-rounded characters. Why, some of Santiago’s shot choices could even be called artful.

Dabei sieht das insbesondere im ersten Drittel so wahrhaftig nach Nordirland Mitte der Siebziger aus, als hätte man nicht 2009 sondern 1975 gedreht. Sowas bekommen sonst nur die britischen Regisseure so milieugetreu hin. Aber auch die restlichen 2/3 sind sehenswertes Kino, denn da wandelt sich der Film quasi zum Zwei-Personen-Stück, in dem sowohl James Nesbitt als Bruder eines vor 33 Jahren ermordeten Katholiken als auch Liam Neeson als eben dieser Mörder, der seine Strafe abgesessen hat und geläutert von den Gewalttaten ist, brillieren. Ungewöhnlich auch, wie Hirschbiegel die beiden Charaktere völlig konträr anlegt und den damaligen Täter ruhig und sympathisch erscheinen lässt, das eigentliche Opfer aber als polteriges Nervenbündel. Angucken, Freunde.

reviews.author: Lise
reviews.text: Truth and Reconciliation processes are all the rage recently. They are formed in countries that have known civil unrest or to address particular past wrongs (for example, Apartheid in South Africa, the forced disappearances in Argentina, deaths and disappearances under Pinochet in Chile and Indian Residential Schools in Canada). Whether they are good or bad depends on your ideas of justice. They may be viewed as an alternate form of justice if one sees the justice system as being primarily about restitution (accountability and repair), or they can be viewed as a rival to justice if one believes that justice is about retribution (paying for one's crimes).

Two winsome truckerettes need to make One Big Haul to keep their rig from being repossessed by Harry Dean Stanton, and meanwhile a pair of murderous cocaine smugglers are after the Bolivian marching powder that got stashed in the cab. Annie Potts lays it on thick with her tough-gal drawl, but she’s as cute as a button so who can be mad. Also, as the late Jeff Frageau used to say, “Any movie with Harry Dean Stanton can’t be all bad.” We even get some Stanton-stlye crooning and yodeling, believe it or not.

reviews.author: Nick Langdon
reviews.text: The Phillipines has long had a robust domestic cinema industry and market, but from the 1960s to the 1980s was also the location of choice for low budget American B-pictures. The combination of cheap yet technically accomplished crews and the almost total absence of annoying things like labour unions and occupational health and safety made it a very attractive place for US schlockmeisters like Roger Corman and Cannon Films, while domestic directors such as Ciro H. Santiago cranked out English language exploitation films, mostly for the booming international home video market. Flight to Fury is a US-Filipino co-production, to the extent that local director Eddie Romero made a Tagalog remake named Cordillera (1964) using the same basic story and cast…

reviews.text: When I stay away from this era’s genre movies too long I tend to forget just how deep their nasty streak can be. This begins as a fun romp—Dick Miller appears early as a cabbie who gets an eyeful when one our heroines has no choice but to change the clothes in the way to the airport—but by the third time the “bad” stewardess is violated by her captors it starts to feel a little excessive (esp. for a movie with such a slim running time). Still, consider that rating a real-world rating. If you want an exploitation time capsule that offers a cheap tour of major East Asian cities and a silly subplot about an overprotective , implausibly Italian mom, proceed.

reviews.author: Richard Doyle
reviews.text: When he started New World Pictures, one of Roger Corman's earliest successes was with the Nurses series of films. Starting with Stephanie Rothman's "The Student Nurses" in 1970, he made a series of light sexploitation films that would follow 4 young women, each with a separate plotline that included topical elements and nudity in films that managed to combine sexploitation with women's liberation. By 1973, he had made four of these, and was looking to take the idea in new directions. Stewardesses are an obvious choice.

He's one of the Emperor's personal guards, but he doesn't have any martial skills, he just invents stuff like a giant fan (to blow away the Yuen clan's assassins' killer leaves) and magnets (to take their swords). Mainly three episodes: he gets kicked off the force for not knowing kung fu, then he rescues the Emperor from the Yuens, then he goes undercover to procure a prostitute (Carman Lee, from The Odd Ones Dies) who may be an assassin. Would be utterly forgettable if it wasn't so much fun or without Carina Lau, who plays his wife. Their relationship is maybe the sweetest thing in any of Chow's films.

It may seem confusing, with its wonderful hybrid mix of elements, to audiences who are not informed about Stephen Chow, Vincent Kok, and Lee Lik-chi's sources. To start with, I recommend a reasonable familiarity with James Bond films and martial arts fantasy films. On the surface, this's a Bond spoof, but actually, it's a bonkers melange in the guise of Bond spoof - its contents are more paying homage to the martial arts fantasy tradition, throwing in E. Asian elements…

The martial arts fantasy, in particular, was influenced by The Miracle Fighters (1982) and The Miracle Fighters 2 (1983), a two-part martial arts fantasy-comedy by the Yuen Stunt Team (Yuen Woo-ping and his brothers), though it also reminisced of the hand-drawn martial arts fantasy series of The Buddha Palm in the 1960s.

reviews.text: Looking increasingly likely I just won’t have time to write at length about this movie, but I absolutely loved it. One of the few long movies lately that needed to be as long as it is — you can’t tell the story of a 24 hour race without giving the viewer the feeling of time passing. It’s filled with many of the elemental components of cinema: Speed, energy, movement, innovation, and handsome men in sunglasses. This has got to be one of the best things Disney got from the Fox merger, and in a subtle way it might speak to the act of creation under those kinds of corporate conditions.

reviews.text: Little more than a feature-length puff piece about Britain's premiere horror film festival, this is nevertheless a heartwarming documentary about a modest phenomenon created by four decent guys. The best thing about it is the insight into who they are as people; even without them stating it outright, it's clear that the quartet are a bizarre mismatch of men who'd never have hung out together were it not for what they've made. There's Greg Day, the conservative-looking businessman; Alan Jones, the camp veteran journalist; Ian Rattray, the stereotypically grumpy Scot; and Paul McEvoy, the relatively youthful bad boy of the group. Several of their favourite and most longstanding punters are interviewed too, and the result is a pretty well-rounded overview…

The story follows Ling Ling chat a bumbling government agent who is sent to retrieve a Dinasour skull and what follows is a chaotic mix and low tech gadgets mixed with absurd villains but it’s always endearing and so effortlessly funny and sharp, honestly not much more I can say it’s a film which acknowledges the silliness of spy films especially bond and turns the dial up while also making a fearless comedy which never takes itself seriously.

reviews.text: A half-assed, flimsy attempt at "First!" logic, getting the jump on Netflix by mere days yet producing a film a tenth as focused. Fyre understood that the subject was fundamentally funny and instead highlighted the slow burn collapse. Fyre Fraud consists almost entirely of jokey reference clips, marrying every pop-culture reference by an interview subject to the actual thing being mentioned like a live-action Family Guy riff. The big draw here is McFarland, who was paid to participate to offer no insights other than to protest his innocence and clam up when confronted, rendering his inclusion meaningless and ethically shoddy. This is trying so hard to be a comedy that it only reveals how little research went into it, and no joke here is half as funny as any given tweet that blew up when this all went down.

Enrico Maria Salerno is rather good as the mobster who hires card shark Luc Merenda. Not major, but the kind of professional genre film Martino exceled in the 70s.

reviews.text: An enjoyable and fairly offbeat Italian crime drama that sometimes plays more like a French genre film. That's not only just because it stars Luc Merenda, but one could easily imagine Belmondo as the smooth and gifted antagonist here. GAMBLING CITY is a slick, engaging, and attractive production, with some good action sequences and highly photographic leads. It was the first Italian movie of this type that I saw (via the re-edited US version THE CHEATERS), so I would probably have a soft spot for it anyway, but GAMBLING CITY is notable on its own merits.

reviews.text: Made possible by the success of Toho's '90s Godzilla films, this slicky-produced Gamera adventure revived everyone's favourite giant flying turtle as a hero not just for kids. Not a reinvention of the kaiju genre, just a very satisfying example of it. Good-looking, fun, and takes the material seriously without being too serious. Has some lulls during the human scenes, but what else is new? Special effects are significantly more advanced than the classic '60s Gamera films, and in fact are about on par with the '60s Godzilla films - in other words, they're perfect.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: Narratively indistinguishable from any number of kaiju jams, although thankfully free of anything but entertainment on its mind. This first color GAMERA film is among the most gorgeous and exciting the genre ever produced, and a tonal counterpart with Jun Fukuda's equally dynamic but very tongue-in-cheek GODZILLA VS. THE SEA-MONSTER, released the same year. Director Shigeo Tanaka uses POV angles, "aerial" shots of the models, and expansive panoramic shots of miniature sets , and makes constant use of wide-angle, short aperture lenses to give the monster fights a depth of field with which Honda hadn't really bothered. The deep focus gives the miniature shots a texture and mass and perspective not particularly present in Toho's features, except for maybe GODZILLA VS. HEDORAH. This actively demands that you suspend your disbelief of the cheap special effects. You have to imagine the scale. and Barugon shoots rainbows.

While I didn't dislike the darker aspects of the story here, I definitely enjoy when the franchise focuses less on adult drama and more on Gamera being a creature who stands for peace and empowering children.

reviews.text: Certainly kaiju pictures never trafficked in realism, but the Godzilla films, especially Honda's, were photographed to emphasize scale, with a lot of wide shots and over-cranking. Poor choice of terms perhaps, but they feel somehow grounded. On the other hand the Gamera series uses a far more expressive arsenal of shots, getting right up close to the monsters, using bright colored lights and lots of detail, lending the sets and miniatures a real tactile quality.

reviews.text: Opens with the Friend of All Children attacking a mysterious spacecraft, but then he's sidelined for most of this in favor of a trippy childrens' adventure story following a couple of boy scouts kidnapped by the alien bad guys. Minus some points for way too much recycled footage, but it compensates (as usual for the Gameras) with gorgeous set design (particularly the interior of the villains' ship with its geometric motif) and fantastic miniature effects (an early sequence with the kids racing Gamera in a tiny submarine is a real blast). I keep harping on it, but this series' focus on visceral impact rather than convincing special effects never fails to be exciting.

reviews.text: Even with the involvement of Looney Tunes icons like Chuck Jones and Mel Blanc, Gay Purr-ee (your guess as to what that title means is as good as mine) just feels like a dull prototype of sorts for The Aristocats, in every way the superior animated cat musical set within Paris. All that makes this notable is Judy Garland's only voice acting in any animated project, which still isn't enough to make such a forgettable work of its type worth watching. The animation itself isn't terrible, with one creative sequence presenting a character in the style of several famous painters, yet the weak musical numbers and paint-by-numbers plot make it sorely uninteresting otherwise. It is a fairly cute waste of time at least, but pretty much a total waste of time nonetheless.

reviews.text: Spike Lee didn’t write Get on the Bus, but he uses Reggie Rock Blythewood’s stellar screenplay to make a movie that’s unmistakably a Spike Lee Joint. He assembles an incredible cast of commanding performers, including Ossie Davis and Brooklyn Nine-Nine’s Andre Braugher, to celebrate and dissect the nuance of activists within black culture. During their voyage to the Million Man March, the characters confront homophobia, gang violence, romance, police, the Civil Rights movement, and countless other fascinating topics in what’s essentially two hours of intriguing conversations.

reviews.text: Gérard Depardieu gets cucked by a child. Oh fuck me, why do I even watch this shit? Modern audiences should call the police. What's the intent here? There's an amazing shot in the movie (one of many) that shows a concertgoer practically frothing at the mouth and rending his garments as Mick Jagger prances in and out of frame, completely oblivious. This guy couldn't even cope with Tina Turner, let alone the apocalypse.

reviews.text: Give Me Liberty, the winner of the John Cassavetes prize at the 35th Independent Spirit Awards is a quickfire assault on the emotions. It smartly distorts narrative time to leverage the consequences of mislaid priorities, and the handheld cinematography by Wyatt Garfield delivers persistent motion which ostensibly serves to accentuate its themes of social fluctuation. Written by Alice Austen and Kirill Mikhanovsky, it’s a substantial and sincere film about real people and the reasonable challenges they face compounded with the unreasonable treatment they receive from prevalent society.

reviews.author: Ashlea 🖤 🐂
reviews.text: Give Me Liberty is part catharsis, part tribute to the personal experiences of director, Kirill Mikhanovsky. From the looks of things, his life contains a high degree of chaos that is outright hilarious in its relentlessness. I think the whole audience was in comic relief throughout without ever feeling guilty for laughing along with marginalised characters. Any time that I questioned that myself I was reminded of the ever-present care and commitment of the director to his subjects. As if the film was bursting out of his heart. This film, without a doubt, is a passion project; dedicated to a life of providing for people, instinctively, while suffering your own, personal roadblocks: the joy and the horror and the laughs and the beauty. Thank you, Kirill Mikhanovsky, for this film 💐❤️

Unfortunately he's sort of got to retell UNBREAKABLE and SPLIT a little bit first, and so boy does this drag -- raising and answering yet again questions we've spent two whole movies now dealing with -- before you get to a terrific centerpiece with the four main characters all in a room together that really ought to be the very first scene of this thing. Still, it's as gorgeous as anything Night's ever done, full of idiosyncratic angles, lush and obviously symbolic color palettes, and his patented cloying portent...it's his movie through and through for whatever that's worth.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Clicked for me on rewatch. Unbreakable was about the stories we tell ourselves so that reality might make sense, giving our pain a larger purpose and Split was about the power of that shared pain; this merges the two in an emotional depiction of solidarity and hope vs. violent control. Repositioning those powerful feelings of purpose and communion within exciting, inspiring images found in comic book history (a history glass refers to as "seeing" and "feeling") and then having them confront the sad, mundane realities of political power. What if the superheroes couldn't even make it to the big third-act showdown because they were too busy being brutally murdered in a parking lot in an overtly reactionary, militant act of counter-revolution? "We exist."

reviews.text: "Goin' South" is a 1978 comedy directed by Jack Nicholson. The film is wrapped up in stylings of a revisionist western, a genre that took off in the 70's but tonally this is film that plays on the irony factors of relationship comedy more than anything. With that being said, the star power of the film (as there is a hefty number of notables in the feature) and the designed setting is plenty of a draw to bring many into the fold of seeing the film. Adding to that, I can also see how some walked away wayward from the production, thinking they were going to get one thing in a film's delivery and absolutely getting something else.

reviews.author: teamgal
reviews.text: Excepting the graciousness of Mary Steenburgen's screen debut, this is a fiasco of the highest magnitude, a star's ego driving a film off-the-rails. Nicholson, the actor, gives an unforgivable performance. Nicholson, the director, hasn't a clue what he wants to accomplish. At times this appears to be interested in broadly spoofing the Western in the same way that, dare I say it, BLAZING SADDLES had a few years earlier. But it lacks that kind of daring. The script is the real culprit here — cobbled together by four writers who, judging by appearances, were never in the same room together. It's a tonal mess, careening from one event to another with no cohesive linkage. Makes the previous year's MISSOURI BREAKS seem like HIGH NOON.

reviews.text: Jack Nicholson stars in and directs "Goin' South," a rascally charmer about a marriage of convenience and a whole lot of gold. The Western comedy finds Nicholson's Henry Moon saved from a hanging, hitched to a woman far above his station, a running afoul of the law, the railroad, and his former gang. The story engages with a smart mix of goofiness and plot tangles, and Nicholson puts together something with a dustily breezy energy and a stellar cast. This is an appealingly visualized, sardonically told, and all-around enjoyable piece of work.

Halicki was no SoCal realist, though, he was just an amateur who loved cars and, due to ignorance of filmmaking craft or frustration with existing examples, wanted to present a car chase with as little illusion as possible. reviews.author: Fred 🇵🇷
reviews.text: You have to know going into this film what it is and what it isn't. Despite appearances to the contrary, this isn't a continuation or prequel to the preceding DC Animated Universe Lantern outing nor is it a standalone Green Lantern story. For all intents and purposes, what this is is a crash course in Lantern lore as told through vignettes. Going into this with that knowledge in your pocket, this is a terrific invitation to enjoy some of the most satisfying, decidedly weirder DC fare out there. I loved just about every story in this anthology and appreciate how much they further endeared me to this corner of the DC universe. It's a highly underrated creation deserving of more adulation than it's gotten.

reviews.author: Kevin Y
reviews.text: Incredibly disappointing given how great the real life story is. Erivo and an underused Monae are both wonderful, and their dynamic is the best part of the film - however, everything around them is aggressively pedestrian and poorly thought out. From a story standpoint, this falls into a typical biopic trap of trying to cover too much in too little time, such that moments are rarely allowed to breathe and develop. The pacing just never pulls you in because it's too distracted with figuring itself out, seesawing between plot points and characters with little purpose. Because of that, the heart of Harriet's story gets lost in all the shuffle, and you can't really make out a clear vision or focus…

reviews.author: Georgia Coley
reviews.text: Gratefully, this doesn’t shy away from Harriet Tubman’s singular religious faith (even the wilder stuff, like her prophetic visions) and Cynthia Erivo is an absolutely inspired choice, capturing her strength with such grace and vulnerability. Still, it’s unfortunate that little elements like a misplaced musical score and misguided editing can totally cripple an otherwise solid movie. It’s perfectly competent, and even inspiring at times, but it could have be so much better with a cleaner job in post-production.

That sad fact of life proves to be an insurmountable problem for Donick Cary’s “Have a Good Trip: Adventures in Psychedelics,” an exasperating Netflix documentary so high on its own supply that it starts to see things that aren’t there — namely, the entertainment value in watching a bunch of famous people tell interchangeable stories about seeing the carpets move or whatever.

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: I know I'm very much in the minority here, but I really struggled with this one. Though John Alton's black and white cinematography is as striking as ever, to modern eyes, He Walked by Night feel like a very static, bog-standard piece of copaganda, weighed down by a barely functional screenplay full of cliches and weak cop "banter." It also carefully — and, presumably, intentionally — removes any and all personality from most of its characters, requiring the audience to awkwardly attach itself to the broad category of 'Cop' as protagonist.

reviews.text: He Walked by Night is one of those police propaganda noirs, complete with serious voice-over. This one is apparently based on a true story and follows a police investigation after one of their own is murdered following a seemingly routine checkup. The film splits the focus between the police investigation and the criminal himself; here depicted as a resourceful individual with a knowledge of electronics, police procedure and the Los Angeles storm drain network. The police aspect is sure to get in the usual range of methods used to catch up with criminals - including undercover work and an identikit presentation in front of a live audience of previous victims. It has to be said that the focus on the…

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "He Walked by Night" is a 1948 film directed by Alfred L. Werker. A short and dynamic noir, the film plays directly to procedural form in its direct crime narrative. Set within the streets of booming city of Los Angeles, the film begins with a patrolman who is killed in the line of duty. The killer, looking like a modest, normal citizen and not the deranged killer type has fled the scene and has caused a metro wide search. The problem is that the killer looks carries themself with the common persona and with that it is anyone's guess where he lies.

reviews.author: noir1946
reviews.text: Semi-documentary films noir aren’t usually my kind of noir. Here, we have Reed “Mr. Voiceover” Hadley bombarding us with facts about Los Angeles and telling us what a swell job the police are doing. Then we have the actors performing with the straightest straight faces imaginable, as if they are real people. But these qualities, which often make for boredom, are balanced by an intelligent screenplay, solid direction, and spectacular John Alton cinematography.

reviews.author: comrade_yui
reviews.text: contains some of the all-time great noir setpieces, blending docu-drama style with john alton's more expressionistic touches. i LOVE the silent ambush scene, and the brutal stormdrain climax, made before the third man, makes that film's famous ending look paltry by comparison -- this is the genuine b-movie article, bereft of any rhetorical pretensions of being anything but a hard-bitten heater. anthony mann is so clearly the director who handled most of this that i don't know why letterboxd doesn't have him credited directly alongside alfred werker, the mann deserves his due for creating such a memorable work from what in other hands would be pretty dry material -- the cops are nasty, the criminal is smug, and the world resembles a rembrandt nightmare, anticipating blade runner's rain-slick corridors and existential paranoia.

reviews.author: Raphael Georg Klopper
reviews.text: Bold and daunting enough to be considered transgressive for its time, even if helded back by a documental obnoxious narration that turns some of its parts dated. But as always, is in the power of the filmmaking that elevates the film above its limitations and lets de artistry dictate its iconic status. He Walked by Night may not be an iconically remembered Noir classic, but is a masterfully made one! With director Alfred L. Werker getting fired mid production, and most of the work going for Mann’s unfairly uncredited work here, I most likely bet to be the reason why the film made it as superb as it is.

The perfect balance between coherence and inspiration, tightness and fulgurance, life and cruelty - a sequence of actions, feelings and social forces that succeed one after another with the clarity and blaze of a lightning bolt. Stroheim’s authorial presence survives the frequent, systematic dismantling of his work in post-production not only after studio sabotage, but even when his films end up directed by others, continuing to bear an unshakable coherence with his art.

reviews.author: TommyLeeMcGee
reviews.text: Akin to “A Hard Day’s Night” (1964), both cinematic cash-ins on wide popularity, but neither film bad because of it. Retains the episodic shenanigans of the show, but decidedly abandons the small scope for a much larger trek through America, to match the jump from TV to theaters, with the addition of a larger narrative, also allowing for the inclusion of thematic elements to bolster the larger scale product. Acts as a loose allegory to the civil rights movement and racial issues of the time, with Yogi and Boo-Boo’s trip down South looking for freedom to only meet alienation, stereotyping, and violence, mirroring the experiences of African-Americans in the early 60s. The best “Yogi Bear” animation up to that point, and as fun and entertaining as the show, possibly more; a pleasant and smile-inducing cartoon, also acting as a cultural and cinematic time capsule.

reviews.author: Michael Brooks
reviews.text: Hanna-Barbera's Hey There, It's Yogi Bear cleverly blends the humour and slapstick antics that children adore with subtle witticisms that will elicit a chuckle from parents. The film captures the essence of the original "Yogi Bear" television series, maintaining its lighthearted humour and simple storytelling. The animation style also remains true to the classic Hanna-Barbera aesthetic of the era, and its colourful and simple animation has a charming retro appeal. The character designs retain their original charm, capturing the essence of Yogi and Boo Boo's personalities while introducing a new array of amusing supporting characters.

But I think maybe he's just way too interested in the idea of disruptor status -- obviously this is only superficially about sports -- and for me at least that got in the way of all the gymnastics (both verbal and cinematic). reviews.author: Chris Hughes
reviews.text: Hollywood Party is an odd patchwork of a film featuring a thin plot. It concerns Jimmy Durante throwing a lavish shindig in order to locate lions for his next film. This meager premise is used as a framework for musical comedy featuring appearances by MGM’s high profile film and radio stars of the day. It has some wild pre-code musical numbers with insane sets, a kinetic turn by Lupe Vèlez, Laurel and Hardy, the Three Stooges, Mickey Mouse and more. It fluctuates between moving at breakneck speed and crawling like molasses. The lack of anything resembling a compelling story is the issue. It’s no Footlight Parade but it isn’t a waste of time either. It’s just crazy enough to maintain interest for its brief 68 minutes and the color animated sequence in the middle is worth the price of admission in and of itself.

reviews.author: Chris
reviews.text: Hollywood Party was initially critically panned at its release, which is completely understandable. There is a feeble framing device that serves as an excuse for the titular "Hollywood Party" to occur in which Jimmy Durante needs lions for his movies from a "lion provider" that is attending the soiree. It feels haphazardly made and disjointedly spliced together, but this may be because approximately seven minutes are missing from this movie because of the various edits that had circulated which cut out some material that was deemed too risque for certain regional audiences.

reviews.text: A little bit insane, kind of needs to be seen to be believed. In one sense it seems lazy, because the concept is so low-effort and the tiny shred of plot covers about as much as Lupe Velez’s dress. On the other hand, everything it does it does wayyy over the top. Music! Dancing girls! Jimmy Durante fighting a lion! Mickey Mouse and a color Walt Disney cartoon! There’s actually plenty to enjoy, if you’re into this sort of thing: Eddie Quinlan & June Clyde are adorable, and Charles Butterworth is his usual funny deadpan self. Even the Three Stooges make an appearance. The high point, however, is the battle between Lupe Velez and Laurel & Hardy; the expressions on Ollie’s face while he has an egg sliding down the front of his trousers are comedy gold.

reviews.text: The premise of this 20-minute short is an Asian-based Hollywood theme party, a light bit of fluff with a few musical/dance numbers. Most of it is entertaining and harmless, but there are some exceptions, most notably with host Charley “Chan” Chase, who appears fresh off of having left Hal Roach. He treats this like a Halloween party of sorts, donning an obviously fake Fu Manchu mustache and traditional Chinese clothes. Several times he mimics stereotypical broken English while doling out his humor (“Old Chinese proverb say, when on visit, always give hostess the bird,” he says, offering his co-host, Elissa Landi, some parrots). There are a couple of other examples of this, including some band members who briefly imitate Mandarin…

reviews.author: Fint
reviews.text: I don't normally log these bits of fluff that the Hollywood studios churned out for their "full supporting programme" offerings, but this one - an early Technicolor tap dancing/fashion showing/musical interluding/awful comedy routining effort - is noteworthy for the appearance of Anna May Wong after a spell in the wilderness (i.e. England). It appears on the disc for The Good Earth (also 1937) for which she auditioned. MGM refused to consider her for the central female role (which won Luise Rainer her second Oscar), a dreadful oversight that only gains in its unfairness over the decades.

reviews.author: Quiller
reviews.text: MGM throws a China-themed party in this inconsequential two-reeler. That means there’s quite a bit of Orientalism going on: a gimmicky performance of “Chinatown, My Chinatown”; Charley “Chan” Chase decked out like Fu Manchu and “speak-ee” like “Chinee”; etc. I can understand why some Letterboxd users rate this short so poorly. A model of cultural sensitivity it is not! But it does offer one remarkable compensation: at one point, we see Anna May Wong, who had recently returned from her first journey back to her family’s Chinese homeland, modeling some of the fashions she had picked up on there. She even reminds viewers that China has two major languages! How many viewers in 1937 even knew there was a difference…

reviews.author: Ben
reviews.text: The ero-guro (erotic grotesque) label is appropriate for many of Teruo Ishii's films, and Horrors of Malformed Men is no exception. However, it feels decidedly different from some of his earlier works because he substitutes frighteningly realistic brutality for surrealistic psychological horror in this film. Ishii films such as Shogun's Joy of Torture, Orgies of Edo, Inferno of Torture, and Yakuza Law are effective at evoking a response because he never shies away from depicting cruelty, but the narratives are straightforward. In many ways, they are visual spectacles whose intentions are clear for everyone to see. Ishii doesn't sacrifice any of his visual flairs in Horrors of Malformed Men, though – instead, he backs his spellbinding aesthetics with a mind-melting…

reviews.text: Teruo Ishii regular Teruo Yoshida plays the main part in this beautifully shot and at times bizarre variation of The Island of Dr. Moreau. But the standout personality here is Tatsumi Hijikata as the mad scientist. An actor, author, choreographer, dancer and the founder of a genre of dance performance art called Butoh. (Google it or listen to the Blu-ray commentary to learn more about that particular kind of performance art.) He already appeared in several other of Ishii’s movies but here he was given a bigger role. He and the, at times psychedelic, visuals make this movie one of Ishii’s more memorable and well-known films.

reviews.text: It is undoubted that the strength of House of Flying Daggers lies in its visual splendour: there are few movies that manage to capture so many shades of colors as Zhang Yimou's, and House of Flying Daggers might be his biggest effort to date in terms of ambition, which is repaid by a movie that presents an artistic vision I thought alien to the live action world. The unapologetically bright and bold colors that construct the picture are the ones you could easily find in an animated movie, but rarely in a live action one. The movie is absolutely stunning in terms of presentation, where red was the dominant color in the director's previous features, it is now green who…

reviews.author: David James 🍩
reviews.text: He's acting, she's acting, but they real-deal fall for each other down through these layers of deception. Actions false, feelings genuine. The state is telling a story and the Flying Daggers are telling their own, both aiming to send bodies into the meat grinder in their struggle for power. Feelings false, actions genuine. Love versus power is the core conflict here, and Zhang Yimou spins these familiar ingredients into hallucinatory magic with dreamy wuxia action and musical editing, affecting a tragic martial arts opera with only one song, but what a song it is. Hearts bleed and the earth turns and seasons change during a final clash of the swords, bamboo shattering all around, snow blanketing the fields of fathomless loss like a sacred shroud. What a romantic gut punch to be left so vulnerable after such a triumphant display of balletic bloodshed.

It took me a spell to get used to the Cinerama look on my widescreen T.V. but I did find it was impressive though I wish I saw it at the actual Cinerama Dome. It is very epic in quality following a family through generations as they go west. It's painted with sorrow, joy, regret and an acceptance. Sure it's a bit much at parts and has a long running time but there is something about everything coming together to try and thwart Television and showcase the grandioseness of cinema. I am quite aware of the irony that I watched this on my T.V. off of TCM but I still admire it for what it is.

reviews.author: Joe Lynch
reviews.text: Look, I like movies shot wide but this may be the WIDEST film I’ve ever seen (at home it’s best to watch it in “SmileBox” format with the curved edges). But a sprawling epic on the history of the Wild West from multiple (sometimes connecting) storylines needs a scope that doesn’t just feel like a gimmick, even if the frame at times seems more like an IMAX demo than a storytelling tool.With a cast this insane and production value through the roof (the expendable horse budget alone must have been immense), it’s hard not to relish in this big, brash, last gasp at earnest Westerns before the more cynical Spaghetti Western became popular.Long live VistaVision and the SmileBox format!

Try an ENTIRE FAMILY OF HIPPOS, leaving behind the titular orphan. There's quite a bit here that frames that G rating as adults asleep at the wheel. But man, oh man, that animation! I've never seen another film in this overall style. It's full of stylized forms with vibrant, psychedelic colors, and every frame looks like a page from a picture book. A movie that got made in Hungary because the producers bribed their government into letting them ship their project over there, a movie funded by a French cosmetics company, and a movie that somehow involved Roger Moore of James Bond fame. reviews.author: Xennui
reviews.text: This Hungarian film tells a story about hippos in Zanzibar, injected with an eye-dropper full of LSD. The images are frequently stunning, and some sequences very impressive. There are some issues with the pacing and writing, not to mention reliance on broad cultural stereotypes, but I'd venture to say it has its heart in the right place. Hugo the Hippo is certainly floating in the wake of Yellow Submarine, but also brought to mind Tezuka Osamu's Cleopatra and Yokoo Tadanori's pop stylings too.

reviews.author: noen
reviews.text: When Abel Gance released this film in 1919, cinema stood at a crossroads. Barely 25 years old, the medium had developed from a technological curiosity into a flourishing art form with its own stylistic ambitions and industrial structures. Before the First World War, Europe (and France above all) held an unrivaled position of leadership in the global film industry. The nation that had witnessed the birth of cinema through the Lumière brothers, and its imaginative expansion through Méliès, had also built an immense industrial infrastructure through Pathé and Gaumont. Film culture was international, dynamic and experimental. German studios cultivated psychological realism, Danish cinema produced sophisticated melodramas, Italian epics displayed a monumental sense of scale and Russia was beginning to explore…

reviews.text: Cuando leí el título de la película me pregunté qué era lo que se estaba acusando. Entendía que la película era de carácter bélico, pero me causó mucha curiosidad saber cuál era el objeto de acusación: ¿los poderosos? ¿los militares? ¿las armas? Para mi sorpresa, aunque algunos de los mencionados también son implícitamente culpables, todo el peso de la guerra terminó por recaer en un grupo más general: la humanidad. Inesperadamente, se toma la decisión de culpar a todos y cada uno de nosotros (de las personas de la época) por el conflicto armado y todos los desastres que este causó. reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: Displaying some of the most technologically advanced filmmaking of the 1910s, J'accuse is an incredible work on the horrors of war, literally filmed in the trenches of World War One. Death lingers everywhere in J'accuse, from a deer bleeding on the floor in an early scene to the corpses strewn across the battlefield later on. J'accuse captures the mood of a nation which lost so much, with a pacifist, anti-war sentiment that condemns those who survived - what makes them worthy of the sacrifice of so many? Early on J'accuse depicts a frenzy of men willing to enlist and children who have no conception of war. Yet by the end it shows a land of sorrow, where the dead rise…

reviews.author: Neill Shaughness
reviews.text: It's always fun to discover antique cinema that holds up. This is not only a great World War One movie, it's one of the best war movies I've ever seen (and at this point I've seen a lot of war movies). Unlike many modern warfare films, this doesn't sacrifice story for spectacle. These are fully realized characters with clear and distinct motivations. The visual language utilized is incredible for 1919, and it still manages to make statement about war without allowing the message to overwhelm the plot. Maybe my new favorite film from 1919.

It is pretty slow at times, especially during the second part of the film, but the payoff is absolutely worth it.

reviews.text: Small-scale science fiction that will inevitably remind genre-savvy viewers of Moon and Ex Machina in equal measure, and that's no bad thing. Really strong performances, terrific robot special effects (it looks like CGI, but it's a robo-suit), and a particularly well-defined environment boost this story up beyond its somewhat basic narrative, which feels like a throwback to Terminator-era science fiction, in a way that makes the more sophisticated modern visuals kind of startling. reviews.text: How come nobody told me that Tobe Hooper churned out one of the low-key gayest horror movies of the 90s? I know this is based on a Cornell Woolrich novella, but it plays out more like a perverted take on Teen Witch or any number of other Disney Channel teen girl empowerment movies. only with Mädchen Amick fighting with Dee Wallace over control of a deadly dress made from an Aztec mummy's burial shroud. Between giving Anthony Perkins and Natalie Schafer roles and at times exposing and lingering on more male flesh than female (including a shower murder), I can only really wonder just how much of the camp value is intentional.

reviews.text: "I'm Dangerous Tonight" is a 1990 supernatural horror film directed by Tobe Hooper. Within the supernatural element, it directly focuses on possession, as the characters in the film trade off a cursed Aztec robe that holds the properties of enraging any person who puts it on. After removing it, the direct person forgets the prior events, showing that they were in a trance while the destruction was done. The beginning of the story seems harmless enough as Madchen Amick, who was Shelly Johnson of "Twin Peaks" (1990-1991) fame, stars as college student Amy. Relatively shy and innocent by design, she lives with her aunt, cousin, and grandmother as she lost her parents prior. There is a bit of a Cinderella…

reviews.author: Dave Edwards
reviews.text: 20% Cinderella80% In Fabric While the made for TV movie trappings of I’m Dangerous Tonight limit Hooper from being able to truly break loose like we’ve come to expect, there are aspects of his film that earn it a mild recommendation. The performances are uniformly good, with Madchen Amick turning in a grounded and emotionally committed performance in the lead. It’s well shot and edited, especially when you consider the standards of USA TV movies in 1990. Still, it’s hard to shake the feeling I’m Dangerous Tonight would have been better off as a short film or as a part of a horror anthology, as the pacing ultimately wears the viewer down a bit, ultimately making the film notable only to Hooper completists.

reviews.author: Patrick Pryor
reviews.text: Tobe Hooper directs this wack Fear Street knockoff where Shelly from Twin Peaks finds a haunted mummy dress that makes her. . . dangerous. After slipping on the evil gown, she becomes a wild delinquent who ditches her bedridden grandma to dance seductively at a college formal. Lots of amazing early '90s baggy fall fashions and a supporting turn from Anthony Perkins as a cursed object occult expert push the movie over the top. The plot gets kinda muddled halfway through, the pacing feels slack, and Hooper doesn't go ape enough with the premise. But if you can find the tape, I'm Dangerous Tonight is a fun enough way to kill 90 minutes and fill in more esoteric patches of the Texan horror maestro's filmography.

Lee Ermey arriving late while smoking a cigarette. That cut includes a lot of what is good about it. There's a certain TV movie quality to it, I'm Dangerous Tonight could use be a little more violent, and pace can come and goes according to its needs to obscure narrative. Hooper does direct it with a very good eye, lots of striking images throughout and the main trust between sexuality, usually female, and repression, based mostly in religious fundamentalism, is observed with more care than usual. reviews.text: Director Julia Hart presents a subversive, cinematic conundrum of “what happens with the gangster’s wife?,” in this stylish but lethargic thriller I’m Your Woman. A sturdy Rachel Brosnahan plays the unknowing, inexperienced gangster wife whose life turned upside down when her husband gets embroiled in a “business” mishap. There are some glaring issues in the film that impacted the film’s overall impact. First, the film’s first half is too lethargic that it sets up the bar pretty low. The film’s second half is the best part, but by then we’re all pretty bored and inattentive. Second, the film has some awkward, half-baked screenplay that doesn’t give us any good judgments to try piece it all together.

A lot of what makes this film work is because of the spot on comedic delivery and wonderful performances from a fine cast that includes Kevin Kline, Tom Selleck (kinda weird seeing him without a mustache), Matt Dillon, Debbie Reynolds, and a show stealing Joan Cusack. reviews.text: There’s something incredibly endearing about Infinitely Polar Bear’s unostentatious simplicity. Constructed on familiar indie tropes – a hand-made, whimsical aesthetic, a period setting, a family unit defined equally by conflict and closeness – the film sidesteps cliché to conjure an utterly charming experience.

reviews.author: Vince The Cinephile
reviews.text: On paper Maya Forbes’ Infinitely Polar Bear might look like a problematic family drama, but the consistent, heartfelt performances from Mark Ruffalo and Zoe Saldana make it all worth it. The film centers on a mentally unstable father who takes over responsibility for his two daughters while his wife attends a graduate school. Mark Ruffalo is outstanding here, balancing the tough act of playing an unhinged individual with nuance and complexity. Ruffalo’s likeable everyman charm suits well together with Saldana’s radiant presence. The daughters are great in supporting turns as well. The upbeat energy, and unabashed sincerity of Infinitely Polar Bear makes it worthwhile to spend some time with this family.

reviews.text: Say what you will about SILVER LININGS PLAYBOOK (for instance, "schematic bullshit ... truly toxic" - D. Dillaman), but at least it's recognisably competent. Here, meanwhile, is a screenplay full of undigested anecdotes that lurches from moment to moment like a drunken sailor, some truly bizarre camera choices (that arbitrary zoom! cutting with static shots!), and enough Ruffalo ham to feed a small village. The title is because one of the girls, despite speaking precociously through the entire film, says her dad has "polar bear" instead of "bipolar". If that doesn't make you flee, then this film is more for you then it is for me.

reviews.text: Intolerance, D. W. Griffith's silent era classic, is definitely a movie that has stood the test of time, and although it can't quite keep up with the flashiness of modern cinema, it has the power to captivate an audience with its powerful message and innovative direction. The story, which follows several distinct storylines across the ages, draws attention to the difficulties faced by those who have faced discrimination and oppression through the ages, and Griffith's masterful direction binds these stories together wonderfully. He crafts one of the most iconic sequences ever, with a series of scene cuts between periods, to show how history keeps repeating itself. The visuals and cinematography also have to be applauded, as the scenes really pull you into…

reviews.author: RigelDC
reviews.text: From Robert Greenwald, focuses on corporate involvement in the Iraq campaign. It covers KBR (Halliburton), Titan, CACI, and a host of other corporate interests that are providing civilian services and military support in Iraq. Half of the film is exceptional, detailing true incompetence, corporate greed, and political corruption rampant throughout the military-industrial relationship. Some of the most shocking elements include how perfectly good but unneeded, erroneous, or only slightly deficient equipment (like a truck with a flat tire) gets destroyed rather than exchanged so that the contract companies can get more money. Or how they run caravans of empty vehicles and claim them as trucking expenses. The other half of the film is questionable filler of families whose members joined the companies and were killed in Iraq in service that was later deemed deficient. While I felt bad for those people, weeping widows have less of an impact than photographic evidence on this topic. Highly informative and depressing.

reviews.text: IRONWEED is the type of movie that’s made for its performances. Both Jack Nicholson and Meryl Streep are at their best in this. And Tom Waits never disappoints whenever he appears in a movie. This movie is pretty depressing, which makes sense since it takes place during the Great Depression. The grimly lit cinematography really sets the mood for the movie’s journey, capturing the bleakness of the era that reflects the hopelessness of the Great Depression. The pacing is a bit ponderous, occasionally feeling aimless and too drawn out. It’s a movie that deserves recognition for its unflinching look at the human condition during one of America’s darkest times, but it’s certainly not an easy watch. Definitely worth watching for its performances.

reviews.text: #28 of MGM’s 49 Crime Does Not Pay shorts serves as a warning against taking the seemingly insignificant slot machine for granted: it’s the foundation of many racketeers’ empires because all those nickels add up. In this entry, racketeer Edwin Maxwell conspires against reform-minded Mayor Joseph Crehan, who’s campaigning against slot machines, while still finding time to intimidate small-time businessmen like Tom Neal into paying protection money. It’s not bad, thanks to an interesting cast and fast-paced direction by Roy Rowland. (It’s one of four Crime Does Not Pays Rowland directed just before graduating to features.) In addition to Neal and ubiquitous character actor Crehan, film buffs can spot Lloyd Corrigan, Reed Hadley, future blacklistees Jean Rouverol and Lloyd Gough,…

It jumps from comical, glitzy scenes set in hell to a reasonably realistic retelling of the Aum Shinrikyo cult then back to gruesome but hilarious torture scenes. Head-scratching stuff, but a fascinating watch.

An older woman - who is presumably Satan or something - gives teenager Rika a sneak preview of Hell, so that she'll be scared into living a wholesome life. I've seen several depictions of Hell, but this is the one that looks the most like an episode of Play School; watching the characters pretend to row down a River Styx made out of shimmery cloth gave me real Brian Cant/Floella Benjamin vibes. reviews.text: all the very annoying & overcooked stylistic choices in this can't detract from the fact that, out of all the big 80s/90s action stars, van damme was overall the greatest screen performer of them, matching a taught, deliberately homoerotic physicality with a slightly-oblique everyman persona, always signifying to the audience an attitude of "wow, can you really believe a guy like me became a movie star?". this is his most affecting acting showcase, probably due to the fact that he's able to actually give a performance in his native language. the director/writers clearly oriented this to be a gracious dog day afternoon-esque vanity project for van damme, but he imparts it with a deliberate listlessness and skilled melancholy that ultimately leaves you nostalgic for a bygone era in which weird european martial artists like him could be beloved by people all over the world just for being an underdog who could do the splits and kick people really good.

reviews.text: Todd Phillips’ “Joker” is unquestionably the boldest reinvention of “superhero” cinema since “The Dark Knight”; a true original that’s sure to be remembered as one of the most transgressive studio blockbusters of the 21st Century. It’s also a toxic rallying cry for self-pitying incels, and a hyper-familiar origin story so indebted to “Taxi Driver” and “The King of Comedy” that Martin Scorsese probably deserves an executive producer credit. It’s possessed by the kind of provocative spirit that’s seldom found in any sort of mainstream entertainment, but also directed by a glorified edgelord who lacks the discipline or nuance to responsibly handle such hazardous material, and who reliably takes the coward’s way out of the narrative’s most critical moments.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: Cruelty and tragedy. Red dye pours into a pool, dirtied hands find a warmth, fabric floats down from above. Ju Dou is less elegant than Zhang Yimou's usual films, and perhaps even a crude movie, but such crudeness gives it character. This story of miserable lives is hard-hitting, as traditions are uprooted and power dynamics abruptly shift. Ju Dou is a quiet film, emphasising the simplistic nature of the text; a story to feel, not to think about. The storytelling is lean but Zhang uses colour to make as many moments as possible count. There's shots of flowing red and falling blue, light bleeds through the onscreen space, and shots are tinted to wonderful effect. This is a film of a secret love and only been able to reveal yourself as a show of pain. There's an imperfection to Ju Dou that stops it being a masterpiece, but as emotive cinema it's tautly constructed.

reviews.text: Reality perceived through memories, but the memory had gotten rather blurry, to the point where it couldn't be differentiated from dreams. Since the beginning we were seated behind frosted glass, it was never meant to be a literal recount of events. There is enough realism for a full immersion, yet also infused with enough inconsistencies to tip us off balance. The human memory is notoriously unreliable. In our minds, the destination was clear, the journey there wasn't, like how yangyang took a large detour by taking a boat to cross the river, then circle back around by bridge, just to attend a band performance a few blocks away. Some details might have been lost in the fog, tangled up and replaced, the timeline is all wrong too. At the end of the day, we were simply reliving a past that is not ours.
