reviews.author: Corey Donovan
reviews.text: If a shirtless, sweaty Tony Dorsett gunning down a bunch of North Vietnamese isn’t a perfect cinematic encapsulation of American bravado then I don’t know what is. I know Dorsett didn’t have the same established acting career as some other all-pro running back alumni like Jim Brown or the Juice. Yet there is something about running backs—the most physically debilitating position—putting themselves into the facades of Hollywood, even if it is at its exploitative fringes. People’s bodies and image being placed in the hands of America’s corrupted institutions for mass entertainment. Cirio’s films, at their best, find an accidental commentary through their low-budget riffs. The NFL, Hollywood, the U.S. military with an equal inhumanity only differing in scope. Institutions led by those with a justified insanity—incomprehensible to the average person—that will get results no matter how ruthless the methods must be. The leader here is David Carradine as a Cambodian invading colonel; searching for a violent ecstasy in Southeast Asia.

reviews.author: Brian Burkart
reviews.text: For years Mickey Rooney had portrayed Hollywood’s all-American teen, but at the age of 27 he was eager to move into grown-up dramatic roles. So he laced up the gloves as feisty boxer Tommy McCoy and scored a resounding box-office K.O. in "Killer McCoy." The story – a retelling of 1938’s "The Crowd Roars" – traces McCoy’s rise from poor kid slinging newspapers and hustling pool games to lightweight title contender. Along the way, he falls under the sway of a big-time gambler (Brian Donlevy), copes with his alcoholic Dad (James Dunn) and finds forbidden romance with the gambler’s daughter (Ann Blyth). This documentary he made on the 2000 election is the best way I know how to do that. All of his work is personal in some way, but this is truly personal, Phil just being himself—dirt under his fingernails, his sense of humor, that Wilco tour shirt he wore to rags, “oy vey,” his brow furrowed in concern and tenderness, big hands covered in freckles, his cynicism and curiosity, listening to Roberta Flack in the car.

His quiet nodding and shuffling from place to place is instantly more compelling because he's doing it, and the whole project has a probably unearned fascination value because of him.

They live in the margins, far removed from the capitalistic power of what Ken Kesey once called the Combine. Some of them, like the destitute 17-year-old Jennifer Lawrence played in “Winter’s Bone,” were simply born there. Others, like the tender but troubled Vietnam vet at the heart of Granik’s 2014 documentary “Stray Dog,” have been too close to the big machine, and can’t stomach the idea of going anywhere near it again.

As much as I admire Russell's audacity, not all of it works -- the worst parts feeling like a filmed version of a Frank Zappa stage routine and with original songs that aren’t much better than if it actually were. It's impossible to not want to compare this to Tommy, but I think that film works better for me -- the stricter adherence to the source album resulting in a work that feels more consistent than Lisztomania's frankensteined mishmash of pop-classical pastiche.

reviews.text: Prior to directing Little Witch Academia, Yoh Yoshinari was best known as being one of the strongest key animators and art designers in the anime industry. reviews.text: I must start off by saying that the opening of the film is simply remarkable. It's a long sequence shot that takes place in a forest and sets up the film beautifully because we only obliquely witness a couple of dead bodies and a machete. The film then begins in earnest as a striking fifty-something man named Vargas gets released from jail in provincial Argentina and starts to look for his adult daughter who apparently lives in an even more remote area. It's a very physical journey, and director Lisandro Alonso keeps the film as such. Vargas, played by a non-pro actor, knows the life outdoors like the back of his hand and it's simply fascinating to watch this quiet, reserved man go about his business. This is a subtly harrowing film and I couldn't recommend it strongly enough.

When their background comes to light they have to face the discomfort of the locals, the identity crisis this brings up in their children and ultimately the acceptance of the…

reviews.author: AntoniusBlock7
reviews.text: There are many who regard 1939 as an amazing year for Hollywood filmmaking, with ‘Gone With the Wind’ of course cited as a part of that. What a contrast this film is, made just ten years later in 1949. GWTW had incredibly lavish production value and major star power, but was based on a novel propagating the Southern myths about the Civil War and among other things, glamorizing slavery. ‘Lost Boundaries’ is quite humble by comparison, but dared to confront white supremacy in America, and most notably, in a northern state (though interestingly, changed the ending of the real-life family, thus doing a bit of glamorizing of its own, but I’m getting a little ahead of myself here).

Their stories are charmingly low-stakes and rife with contemporary pop culture references ("Terminator 2"! Madonna! Garfield, lots and lots of Garfield), with Stephen Chow offering a blend of zany visual gags and comically over-exaggerated martial arts action. I don't watch older Chow comedies as often as I could, simply because I'm not looking forward to the day when I run out of them.

reviews.text: From Curt Siodmak, the man behind the screenplays of many 1940s Universal monster movies (The Invisible Man Returns and The Wolf Man, to name just two) comes this spectacularly-silly jungle picture that feels as if it's been ripped from the pulpy pages of a men's adventure magazine. From the very first frames of the film when we meet a jungle girl (Brazilian actress/singer Yara Lex in her debut) painted in green as she looks at the viewer and sings wordless soprano notes over a menacing score, we know what we're in for: this is the world of exotica, where danger and beauty and intrigue coexist. It's a Martin Denny album come to life. The ritual of the savage awaits!

Bad movie fans should be much more appreciative and would have a great evening pairing this with the similar QUEEN OF OUTER SPACE. LOVE SLAVES OF THE AMAZON was apparently never on home video anywhere before Kino Lorber issued their Blu-ray, though the lack of notable special features suggests that even they weren't sure the world was quite ready still.

reviews.text: i think it's ultimately a bit too writerly (i was not surprised to see this was adapted from a play) but was still fairly impressed by the ease with which it adds code-switching and identity politics to the taut, gaslight thriller. the weaponization of ideological ambiguity and social dynamics into larger ideas of political/personal expectations is solid, the performances are a little more complicated than the writing is and it most impressively has very few illusions of grandeur. a couple of scenes reveal a bit too much of the game ("our lives didn't have to be a political statement") but the film ends appropriately on notes of confusion and ambivalence, offering very few answers to its many questions on racial stereotypes, cultural assimilation, and liberal respectability; only a slow ramping of unsettling contradictions.

reviews.author: Kevin Y
reviews.text: It’s a very interesting premise delivered by very capable performers, but this is another example of a premise stretched thin when converted from play to screenplay. I like everything the film explores as ideas - most notably performative black masculinity and the ways in which it is shaped by white anxieties and biases. However, the film slowly but surely loses control of the plot until it’s spinning in place, with nothing new or interesting added to the story beyond superficially tense confrontations. It therefore ends in a place that is more muddled than purposefully ambiguous or provocative. I’m also not a fan of its treatment of mental illness, which comes across as dismissive and driven by shock value. Overall the film has plenty of great moments, but it can’t get beyond its own trappings on the whole.

reviews.author: Greta T. Narrator
reviews.text: Starting with the positive, Bill Pullman is kind of fantastic in this as a cop who resents every action devoted to his job. He's also the only person involved with this who understood what tone to go for (certainly Travolta doesn't, giving a performance as a TV weatherman that seems to have been inspired by never having seen a weatherman nor having interacted with another human). This movie clearly hates its characters and yet refuses to just let them be bastards, even giving most of them incongruously happy endings. And the plot around them gets violent bizarrely early and yet the whole thing is paced so jauntily (and scored with such banal pop hits and generic wacky-comedy music) that there's never a sense of threat even when skulls are getting caved in. It's all just faintly baffling, a combination of mean-spirited and anodyne never before seen in cinema.

reviews.text: Compared to a Ken Russell film like Lisztomania, Mahler feels downright normal, though it has its moments of bizarre visual splendor and political provocation that are what Russell is probably best known for today. Perhaps because of his penchant for maximalism through Christian iconography, perverse displays of sexuality, and silent cinema aesthetics, the more tempered but equally as strong and impactful side of Russell's work that is rooted in 19th and early 20th century literary and musical movements gets less recognition. Mahler fits snugly between The Music Lovers, Russell's Tchaikovsky biopic that is more rooted in reality, and the aforementioned Lisztomania, Russell's Liszt biopic that starts off the rails and only gets wilder. Appropriately, Mahler was released before Lisztomania and…

reviews.text: You don't get "making of" films like this anymore, much less ones among masters. This is not a studio dictated, bonus materials featurette where actors speak vaguely in front of well lit portions of the set. No, Making 'The Shining' is breathtakingly candid. Vivian Kubrick captures the humor, anguish, and romanticism of movie-making. It gives tangibility to the legend that is Kubrick and the genius that is Jack. To be on the ground with them and see them as exhausted, working humans is a real treat. It feels like peeking from behind a curtain and gazing into the mystique of one of the greatest American films.

This certainly has less humour than most of Burt Reynolds' usual films and it is a straightforward action pic that follows a number of genre conventions but does so in an enjoyable fashion and little fuss. The 92-minute runtime means that there isn't much fat on the bones here and Reynolds leads a solid cast who all do their jobs well even though the story is pretty bland and average. It does have the benefit of having some nicely helmed violence that fulfills the tagline's promise of being "ex-plosive" (love it when a movie's blood squibs make it look like someone gets chunks blown out of them when they're shot) which adds more to Malone as a suitably fun, if extremely standard, action flick.

reviews.text: "Sie nannten ihn Gringo" ist ein billig produzierter aber trotzdem recht unterhaltsamer kleiner Eurowestern mit klasse Besetzung. Die Geschichte ist allerdings nicht besonders originell und spult das im Eurowestern oft gebrauchte Schema des von Banditen terrorisierten Städtchens ab, wobei auch ein fieser Oberschurke, der sich im Hintergrund hält und von dort aus die Operationen leitet, nicht fehlen darf. Wie bei solchen Filmen üblich, kann man natürlich von Anfang an nicht nur ahnen wer dieser Bösewicht am Ende sein wird. Der Plot ist also ziemlich simpel gehalten und sehr leicht zu durchschauen. Natürlich orientiert sich der Film noch sehr stark an den amerikanischen Vorbildern oder den Winnetoufilmen, kann so gut wie keine Spaghetti-Elemente vorweisen, ist aber solide inszeniert und glänzt, wie schon erwähnt, mit einer hervorragenden Besetzung. Ich persönlich bewerte diesen Eurowestern als ein relativ naives Cowboyfilmchen, das man sich allerdings ohne Bedenken anschauen kann. Explosive Hochspannung kann man nun nicht erwarten aber unterhaltsam ist der Film auf jeden Fall.

reviews.text: In his most obscure movie since about 1970, Jack Nicholson plays a sketchy, womanizing guard dog trainer. If Nicholson didn't have A Few Good Men right around the corner and As Good As It Gets five years later, this is when you might have started to write him off as movie star and counterculture icon. Here, he's mostly just coasting on his signature personality of charming devil and while that persona historically has taken us far and would continue to do so for decades, it doesn't help Man Trouble much. Nor does a fairly stacked cast that includes Ellen Barkin as leading lady and Harry Dean Stanton, Beverly D'Angelo, Michael McKean, and Veronica Cartwright filling supporting roles.

Regardless of its merits as a movie, the fact that it even exists in such a dire time for animated cinema is something worth celebrating. It was only a few years ago, in August 2014, when the peerless Studio Ghibli announced it was re-evaluating its future in the wake of financial hardships and Hayao Miyazaki’s supposed retirement — the move seemed to confirm the collective fear that the world’s most consistently brilliant film studio was lost without the visionary storyteller responsible for so much of its immortal output.

reviews.text: The great pleasure of historical biopics often lies in their visceral power to remind us that history is always personal for those who make it. From the Middle Ages to our first walk on the Moon — from Jesus of Nazareth to Freddie of Kensington — even the most mythic figures were flesh before they were folklore. Josie Rourke’s “Mary Queen of Scots” is an epic look at the intimate frustrations of two massively powerful young women who spend most of their energy navigating between who they are and what they represent.

reviews.text: A man is set up to dream, to keep moving, looking for something until satisfaction just arrives in the simplest of ways. From Melvin and Howard nocturnal meeting on, Jonathan Demme keeps a visual style that is never artificial but is also embbed of a film fable quality. Warm and funny and never condescending to its characters. Much more than other major American auteur films of 1980, Melvin and Howard does feels like a true end point for 70’s American cinema.

reviews.author: Chris Cabin
reviews.text: One thing that always sticks out to me about Demme is how unburdened his films feel. Any other director makes a film like this and you feel the gears turning the entire time, attempting to logically explain the actions of the characters and the turns of the plot so everyone understands. Demme never did that and the result is that his films feel completely untamed and without a pre-set narrative destination, both in how they are shot, paced, and scripted. Someone needs to put this out on Blu-ray as soon as is humanly possible.

He’s supposed to drive main plot lines but never understands how to inject any form of energy, enthusiasm or convincing heartbreak into the film. He is this semi-handsome loser who makes bad decisions that don’t ever feel justified and they never feel exciting despite how “shocking” they’re said to be. Paul Le Mat’s performance is horrendous as he is somehow over-the-top and boring at the same time and doesn’t do anything to elevate or explain the material at hand. Mary Steenburgen won an Oscar for her role here and she’s fine as she has…

reviews.author: Geoffrey Broomer
reviews.text: Early Sergio Corbucci western sees Cameron Mitchell as our titular soil sample, who upon learning that he is losing his eye sight, breaks out of prison to put a man in the ground. This lack of vision is a trait shared by both our protagonist and the film itself. It enjoys a similar structure to a Fistful of Dollars - released a few months earlier, and whose success afforded Clay a theatrical run in Rome - but for all the spaghetti staples, the end result has more in common with the traditional Hollywood west.

reviews.text: What’s lovely about this movie is there is no miracle on 34th Street — at least not an overt one (unless you count Macy’s encouraging its customers to shop at other department stores if they don’t stock the item they want). Kris Kringle may be Santa Claus; nothing in the film rules that out. But by design, nothing conclusively proves he is the real Santa either. He might just be a delusional old man. Even the last shot, meant to suggest a divine presence, can be easily explained without any supernatural shenanigans — it’s basically just a Rorschach test for the audience.

reviews.text: Part “Raiders of the Lost Ark,” part “Mighty Joe Young,” and part “Planes, Trains & Automobiles” — to cite three of writer-director Chris Butler’s most explicit references — “Missing Link” is a sweet, touching, and seriously fun adventure comedy about two lost souls who are struggling to reconcile yesterday with tomorrow in their bid to belong in a world that refuses to make room for them. Set in the Victorian era but progressive in almost every major aspect of its narrative and design, Laika’s fifth feature may lack the weight and urgency of the studio’s previous work, but it reaffirms the studio’s commitment to a future that comes in all shapes and sizes.

reviews.author: Neil Bahadur
reviews.text: Post-war moral blackout: The end of the world, a totality in form/content, a thriller more Brechtian than Brecht. Tracing the history of the world between 1929 to 1945: Wall Street Crash leads to Great Depression leads to rise of fascism leads to atomic bomb. We've covered three of these since 2008, its no wonder Straub called it the best film of the last ten years. Utterly profound - a man born into poverty makes the greatest film about how capitalism destroyed the world. Chaplin's highest masterpiece. We're alerted to the first murder by the black smoke of an incinerator - this is the first post-Holocaust film.

reviews.author: Will Sloan
reviews.text: It's becoming a tradition for me to watch this movie after U.S. presidential elections. The last two have been incredibly depressing - seemingly engineered to extinguish any hope that a better world might be possible. Like anyone, I have sometimes turned to art for comfort, but in moments like this I don't necessarily want "escapist" art. Sometimes it's comforting to see art that's brutally honest about the mess we're in. In this movie, even the streetwalker who Verdoux chooses not to kill - the pure, virtuous creature whose optimism in the face of despair makes Verdoux briefly reevaluate his cynical worldview - only rises out of poverty by becoming the kept woman of a munitions manufacturer ("That's the business I should have been in."…

reviews.text: A comedy of manners post civilization. Chaplin the actor has always been Chaplin the filmmaker's main subject and weapon, henceforth it makes sense that his finest on-screen work happens to be his finest movie. Very funny (even more so because of the tramp ghost hanging over it), surprisingly generous towards its ensemble, horrifying and guided by the contrast between the bleakest inevitability of its world view (the certainty that 20th century main strands just lead towards more barbarity) and Verdoux himself and all the contradictions he and how Chaplin camera lovingly captures him.

reviews.text: Eroding pasts and, subsequently, futures in the name of "progress." Jia fills this film with all kinds of gorgeous and subtle complimentary compositions, as any story that deals with the cyclical is bound to do (the opening & closing ones, in particular), but the matching shots of planes - one carrying seeds to replant a local forest, the other Tao's estranged son - signaling the helplessness and agony of an irreparable stasis absolutely floored me. History (emotional & otherwise) informs our future, so we better learn to reconcile the two.

reviews.text: Nothing more to say about this really - but amazing how of all things, how well the 2014 section has aged. Jia at his most Antonioni: the saddest thing about modernity is that leaving someone behind is a condition of it. The 2025 section remains one of the wildest third-act gambles I've ever seen, but even with its clumsy dramatic elements the emphasis on alienation within diaspora - and the need for emotional connection because of that - is touching on something so profoundly modern and still literally nobody else is getting close to that today.

reviews.author: Chris Hughes
reviews.text: This was one of my mom’s favorites. When RKO made Mr. Blandings Builds His Dream House they ran a promotion in which they built 73 replicas of the finished Dream House from the film in various locations around the country. The houses were then sold, often by raffle. Over the years most of the replica Dream Houses have been torn down or drastically remodeled. There’s one here in Portland Oregon that’s mostly original and every time we’d drive by it my mom would say “Oh! There’s Mr. Blandings’ Dream House!” as if it was the first time she’d ever noticed. It’s a fond memory that would earn any film 5 stars in my book. The fact that this is actually a really great film is just a bonus.

reviews.author: Bob Hovey
reviews.text: Last feature from the troubled Fleischer Brothers animation studio is notable as the first animated feature from an original script and the first to be set in the present time. Fleischer animation was not quite as polished compared to Disney but was extremely creative and often quite a bit darker and more risque than Disney (and quite a bit more in tune with contemporary music and culture). While they primarily produced shorts (notably Betty Boop, Popeye and the Superman serials), their previous feature, Gulliver's Travels, met with some success so a followup was to be expected. Unfortunately, the film was a failure owing to it's release two days before the attack on Pearl Harbor, and soon the brothers were fired…

It's impossible to know what the medium might have looked like - and I am not going to argue it mightn't have ended up looking much…

This is a great animated film and those Fleischers sure had something cooking. I will never not bang the drum that it's a shame Disney outpaced them. Disney had something special too but look at them now. Of course, there's no guarantee that Fleischer/Famous Studios wouldn't have gone the way of absolute dreck same as Disney. I'm just curious what the world would look like if Popeye and Mickey Mouse switched places, or if they at the very least maintained the same amount of relevancy and remained rivals.

Adapting from Shakespeare and bringing his detailed and subtle characters along with their elegant dialogues to the modern world has always been a challenge for script writers, but Joss Whedon finds a genuine solution. The story is told in the modern world but the modernity of the film is not a factor here. It gives the film the freedom that it wouldn't have had if it was a typical period drama. There’s no need…

reviews.author: Jenny
reviews.text: Lazy, bland, mostly charmless adaptation of the wonderful Shakespeare comedy. This black-and-white movie has a modern setting and costumes, but it repeats the original Shakespearean dialogue from the play, which has a very pre-modern story (centering on the importance of chastity and virtue before marriage). The clash between the modern visuals and the old-fashioned story is disorienting and doesn’t work at all. And although some of the actors do a good job with the Shakespearean language (Clark Gregg and Fran Kranz are especially plausible), Alexis Denisof is genuinely terrible as Benedick and doesn’t manage to convey any of the character’s wit or charm. Denisof made me miss Kenneth Branagh’s joyful turn as Benedick in his rollicking 1993 adaptation of the same play. Watch that movie instead!

reviews.text: Joss Whedon directing a modern Shakespeare movie?? I'm in. This film was entertaining and witty. As this was an interesting take on the classic comedy of Much Ado About Nothing, it was sweet and uplifting. The performances were great, especially Beatrice and Benedick. Although sometimes the acting seemed flat. The story itself does no wrong as it is told as the classic Shakespearean play. Much Ado About Nothing is my favorite Shakespeare play; therefore, I enjoyed this film. However, I prefer the 1993 Kenneth Branagh version better. Overall, charming, witty, and in some sorts of ways, wholesome.

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Navajo Joe" is a 1966 Spaghetti Western featured directed by Sergio Corbucci. Starring a younger Burt Reynolds in the central role, Joe takes on a group of train robbers and illegal scalp hunters with no remorse whatsoever. This all comes about as a town seeks his aid from the group of bandits, but not before the townsfolk themselves have to get over their preconceived bigotries to work with a Native American. It is with this theme that the film holds closely, as Joe aid challenges the element that many of the townsfolk seek to avoid in their established prejudices but quite frankly Joe is the only one who can save them at the same time.

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: Inside the first half hour of Sergio Corbucci's Navajo Joe, we're treated to: scalping, the use of bows and arrows, and what American westerns have trained us to hear as the war whoops of Native Americans. The twist, however, is that all of these things are either wielded by white people, or in service of their causes. From the start, then, Corbucci makes his position clear: the hypocrisy of an American west that vilifies indigineous people even as it uses them and appropriates their culture is on full display.

reviews.author: Andy Summers 🤠
reviews.text: Sergio Corbucci's legacy has been genuinely enhanced by the various modern directors who've been both influenced and inspired by him. Tarantino's glowing references to him in both film and literature introduced him to new generations of film fans looking to expand their horizons by exploring deeper into the Spaghetti Western subgenre. Most have seen Leone's Spaghetti Westerns, but Corbucci's, with the possible exception of Django, aren't quite as well known outside of the real Western fans. Even as a huge Western fan, almost all of these Spaghetti Westerns are new to me, I'm learning as I go, and I'm experiencing plenty of interesting films, but why did Corbucci call his films Zapata Westerns?

reviews.author: Edgar Cochran ✝️🍋
reviews.text: So, why are so few films that capture the nature of Jesus Christ accurately? Let's throw away the fact that the Hollywood stamp, false rumors and flat, hypocritical and inaccurate characters are always present. Also, let's exclude the religious fanatics with a narrow-minded perspective. Buñuel always exalted religion and destroyed the Catholic Church as the monstrous, almost bourgeois human institution it always represented throughout the centuries. Nazarín is shown as a modernist Christ, and through the surreal and experimental, neorealist scope of Buñuel, this testament is innovation in avant-garde storytelling. It's a more conventional film by this giant auteur, but words won't suffice for describing the genius, accuracy and originality of divinity and faith seen through the eyes of a vulnerable man, featuring one of the most grandiose catharsis ever put to celluloid.

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Based on Benito Pérez Galdós' distinguished eponymous novel, Nazarín follows the excursions of Father Nazario (Francisco Rabal), a priest who experiences several episodes that echo incidents in The Gospels. Director Luis Buñuel is once again in the territory of exploring themes relating to morality, here it's the conflict between subjective impulse and social convention and the conclusive collapse of the latter. Nazario appears to seek conclusive subjective ruin by behaving strictly according to his principles as he wanders through the secularists' world of blights, shortages and sins. The film, which was awarded the Palme d'Or and denounced by the Pope, stikes a restrained yet profound tone and is certainly sober by Buñuel standards; nevertheless, the film impressively illustrates the catholic education he rejected, the imprint of which never left him.

reviews.author: Lexzilla
reviews.text: An Italian schlock riff of Dawn of the Dead was never going to be a bad time. Sure, the dialogue was poor, the acting questionable and it was way too reliant on stock footage of birds. But that’s just part of what makes it so entertaining. The other parts, of course, being the bountiful blood splatter mayhem with bits of butcher shop off-cuts doubling as human intestines and the over-the-top zombie make-up where it was either relatively creepy grey face-paint and gore or very silly green face-paint and gore. It was probably a bit too leisurely paced, but at least that allowed for shadowy-government-conspiracies to be shoved into the goings on, giving it a nice fake depth to prop all the flesh tearing onto. So, clearly, fun stuff from Bruno Mattei.

The production is noticeably cheap and I was not surprised to see the name globus alongside very obvious Israel location work but Hooper clearly relishes the opportunity to make something with historical elements so strange and lurid; lots of castles and period costumes giving way to surreal nightmare sequencing and sexualized, religious torture that'd make Ken Russell proud. Tobe still had it much later than he's given credit for. Always nice to see William Finley show up in something for a little while as well.

reviews.text: The difference between comfort and luxury is an important distinction when discussing the distinction between life under socialism and life under capitalism. Having what you need, not having to worry about dying of treatable disease, starving to death, losing your job, losing your home, or being subjected to racist, sexist state violence is basic comfort that was and is available under socialism in most socialist states. Billions are provided with basic necessities. They might not have access to mansions, Mercedes, and Moet, but they have what they need. (For the most part--invasion by capitalists and fascists, natural disasters, and sanctions imposed by capitalists do cause disruptions, but the state does its best to support the people during these times.)

reviews.text: This is the first silent film Mountie review on Phantom Empires, I'm pleased to report. Abu Osama (a pseudonym) was the 40ish, bearded father of eight children, avowed partisan and fan of the Afghani Taliban. Of his children, we only follow the boys, never see the mother or girls at all. The father is a confirmed jihadist, who until an accident off screen which cost him a foot, was a sapper for his group, finding and disarming mines. The father's story in itself, his dedication to his cause up close and personal, would make in interesting documentary.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: Okko's Inn is yet another anime film about a kid moving to the countryside, but it's an absolutely charming children's film. The visual design is simplistic and broad, but what really matters is the heart of the film. Whilst it is a film about loss, Okko's Inn doesn't embrace sadness, instead being valuable for showing the happiness that can still be found. When it does eventually become sad, it only happens to allow the film to snap into focus and showcase the love and happiness that can be found in the world. For a film about healing everyone, it is actually a healing and heartwarming watch. There's nothing inspired about Okko's Inn and it is really clunky, but it's a very pleasant film that is likely to better all who watch it.

reviews.text: Barbra Streisand joins forces with Vincente Minnelli in the charming psycho-fantastical romantic roundelay of a musical comedy, On a Clear Day You Can See Forever. Streisand immediately endears as the chain-smoking neurotic Daisy Gamble—outfitted with yellow fingers and one seriously green thumb, she seeks out the professional help of psychotherapist Dr. Marc Chabot (Yves Montand) to help her kick the habit via hypnotic suggestion—intriguing him with her casual clairvoyance. When the hypnosis accesses a past-life regression in the form of formidable, sexy Lady Melinda Tentrees, the frosty, dubious Dr. Chabot becomes bewitched by Daisy’s past incarnation, while Daisy feels torn between her feelings for her therapist and her duty to her jerk-off fiancé Warren.

reviews.text: It’s not saying very much to declare Ueda Shin’ichirô’s debut feature the best zombie comedy since “Shaun of the Dead” — no disrespect to the likes of “Life After Beth” and “Scouts Guide to the Apocalypse,” but the decomposing sub-genre has been in desperate need of fresh brains ever since Edgar Wright brought it back to life. Enter “One Cut of the Dead,” a low-budget, high-concept work of tongue-in-cheek genius that not only matches the best of its predecessors, but also lovingly articulates why people are drawn to these movies in the first place.

reviews.text: Sentimental story of Norwegian farmers settled in the US. As a Norwegian myself, that got me extra invested in Our Vines Have Tender Grapes (1945). Robinson was the draw, but it was really the kids that mead this as pleasant as it was. A truly great one for 8-year-old Margaret O'Brien and her little sidekick, dopey-eyed Jackie 'Butch' Jenkins. There's a dramatic climax to a otherwise human and slow-paced movie, which was needed. And that helped make this a positive for me. Very positive, in fact. Showed how much their simple lifestyle meant to them.

reviews.text: Simplistic slice of life tale, the sort that just doesn't get made anymore, unless it has some ham-handed religious message to beat into your brain. At this point in our harried lives and modern society's bullshit, it's nice to take a nostalgic trip to a childhood untainted by social media, which I suppose I can say I was lucky to have. It does a nicely rounded job of portraying the trappings and advantages to simple, rural life, viewed from the innocence of well-intentioned children. Edward G. might feel out of place at first not snarling at someone, but you quickly become accustomed to the warmth he injects into the film, passing more than a few resemblances to my own grandfather, making it easy for me to fall in with him.

This is a fairly substandard documentary in terms of its productions values and could have been a lot more interesting, let alone entertaining. Making a film with the premise that 'Fox News' is biased is akin to making one on the premise that the sky is blue. Hindsight isn't even necessary to know that either, Fox's reputation hasn't changed in the thirteen years since this was made. Maybe if they had contextualised Murdoch's methods and motives a little more and the effect that they have had it might have been more compelling, instead we get a barrel, some fish, a big shotgun and a bad score.

reviews.text: DVDs are bringing about rapid and substantial changes in the way we consume movies, and in film culture itself. A case in point is Robert Greenwald’s OUTFOXED: RUPERT MURDOCH’S WAR ON JOURNALISM, which premiered July 13 on DVD and video rather than in theaters. You could have seen it at one of more than 3,000 “house party” viewings organized by MoveOn.org two Sundays ago, or you can just buy it online for $9.95 plus shipping as I did. There must be lots of others like me, because OUTFOXED has been Amazon’s top-selling video title for over a week now, and the last time I looked it had 133 customer reviews.

reviews.author: Violet Kay
reviews.text: Outside the Law is a genuine treat to witness as all events play out unexpected ways in many flavourful performances. Lon Chaney magnetising effect on the viewer is so evident here more than ever in a sublime double role. The supporting cast, pacing, setting of Chinatown are fantastic in a murky background that oozes that hard hitting early 20s feel. A groundbreaking step in cinema for 1920 bringing the gangster genre into a new direction, adding psychological elements to the forefront. Tod Browning grandest achievement in filmmaking I’ve seen since Freaks (1932) the atmosphere, tone, costume design are expertly displayed and the filmmakers are respecting Chinese culture, for the 1920s in a rarity. The film hasn’t dated in the slightest…

reviews.author: Jim Dooley
reviews.text: Very soon after becoming a film collector (in 8mm and Super 8) during my pre-teen years, I read about OUTSIDE THE LAW as an example of Lon Chaney’s earlier work. However, I never had the opportunity to see it until today on a beautiful Blu-ray restoration. Significant portions of the film had deteriorated, although it was still possible to understand what was happening. It made me grateful for what we still had available! Director Tod Browning, especially known for Bela Lugosi’s version of DRACULA and the astonishing FREAKS, delivers a crime drama headed by Priscilla Dean as “Silky Moll,” the criminal daughter of a noted gangster, and with Lon Chaney in two different roles (most notably as the…

Thankfully the "exotic Chinatown" aspect of the story took back seat to a chamber piece centering around two good-at-heart young people hitting rock bottom thanks to the shenanigans of a decidedly not-good-at-heart criminal ("Blackie" played expressively by Lon Chaney). At one point there's the world's most passive three-way stand off in which each of the three main characters has a hand on a gun in their pocket pointed at each other while pretending not to notice this is taking place. It's remarkably tense and well executed, as is…

reviews.text: A crime melodrama in which redemption comes courtesy of the holy trinity of Jesus Christ, Confucius and a cutesy-wutesy moppet with the most incredible pudding-bowl haircut. Tod Browning directs Lon Chaney for the second time, but top-billed is Priscilla Dean who convinces as a feisty gangster heroine. Chaney plays two roles - a nasty gang boss and a Chinese lackey. Despite what Kim Newman says, I think the makeup transformation for this second characterisation is impressive.

reviews.text: Fascinating film. Dramatically compelling and it makes a 1920s argument for prison abolition. Unfortunately, the yellow face and the division between criminals who can fit into domesticity (good, worth saving) and those who can’t (bad, need to die or still be imprisoned) prevents it from being truly great. Still super interesting though.

reviews.author: 27altoids
reviews.text: What is this movie? Is it a look at the sordid underworld of San Francisco in the early 1920s? Is it a romance about lovers cast adrift in a world where trouble threatens to split them apart? Is it a gangster picture where guns are shot, mobsters are killed and a variety of hats are worn to varying levels of success? Or is it a public service announcement with the most eye-rollingly cloying ending to a movie featuring Lon Chaney? It’s all of those things, really. I suppose I could just say it’s mishmash of genres that never quite fit together properly but even that doesn't sum up this convoluted Tod Browning entertainment experiment.

Its protagonist Suzy, played by Maggie Stride, is a blank young woman who comes to London and immediately sinks into the rock underworld. It's an exploitation film, but a British one, so there's a heavy dose of miserable moralising along with the nudity. It might have been less of a drag had the band she ends up being passed between, Forever Young, not been so terrible: the most lumpen, joyless, tuneless blues-rock…

reviews.text: O filme narra o famoso caso Dreyfus na França. Alfred Dreyfus era um capitão do exército francês, de origem judia, que foi acusado de traição e preso na Ilha do Diabo. O exército, decidido a encerrar o caso, escolhe o coronel Georges Picquart como chefe da seção de contrainteligência. Porém, Picquart acaba descobrindo provas inocentando Dreyfus e acusando outro oficial, o major Ferdinand Esterhazy. A partir daí, iniciou uma crise na França, dividindo o país em defensores e acusadores de Dreyfus, com o Exército tentando colocar panos quentes na situação. O roteiro descreve muito bem toda a questão, mostrando os acordos para manter o que estava, enquanto outras pessoas lutavam pela absolvição de Dreyfus. O que espanta aqui é a filmagem burocrática de Ken Russell, mais conhecido por filmes bem mais psicodélicos. Talvez a maior surpresa é descobrir quem é o narrador da história.

reviews.author: PTAbro
reviews.text: Absurdist satire of the highest order, Putney Swope is painfully funny, ludicrous, and jarringly incongruous. Among the subjects that find themselves under its scathing gaze are commercialism, ideological extremism, and racial and gender rights. Nothing is sacred, nothing is safe. From today's viewpoint, it's easy for the viewer to distance themselves from the issues thanks to the film's dated language and delivery, but Swope's power lies in the increasingly prescient presentation of those issues. Advertising that relies on sex and crudity, the government's role in corporate dealings, and the cult-of-personality applied to nearly anyone in show business; to think that we were warned of these things in 1969 makes their reality today all the more sadly hilarious.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: Both original and obscene, Putney Swope is a classic 60s "fuck you" to the system at large. It's a sweeping satire on corporatism, masculinity, race, sex, revolutionary politics, pop culture, and social responsibility. Putney Swope is crude and coarse, being gloriously incoherent at times as it overflows with ideas and lets individual moments take precedent over the story as a whole. This is low-budget, minimalist filmmaking, with empty rooms and provocative pictures. Culturally this is about attempting a revolutionary set-up within an established power structure, and how such revolutions fail due to corruption or logistics. Putney pushes for change but ultimately creates something as soulless as before. The establishment, such that it exists when you're an outsider entering their world, will crush the competition of an opposing ideology. Putney Swope is a rollercoaster of scathing critique and hilarious execution, a film with a lot to say and little to lose.

For Georg Lukács, its emergence as a popular literary form in the wake of the French Revolution offered proof of ordinary readers’ newfound sense of themselves as agents of history, not just as pawns of so-called “great men of history.” Building off of Lukács’ dismissal of later, “decadent” historical fiction (think: Gone With the Wind), Frederic Jameson singled out E.L. Doctorow’s 1975 historical novel Ragtime as a representative example of postmodernism’s tendency toward “blank parody”: Ragtime isn’t especially interested in history as such, but rather in the idea of history. Its history is “pop history,” a blend of pastiche and stereotypes about the past without any real sense of how ordinary readers might intervene in…

reviews.author: MichaelEternity
reviews.text: Real people and events from turn-of-the-century American history are interpreted through a significant filmmaker's decidedly unromantic, large-scale ensemble vision of very early New York. No this isn't Scorsese's "Gangs of New York" (though it racked up nearly as many Oscar nominations), it's Milos Forman adapting an acclaimed mid-'70s novel by E.L. Doctorow. A handful of somewhat average subplots about life during these times for different people, the relationships and scandals they endure, threaded by a wealthy family's involvement with all of them, eventually narrow into one dominant, gripping story, of a black pianist whose cruel mistreatment by an insidiously racist society sends him down a dark path of vigilante justice.

reviews.author: FilmsInSight
reviews.text: In hindsight, who was better to fit for Easy Rider than Jack Nicholson, Peter Fonda, and Dennis Hopper? All of which had starred in biker movies previous to their pleading pitch to Bert Schneider/Bob Rafelson: Fonda in The Wild Angels (1966), Hopper in The Glory Stompers (1967), and Nicholson with Rebel Rousers (1970) — which was filmed in ’67 but ultimately shelved until its release in 1970 after Nicholson’s breakout success. While The Wild Angels attempts to partially base itself on The Hells Angels — with Sonny Barger openly criticizing the film — The Glory Stompers and Rebel Rousers encapsulate the essence of what a reckless, outlaw-biker, counterculture film, more aligned to a schlockbuster reimagining of The Wild One (1953), would look like.

reviews.author: David Weigel
reviews.text: The subject is 24-carat documentary gold. Stokes, an eccentric black intellectual who married into wealth, had VCRs humming for 35 years to record every second of live television across eight major channels. This was high-level form of hoarding - Stokes would end up filling nine apartments with everything from the tape archive to every Apple product to piles of junk. But it had a wise purpose that nobody else could see in the late 1970s, a record of the "flow" provided to Americans by media companies that demanded their attention and shaped their views.

reviews.text: Zhang Yimou's acclaimed debut focuses on the life of a woman who takes over a sorghum liquor distillery and the difficulties, personal or labour related, she has to face. Initially, Red Sorghum resembles an ethnographic document about rural and rudimentary life somewhere remote in China at the beginning of the 20th century. As the harshness of rural life unfolds, a particular love story develops between the young protagonist and a visceral man. When everything seems to have reached a balance, the story takes an abrupt turn and the film becomes a denouncement of the crimes perpetrated by the Japanese army. A work of great visual power dyed in red that resembles blood and in which one can already see glimpses…

reviews.text: Warren Beatty's Reds has to be considered perhaps the most ambitious, frankly crazy, film released by mainstream Hollywood. It is, in 1981, a sympathetic, if critical, look at the 1917 Russian Revolution. The film focuses on the life and career of John Reed, the journalist and writer who wrote Ten Days That Shook the World. It mixes the personal and the political, spending a good deal of time looking at Reed's relationship with Louise Bryant (the amazing Diane Keaton, more of whom later), while also chronicling the revolution, through 'witnesses', montage, song, interviews. It is a mosiac of a period of time, earthed by Beatty's natural charm and the romance of Bryant and Reed.

reviews.text: I can't believe it's taken me so long to watch this movie, since the subject matter pretty much defines my wheelhouse. Unfortunately, for most of its run time, Reds plays like a pretty stock historical romance, with the revolutionary politics as colorful backdrop. The first half is pure romance, culminating in that absurd montage of Reed and Bryant falling back in love while the Winter Palace is being stormed. The second half foregrounds the politics, but since the film isn't really interested in that, it loses the snap and drama of Beatty and Keaton's verbal jousts and passionate clinches. It's a strange paradox: the revolution is more objectively interesting than familiar romance beats, but the relationship is so well drawn,…

reviews.text: "You speak with the authority of feeling!" so shouts prominent Bolshevik Grigory Zinoviev to American journalist John Reed, a compliment he wields as a weapon while trying to strongarm Reed into staying in Russia. Zinoviev understands that people like Reed are essential to the revolution to translate the knotty, often joyless intellectualism of theory into something that inspires the masses. You could also say that Beatty applies a similar notion to the film itself. Though much of this 195-minute feature involves endless back-and-forth debates and intense discussion of how to enact and support revolution, this is fundamentally a romance, not merely between Reed and Louise Bryant but of radicals with their ideas. The heated exchanges are less about the content…

reviews.text: A snoozy, small-scale historical epic that finds Angus Macfadyen's Scottish King in hiding while traitors plot for his head, Richard Gray's "Robert the Bruce" carries with it enough solid stretches to earn a reserved recommendation. The film takes on history and politics in overly broad strokes while attempting to focus on the hearts of its characters, leaving a story where dullness is thankfully punctuated by rousing bits. With its neatly appointed production and capable performances, that story is suitably supported; and the experience is mildly satisfying.

Not only that, Angus Macfayden's Robert spends roughly half of the film incapacitated and the focus is instead on a peasant family, all of whom are charming and interesting characters but Robert's absence from the story is conspicuous.

reviews.text: One of the lesser known legacy sequels, Robert the Bruce sees Angus Macfadyen reprise the role he played in Braveheart over two decades prior. Focusing on Robert the Bruce's in-between years, after William Wallace’s execution but before his rousing victory at the Battle of Bannockburn, we see him as a defeated man; weary from constant conflict and burdened by the weight of a crown he can barely even maintain. In the central role Macfadyen shines. He brings a tragic air, often avoiding words but still evoking a world weariness that suits this stage of the outlaw king (even if he is much too old for the role). Big mistake killing off West, who could so easily exaggerate the stereotypical rugged stoicism of masculine stoicism into something approaching camp, to follow Mantee, who is just the surface of that absurdity. But Winton C. Hoch's cinematography and the incredible matte painting and set design are the real stars here, drawing from sci-fi book covers to paint Mars in shades of fauvist purples and greens that accentuate the surprisingly subtle use of red. All hail Mona.

reviews.text: Brothers Chris and Eddie are devoted to being great cops despite Eddie's insistence on following every rule in the book and Chris' reliance on the handouts and scams coming his way from the Mob. When they witness the wrong murder, twitchy psycho mobster Beaumonte (Raft) gives Chris (Taylor) the ultimatum to sort out his holier-than thou bruv (Forrest) who is clearly aiming to squeal to the Feds. Which means, I guess, bribe him with benjis or shoot him through the face. Thus begins the dilemma for older brother Robert Taylor in this genuinely compelling and classy up-scaling of the usual B-flick crime thriller. "Rogue Cop" sees the gruff and cracked Taylor desperate to find a way out for his kid…

reviews.text: Robert Taylor was at his best when playing the sort of uncompromising hard-ass he portrayed in Roy Rowland's 1954 crime film Rogue Cop. A top flight cast "classes up the joint" you might say in what could otherwise be a somewhat rote tale of police corruption by way of the mob. Anne Francis and Janet Leigh are both excellent as the gang-moll and nightclub singer respectively while George Raft does his George Raft thing as the mobster. Also delivering quality supporting performances are Steve Forest, Robert Ellenstein (in his first film role) & Olive Carey. Roy Rowland was always a bit of a no frills director and it shows here with the fairly brisk pace and flat back lot atmosphere and…

reviews.author: AndreIron
reviews.text: Strikingly unusual for an MGM noir, or any film of the period, really. The most notable stylistic element is the complete absence of a score-there is a lot of outstanding sound design in the atmosphere of the station and the diegetic music. Even more striking is the minimalist storytelling-B-crime thrillers are often economical, but this approaches Bresson in how much fat it eliminates and the emphasis of Taylor's actions. Finally, Taylor himself-very bold to have the lead be such an unqualified rotter in so deep even his considerable wiles cannot absolve him completely.

reviews.author: Jeremy N.
reviews.text: Routine and moralistic police procedural from Roy Rowland (director of The 5,000 Fingers of Dr. T. and a dozen other movies not The 5,000 Fingers of Dr. T.) that occasionally feels more modern than it actually is because someone forgot to set a music score to the action scenes. It's fairly brutal in spots, too, mainly towards its female leads, with Janet Leigh being smacked around and Anne Francis gang-raped (offscreen, thankfully); where's Gloria Grahame and her coffee-scalding vengeance when you need her? At least Rowland's dialogue offers some campy entertainment in its endless stream of gumshoe idioms circa '50-54, at times even giving Tex Avery's Symphony in Slang a run for its money.

reviews.text: The ritual of Catholic confession is not only aimed to purify the soul of the penitent who may have offended God; rather, it is a warning. It is used to make us remember that evil (and the related abyss of sin) is an unstoppable force that never rests, a monstrous mechanism that works well, always finds victims and excogitates tricks to fool us while we experience the unavoidable ethical ambiguity of life. Of course, I am not argumentative, nor I have resentment, I am just a non-practising baptised Catholic fascinated with myths and beliefs. “Rome, Armed to the Teeth” is one of the most ruthless “poliziotteschi” (police movies) ever made and its whirlwind series of secondary plots, sub-plots, excesses of…

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Rome Armed to the Teeth doesn't really have a plot, it's just ninety minutes of bad tempered Poliziotteschi action. Maurizio Merli once again reprises his role as the badass Roman police captain, this time facing off against a bunch of Italian criminals and an Italian justice system that just keeps on letting them out! The action basically doesn't let up from the word go - so many things happen in this film that it's almost unbelievable. The best way is simply to relax and go with it. Umberto Lenzi's delivers all manner of violent sequences and it's all done with such a grimace. Be thankful you don't live in the world depicted in this film! The standout performer is of course Merli who chews the scenary well and gets good support from regulars Tomas Milian and Ivan Rassimov. Franco Micalizzi's soundtrack is thunderous. Surely one of the best films of the genre.

reviews.author: Ziglet_mir
reviews.text: If anything this entry of poliziotteschi is more memorable than any of the others I've seen strictly due to Tomas Milian's wily checkered-scarf wearin', bowl cut lookin', greasy hunchback walking' mofo. Secondly, I do dig the funk-a-licious tunes that help the film keep pace. The film feels breezy and has minimal expository scenes compared to others of it's ilk. Rome, Armed to the Teeth still maintains many of the genre's bizarre traits such as clunky editing, whiplash dialogue, and strange scenarios that escalate from seemingly random items (i.e. burning crates, ambulances) as well as unique locations (i.e. junkyard, farmer's market, clothing warehouse). The final punctuation is also pretty revelatory, in how from what I've seen, the good guy always has to have the last minutes-long-soliloquy about his reputation, but here, the groveling namby-pamby remains the coward while the final statement is made -- wordless. Seconds later, the credits roll. That's what I'm talking about!

Maurizio Merli handing out punches and bitch slaps like they are going out of style and Tomas Milian doing what he does best, playing a creepy, unhinged sociopathic killer. reviews.author: Dennis Vehlen
reviews.text: The classic tale of Romulus and Remus told as a peplum epic by spaghetti western maestro Sergio Corbucci and starring two of the most popular he-men of the day with Steve Reeves and Gordon Scott. This is one of the biggest and lushest Italian sword & sandal movies I've seen so far and it actually seems to have a much bigger budget than Corbucci's more well-known gritty western classics. It does however feature some traces of his trademark violence, though it isn't as cynical as his later work would be. It's also worth pointing out that Sergio Leone and Duccio Tessari among others worked on the script. Gordon Scott and Steve Reeves are not the greatest actors but they do really fit in this genre like a charm and especially Scott as Remus was pretty decent here (being dubbed by Rainer Brandt helps, though).

reviews.author: AndrewC
reviews.text: This is the first of Sergio Corbucci's films I've seen that wasn't a Spaghetti Western, and while I'm not that familiar with the Italian sword-and-sandal genre outside of Leone's The Colossus of Rhodes, Duel of the Titans (AKA Romulus and Remus) is pretty fun. It's cheesy as hell and the acting and (especially) the dubbing are sorta hilariously awful, but it's enjoyable stuff. The production values actually don't feel too cheap since there's some great sets, battles, and large crowd scenes, and I like the retelling it does of the Roman foundation myth that translates well into a fun action flick.

Ryan's Babe tells the story of Ryan, just a happy-go-lucky guy whom every woman he comes across ends up being bad luck in some form or another. reviews.author: David Conner
reviews.text: With this louche adaptation of Oscar Wilde’s least produced play, Ken Russell solidifies his status as an honorary gay. To this day, I’m gobsmacked that a straight man was able to crack the genetic code of camp sensibility so completely and definitively. And the fact that he was able to do it so quickly and on such a low-budget — the film was cranked out as part of a three picture deal with Vestron — makes the accomplishment all the more astonishing.

reviews.text: Kind of an outlier in that crazed run from The Devils through Lisztomania, but Russell's portrait of Henri Gaudier-Brzeska is no less maniacally ambitious than those other films. Here, that energy expresses itself not in artificial visuals or booming music, but in the arch performances by Tutin and Antony, who take a literal jackhammer to what could've otherwise been a dull or overly dramatic biopic. This is a dirty, earthy movie, but that feels true to its subjects and their environment -- when Russell's trademark visuals finally do make an appearance at posh (Jarman-designed) nightclub, the contrast couldn't be any more striking.

I guess he used up all his energy in this performance. It's another of Russell's helter-skelter artist biopics and I think one of his most accessible. Dorothy Tutin is marvellous as the older muse of the young artist and I really liked Lindsay Kemp's peculiar portrayal of the wonderfully-named Angus Corky.

reviews.author: nick
reviews.text: Instantly underrated. Scare Package qualifies more as feel-good comedy sketches than a bona fide horror anthology. Each sketch can be seen as a parody of/homage to certain horror cinema trope, threaded together by a refreshingly creative storyline, with extra slimy gore and effective, borderline juvenile humor. The quality of each sketch admittedly gets watered down as the series goes, to the point where it becomes the cliche it tries to mock, but it's undeniable that Scare Package is a guaranteed joy ride that's not like any other anthology you've seen before. Highly recommended.

reviews.text: I didn’t realise before going into this one that this was one of Teruo Ishii’s later works, meaning I was in for something pretty wild. I kinda… loved it?! Little weird take to some here, but I have a major soft spot for shot-on-digital indie films from the 90s and the way they look. Despite it making it pretty hard to get some of these films looking good quality-wise nowadays; times like here it complements the whole surrealist feel and dreamlike energy. It's a wild one; it's uncomfortable at times, it's extremely strange in its humour, and can be pretty gross - so it's definitely an Ishii film - but don't get me wrong, that is also a lot of its strengths. It's wonderfully bizarre, visually gorgeous with great usage of harsh lights and colours (helped amplified by the early digitality), and it has Tadanobu Asano being so effortlessly cool.

There are elements of suspense as Banyon tries to figure out who the collaborator in the crew is; elements of romance when Banyon takes on-board the beautiful Margaret MacLean (Carla Balenda) and plenty of derring-do as the trawlermen seek to outgun the Nazi's. A tight script and some nice black-and-white photography help make this an entertaining, if hardly world-beating, little low-budget adventure.

reviews.text: Perfect perfect perfect - more or less everything I could want out of experimental film, offering up a space to reflect and to be reflected, seeing all my emotions playing out in front of me with colour and light. This is a pristine and delicate object that nevertheless carries sheer awe-inducing force, taking you somewhere so beautiful and wondrous and personal that it feels akin to sharing something intimate with another living thing. Stan and Phil are baring their souls here by virtue of their craft; the resulting work is the union of the essence of two beings, and we are all welcomed to be part of it and subsume ourselves in its beauty, humbled and overwhelmed.

Director Hugh Ford is trying to be sophisticated with cinematic staging and editing - emphasis on "trying", since I think he very rarely gets to anyplace worth going. I wish this had been made even just two or three years later; it's crying out for more, and more purposeful, analytical editing, which was almost a realistic possibility for an American film in 1917. reviews.author: Willow Maclay
reviews.text: This works best as a metaphor of the unraveling of childhood naivete. When Uncle Charlie is revealed to be, not a hero, or a twin, to the heroine of the film (also named Charlie), but a villain it unseats expectations she has had her entire life. The reveal is torturous, due mostly to the audience having known Uncle Charlie's true nature from the very first scene in the movie, and this is all brought to light by Hitchcock's close attention to detail throughout, and Teresa Wright's incredible performance which slowly erodes her character as the truth of Uncle Charlie is revealed. Hitchcock's work in the close-up is especially relevant, and that one frame of the ring is searing. A few miscommunications with the pacing and a slapped on romance hold this back from being a masterpiece, but Alfred has nearly arrived, and his confidence is brimming underneath the freedom he gained from working within the Hollywood system.

reviews.author: Tim Brayton
reviews.text: A wholly bizarre object: it's no surprise that it couldn't find an audience, because it clearly doesn't seem to have been made with one in mind. The look anticipates the scratchy, rough-lined work of Ralph Bakshi, as does the scabrous New York attitude, focused on fallen hipsters, streetwalkers, drunks, and assorted lowlifes, who are praised as the only truly authentic souls in the rotten city. But it also feels like it could have been produced for contemporaneous children's television by Hanna-Barbera. The result is at once childish and thoroughly caustic, and the weird sweet-cynicism imbalance pushes it hard through its short running time; it's strange as hell, and arresting for how much it doesn't feel like any of the several things it resembles. That being said, the story doesn't really go anywhere, and goes there slowly; and the soundtrack leaves very little mystery as to why the source material flopped so badly on Broadway.

reviews.author: boardsofcinema
reviews.text: Who exactly is Shinbone Alley made for, and what could they possibly find appealing about it? This is far too childish for adults, yet far too off-putting for kids despite the inexplicable G rating. It's ostensibly an animated children's musical with talking animals, but also places suicide, sexual overtones, and alcohol use front and center. Despite actually predating Fritz the Cat by a couple years, Shinbone Alley's crude animation feels more reminiscent of Ralph Bakshi's scratchy roughness than anything Disney released in that era, making for an ugly visual style without any real charm. It doesn't help that every character is just shrill and unlikable, stuck within a disjointed story that goes absolutely nowhere. Shinbone Alley may stand out as an unusual curio of 1970s animated fare, yet all things considered, it's kind of unbearable to actually watch.

reviews.text: Based on real-life instances of torture that took place during the Tokugawa Shogunate's reign, Teruo Ishii's Shogun's Joy of Torture never fails to be simultaneously absorbing and unsettling. There are three tales to behold, each depicting men who grossly abuse women and use their political power for evil. It's revolting yet is so masterfully constructed that one can't help but look away. It's an exploitation film through and through, but it possesses many qualities that separate it from typical exploitative efforts. The biggest standout qualities are Ishii's skill behind the camera and the overall production of the project.

reviews.text: Shogun's Joy Of Torture is a foundational piece of Japanese horror cinema. Ideas in Japanese exploitation films like Female Prisoner 701: Scorpion and Lady Snowblood, and in genres like pinku stem from this era in Japanese cinema. This anthology shows three tales of brutality and violence, based on true-life cases that occurred during the Tokugawa shogunate. These tales show how men in positions of power abuse and take advantage of their stature; treating women in sadistic and torturous with very little repercussion. What starts out with a beheading on a hillside, slowly morphs into an unfathomable canvas of depravity, think a Hieronymus Bosch painting but stuck in Edo period Japan. The Arrow restoration looked fantastic, which made this all the more difficult to watch.

The pleasure I derived from the picture wasn't in witnessing the rather tired 'seen it all before' storyline unfold before my eyes but rather it was in seeing this particular couple of magnetic Hollywood stars together on screen for the only time, sparring wonderfully well and really making you believe in the shared history and mutual love…

As well as that interesting list of last films during the 70’s of once popular directors of earlier eras (Hawk’s Rio Lobo, Wyler’s The Liberation of L.B. Jones, Jerry Lewis’ Which Way To the Front, George Stevens The Only Game In Town). However when it comes to that cluster of clunkers, “Showdown” is a very likable entry.

reviews.author: Michael Shawn
reviews.text: An okay, but on-the-slow-side, chase-themed western with the tried-and-true "buddies on opposite sides of the law" trope. Rock Hudson is the sheriff and Dean Martin is the train robber. Hudson brings him in once, promising to get him a deal, but the officious prick prosecutor tries to string him up while Hudson is out of town with his wife. Martin escapes, only for Hudson to track him down again, this time with the crime partners Martin left empty-handed on the trail. The middle section gets a mite tedious, especially after the umpteenth nostalgic flashback to their youths growing up together, which are really unnecessary. Without truly impressive cinematography there isn't a whole lot to latch onto at times and the film rides on its stars' charisma. Susan Clark, always an underrated actress, adds a lot in that department. But it's just not enough to take this movie beyond mediocre territory. The score by David Shire is nice, though.

reviews.text: Simon of the Desert is a satirical abstract art film about religion, and as you might expect coming from the enigmatic surrealist director Luis Buñuel, there's a lot of dense material here that's difficult to unpack in a single viewing. The script is filled with theological dialogue, and the frame often offers heavily ambiguous imagery (e.g. the camera cuts from a shot of priests praying to a shot of an old woman covering anthills with sand), so to say this this is a challenging or difficult film would be an understatement. If you can get into it, however, there's plenty of ironic comedy and beautiful cinematography to keep it entertaining and prevent it from getting bogged down in thick ecclesiastical…

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: Simon of the Desert is an allegory with a harsh view of Christianity. It depicts religious devotion as extreme, an unnecessary demand of God. Simón stays on a pillar but the people who pass him by continue their lives. His sacrifice and resistance to temptation becomes pointless. In the present day, of youthful freedom and secular living, Simón's sacrifice has achieved nothing. The film depicts a world of common miracles, where God exists but isn't sacred. In a world of believers, religion becomes reality and therefore mundane. The film also hints at the fakery of religion and the way it is upheld by social pressure. Now the world has changed we look back at this past as just a curiosity. Simon of the Desert is surreal and compelling, made by a director with firm ideas crafting something special. It's a very solid work from a fine filmmaker.

The Devil is played with a beauteous malice by frequent Buñuel collaborator Silvia Pinal and on 3 separate occasions, she comes to test Simón by way of temptation and lust for bountiful food, as a wolf in sheep’s clothing and, finally, sensuality and seduction. Though moralizing so absolute — the movie ultimately seems to advocating just shooting people who run such publications — can be tiresome at best, Slander is anchored by some performances good enough to significantly improve its quality.

reviews.author: theironcupcake
reviews.text: Directed by studio workhorse Roy Rowland, MGM's Slander is an inconsistently entertaining tabloid melodrama that ultimately falls short of the similarly titled Libel from the same era. We get Howdy Doody-wannabe puppets, blackmail and a bit of a Pee-wee Herman situation for Van Johnson when his lucrative gig on a children's TV show is jeopardized by a tawdry rag's publication of his prison record for a felony committed in his youth. I have to say I really enjoyed Steve Cochran as the magazine's sociopathic and ruthless managing editor, a mama's boy - I assume gay coding; would a straight man care as much as he does about ruining the reputation of a maître d' who refused to seat his mother…

reviews.author: Blake VP
reviews.text: Slander is if The Sweet Smell of Success was devoid of all of its charisma and humor and left only with the cynicism. Starring two well known Hollywood actors - Steve Cochran and Ann Blyth - this film is all about the worst aspects of humanity. It's unintentionally anti-capitalist in it's messaging and a forewarning to the industry of sensationalism and tabloid reporting and where it could lead. It's got *nothing* to offer in terms of hope and is truly one of the most dour scripts that ever came out of Hollywood. Furthermore, the characters are simply not interesting enough to engage heavily in the depravity of the situation, so it ends up being a miserable 90-minutes of fear and anger. And I usually love noir films like this one (especially at that runtime), but it was missing the hardboil detective or more acceptably, an interesting protagonist rather than the focus be entirely on Steve Cochran's psychotic antagonist.

reviews.text: Yes, it veers into melodrama and the third act takes some wild, often unbelievable turns, but Slander ended with me as a fan. I've always felt that Van Johnson never got the appreciation he deserved and perhaps I'm just fond of the "friend of Dorothy" underdog story. Its Johnson and Ann Blyth's performances that give this otherwise cut and dry morality tale some much needed depth. Is it the best criticism on tabloid culture? No. But there were enough compelling scenes to make me shed a tear or two. If only that third act hadn't felt so rushed, Slander could have been great.

reviews.text: Troy Donahue is a very, very long way away from ROME ADVENTURE as the star of this Filipino production best known in English speaking markets as SOUTH SEAS MASSACRE. He plays a criminal who ends up stranded on a remote island with his law enforcement captor when pirates attack their ship. The natives turn out to be peaceful and accommodating and Donahue is more than happy to stay marooned, but, naturally, the pirates eventually show up. Amusingly goofy in spots (especially the islanders' hilarious "traditional" songs), but also surprisingly dull considering all of the raping and pillaging.

IVES always comes to mind). Bo Svenson was almost an A-lister just before opting to spend the rest of his career in American and Italian B-movies, and Cybill Shepherd on her way down after a pair of costly Peter Bogdanovich flops with DAISY MILLER and AT LONG LAST LOVE. It's directed Paul Wendkos, who made about 800 TV-movies and only a few theatrical (this would be his last big-screen credit and he would work for another 23 years before…

reviews.author: comrade_yui
reviews.text: fritz lang is the ultimate director of negative space, which makes him not only the master of cinematic darkness, but also of acausality: his montage is not dialectical in the eisensteinian sense of relating two subjects together to express a dichotomy, but is instead what i would describe as a sympathetic montage. via match cuts and elliptical paraphrasing of time, lang bridges together his narrative by collapse, not by comparison; he uses the negative space of the invisible cut to mirror two people in different situations, or an object in different contexts, yet the subject of his frame remains identical regardless of the space that it now occupies as a result of the edit.

reviews.author: san
reviews.text: This is probably the last film from the 1920s that I’ll be seeing in a while, and what a way to end it off with (literally) a bang by watching one of Fritz Lang’s superfilms. Spione is an action-packed espionage film with each scene feeling more intense than the last. The piano score is energetic and complex. It stars Lang’s superstar, Rudolf Klein-Rogge, as the evil mastermind, and for the majority he’s just blowing smoke from his right nostril — what a power move. With an odd but entertaining blend of high-stakes events and goofy sequences, it’s hard not to enjoy this movie despite the epic runtime.

Nevertheless, Spies is more than a match for any of the other entries in Lang’s filmography, and its influence on the modern spy thriller as we know it cannot be understated.

reviews.text: What I really appreciate about Hooper is that he seems to study and research old traditional horror movies very well. But then, he manages to adapt them to contemporary settings. I also like to study and research the old films very thoroughly. But then, you can't just remake them. You have to think how to adapt or adjust them to a contemporary setting. So when I watched Spontaneous Combustion, I started to think that maybe this guy had the same idea about making horror movies as I had. So I feel something in common with him. If you look at the old ghost or horror movies, there's always a graveyard, a cemetery, or an old castle. And that's where the ghosts appear. But there is nothing surprising about that anymore. So…

reviews.text: Torqued with savage ironies and unreal pyro, Tobe Hooper's Fifties-Into-Eighties Nuclear Family Melodrama transposes the threat from without into the threat from within. Spontaneous Combustion is less a parable about the dangers of the great atomic power, and more about awakening to the legacies of damage and imperfection left to us by previous generations, how the choices they made, their successes and failures end up being the very ground, the very matter, from which we come forth, never our own masters, always written in advance the elemental arrangement of who and what we are. This discovery is frequently maddening, that no matter how far we flee or to what lengths we go to disentangle ourselves from the conditions of our…

reviews.text: more than anything else, a family melodrama (hooper is infinitely better on filial neuroses than spielberg, whatever people might say), "america's first nuclear family" caught in the conflagration of atomic flame as it scurries surreptitiously across a generational gap to devour new bodies. hooper has us dining at cafe kitsch with b movie flair - hope everyone who loved twin peaks the return part 8 appreciates that hooper saw those demons first. it melts - nothing else - just plastic; but the charred merry-go-round spins still, our gifted trinkets always outliving us, in lovingly preserved boxes or in landfills. you get out of a child exactly what you put into it - so what does the child of a nuclear family look like? grotesque, shambling, scarred, rageful, everything around him alight with his anger. on our radios, preachers and psychics already know what's coming. expect power surges in your area.

It didn't look like a stand-alone movie though, more like a bigger budget television special where we were meant to already know who was who and all the backstories that had gone before. That was an issue for me, but I'd soon worked out what was going on despite the complex plotting and double-crosses galore. Kit Harrington's never been a great actor, even in GoT, but he carries the majority of the film alongside Peter Firth and Jennifer Ehle. It's stylish but predictable, and this is no Bond movie by any means, but it wasn't a bad way to spend 104 minutes.

reviews.text: The original Spud was a pleasant enough South African teen comedy about a group of eight first term schoolboys at a tony, mostly English and white prep school at the period of time when apartheid is failing. The sequel takes place a year later with the same group of boys. "Spud" (again played by wanly youthful Troy Sivan) has finally achieved puberty (defined by 3 pubic hairs at the start of the film). This time out the adventures and mischief seem more forced, and Spud's favorite English teacher (John Cleese) more melancholy than amusing. But the series remains an amiable and fairly inventive rehash of all the schoolboy bullying clichés.

What at first feels like nonsense ends up more of a Zen Koan, like the one where the monk writes a good luck saying to hang over your doorway that reads, "Grandfather dies, Father dies, Son dies," because that's the natural order of things, and everyone dies eventually. If it happens out of the natural order, it causes more sorrow.

Did he kill an anchorman and his entire staff to get the disguise? If he WAS working for a TV station, why didn’t the Feds arrive immediately as they did? Why was he wearing so much bronzer?
