reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: It's a terrible thing to define a movie by what it isn't. That the subject of this documentary is homeless youth, however, makes it's too tempting to not point out the obvious pitfalls it avoids: It's never didactic, saccharine, condescending, judgmental, preachy, or exploitative. It is loose, ambiguous, well photographed, probably staged in parts (if not by the filmmakers by their subjects), and 100% focused on the human drama inherent in its subject matter. It works simultaneously as a time capsule of a specific place and era and a timeless examination of poverty and humanity. I'd dare say it's The Bicycle Thieves of documentaries.

Many of the girls in this are prostitutes even though they're 14 years old or maybe younger. Many of the girls and boys talk about their experiences hitchhiking, robbing people, getting robbed, getting attacked, and other pretty horrible experiences. reviews.text: Beauty in Hell—humanity at its rawest and most sincere. Streetwise manages to be one of those rare pictures that is incredibly difficult to watch at times, but ensnaring as well, so full of care and genuine love for its subjects. In the midst of all this chaos and nefariousness, there is an abundance of compassion and tenderness to be found. The way everyone looks out for each other, the fleeting moments of beguiling allure and innocence in an otherwise unforgiving and relentless concrete jungle where one must be as wise as a seasoned elder, but savage as a callous criminal. There is no lying or pretense to be found in these youths; they simply are who they are, and their faults…

reviews.text: Had to let this one sit in my head before I could write anything about it, but I'll be amazed if I ever find myself watching a more harrowing documentary all year round. There's never a moment in this that feels intrusive, for you're always in the spot as an observer of a lifestyle that these people had been made to adapt to over time, and it leaves you to think about what could be in store for many children younger than the film's subjects that live the same way that they do.

Herein lies a film where a peevish conversation over a radio with coast guard bureaucrats was almost enough to make me lightheaded from anxiety; if that's not worthy of some love and praise, I don't know what is. reviews.author: Criterion
reviews.text: A landmark of Black and American independent cinema that would send shock waves through the culture, Sweet Sweetback’s Baadasssss Song was Melvin Van Peebles’s second feature film, after he walked away from a contract with Columbia in order to make his next film on his own terms. Acting as producer, director, writer, composer, editor, and star, Van Peebles created the prototype for what Hollywood would eventually co-opt and make into the blaxploitation hero: a taciturn, perpetually blank-faced performer in a sex show, who, when he’s pushed too far by a pair of racist cops looking to frame him for a crime he didn’t commit, goes on the run through a lawless underground of bikers, revolutionaries, sex workers, and hippies in a kill-or-be-killed quest for liberation from white oppression.

reviews.author: Dave Jackson
reviews.text: Wow. I am a seasoned watching of horrible, nasty shit, but this film's opening scene involving a child Mario Van Peebles fucking an adult woman made me extremely uncomfortable. Really gross. While thankfully there's no more borderline child porn after that, Sweet Sweetback’s Baadasssss Song remains insane. Almost plotless, it barrels towards an anti-ending. A jarring soundtrack constantly blares over everything. Dead dogs are left in Sweetback's wake. There's shocking violence. There's stupid violence. The camerawork is Jess Franco-esque. Its place in history is undeniable. I swung from hating it to loving it, from scene to scene. This film is fucked.

reviews.author: Patrick Pryor
reviews.text: Waaaaay more fractured and experimental than the typical blaxploitation run and gun action I had in mind. Time slows and loops and shatters to show the lingering impact of trauma. Sweet Sweetback feels both suspended and hurried, alive and somnambulant, intimate and mythic, angry and frightened like being trapped in a neverending nightmare that is the U.S. of A at the turn of the '70s. An arty'n'gritty distillation of urban anxiety stitched together from a variety of film stock on a shoestring budget that looks better and more distinct than most movies I've peeped in a long while.

reviews.author: Joshua Dysart
reviews.text: Don’t call it blaxploitation. Call it cinema liberation. Call it chaos free jazz energy. Call it the Los Angeles avant garde. Hallucinatory political agitation. Call it revolutionary, perhaps politically (some dispute this, see below) but certainly aesthetically. Call it, historically, required viewing for members of the Black Panthers.

I think that misunderstands what Gatlif is on about but, even if that was true, Swing does not fit that pattern. While the music is central to the story, Gatlif’s treatment of one summer as seen through the eyes of two ten year olds - Max (Oscar Copp) and Swing (Lou Rech) - bears comparison with Lasse Hallström’s My Life as a Dog (1985), Behn Zeitlin’s Beasts of the Southern Wild (2012) or Sean Baker’s The Florida Project (2017).

There are also added forces here - not only the craving for creating life but also one for saving it; for avoiding death. It defies nature in its genesis and its demise. In both, it proves to be a cursed endeavour. The whole thing really works as what it proposes itself to be - a Frankenstein tale with wisely handled limitations.

reviews.author: Michael Brooks
reviews.text: 1958's Tales of Frankenstein is a noble little failure, the kind that collapses under the weight of its own ambition in under thirty minutes and then politely asks if anyone noticed. Telling a Frankenstein story is hard enough. Telling one at sitcom length turns out to be borderline masochistic. The result is a pilot that races through plot points like it’s afraid the monster might unionize if it pauses too long.

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: The saying goes that some people eat to live, and some people live to eat. Juzo Itami’s “Tampopo” is the rare serving of food porn that brings both groups to the table. First released in 1985 (and now returning to theaters with a delectable new 4K restoration), this timeless Japanese classic begins with a petulant gangster bringing a full picnic into a movie theater, and ends with a hungry infant instinctively suckling on his mother’s breast. In between, Itami’s fiercely beloved film unfolds like a prix fixe tasting menu of strange comic delights, the director’s fabulist sensibilities feeding into an episodic foodie fantasia about all of the things that give life its flavor and make it worth savoring.

reviews.author: Michael May
reviews.text: The first Tarzan film was the silent Tarzan of the Apes in 1918. It was apparently a two-hour film, but half of the footage is lost. What’s left appears as a special feature on Al Bohl’s documentary about the making of it: Tarzan, Lord of the Louisiana Jungle. It’s probably not fair to judge the film on half its footage, but that’s what we got and there’s enough there to get a feel for what the filmmakers were after.

reviews.author: Frank Diaz
reviews.text: It’s cool to watch this and realize it’s literally the blueprint for the whole jungle adventure genre. Since it’s 1918 I expected it to be pretty tame but there is a surprising amount of rawness here that you don't really get later on. Because it’s Pre Code Hollywood they get away with some visceral stuff like full on nudity and actual animal violence that feels genuinely dangerous. There’s a scene where Elmo Lincoln kills a lion and apparently that was real which is pretty fucking crazy 😅

reviews.text: I like archival/stock footage collage, but there's almost no way for me to approach criticizing this movie without suggesting something very broad like, "You shouldn't have made this movie the way you made this movie." Faked old-tymey footage (digital with "film-look" effects?) of gorgeous young costumed actors does not cut well with the real deal. The constant, Ken Burns style first person voice over remains largely anonymous (deliberate, I know), slightly dubious, and frequently insipid: "Sally wanted some kicks so she joined the Hitler youth." Fuuuuuck. Teenagers, as it turns out, are the age group always on the verge of being the future. The pendulum of history is heaviest over their head. This pressure and their desire to break free…

reviews.author: The Spork Guy
reviews.text: Teenage is an experimental appropriation documentary by filmmaker Matt Wolf. The film is essentially a narration of preserved diaries from teenagers throughout the last century. Journal entries from the 1920's, 50's, 60's, 80's etc. are read by actors while news reels and archival footage of the time period in question are shown on screen in order to finish the painted picture. The movie is immensely interesting, especially for those who are into history. This is such a simple idea, but seeing it realized in full tells you just how brilliant it is as well.

reviews.text: One of those films built purely around the ability of Margaret O'Brien to cry a river on command. As usual, her lachrymosity is impressive but her character is a completely incredible construction. We are expected to believe that the (11-year-old?) girl she plays can recite by heart and with meaning a lengthy speech by FDR but also believes that mice turn miraculously into cash. The screenwriters want to capitalise on O'Brien's precociousness as well as her cuteness, and want to combine a realistic drama with ridiculous flights of fancy. None of it gels and the film concludes with an absurd set of occurrences on Christmas Eve, making Margaret blub like someone had been sticking needles into her before the cameras rolled. My tear ducts remained dry throughout.

reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: I’m working my way through the last couple Best Picture Oscar winners I’ve never seen, and for the most part the assignment has been the opposite of saving the best for last. Terms of Endearment is a welcome exception; this is a beautiful, funny, heartbreaking movie. It’s about subjects and people and relationships that are all too rare in Hollywood. In Aurora, Emma, Flap, and Garrett I recognized things I love about the people in my life, and a couple of things I hate about myself. No would ever call James L. Brooks a dynamic visual director. But he sure as hell knows how to work with actors, and to write for them too.

reviews.author: anna nomaly
reviews.text: Relationships peak into love and valley into selfishness. Mothers and daughters, husbands and wives, friends and lovers, they cycle in and out of each other's trajectories, waltzing through circumstance, their bonds never stronger than when each party values who the other is instead of judging them for who they are not. Brooks clearly takes that notion to heart, refusing to frame any of these characters' decisions as malicious, embracing the wonderful and often painful complexity of lives lived and lives cut short.

reviews.author: Evan “Raymond Gun-Virus” Pincus
reviews.text: Seuss's only foray into writing for the live action screen ends up as some deranged sort of kiddie Caligari- demented, hallucinatory, and oh yes, very atomic. There's lot to be said for how much torture, misanthropy and general insanity remains in this version, which reportedly has a whopping 11 musical numbers cut (that's more than are actually in the movie!) due to their being too depraved for general audiences- but even still with the horrors left in the final cut, it manages to admirably keep up its wholesome appearances with a 50's white-bread nuclear family smiling in suburbia. I wish the claim this made to being the "wonder musical of the future" was an accurate prediction to the way cinema would progress in decades to come- we need more kids movies this stylishly nightmarish.

reviews.text: Produced by Stanley Kramer out of all people and based on a Dr. Seuss story, this has to be one of the wildest and most inventive kids fantasy movies that hasn’t gotten the reception it might deserve. The production design is magnificent and the musical numbers along with the costume design does what films like Wizards of Oz and Willy Wonka and The Factory Chocolate have archived, and that’s build this creative world capable of immersing its audience into its world. Performances are also pretty good, and the use of fourth wall breaking (especially for that time) was so unexpected and mostly done right.

reviews.author: Carlos Valladares
reviews.text: In my wildest dreams, I didn't believe this could have ever existed: a live action Dr. Seuss musical about McCarthy witch hunts, nuclear destruction, and that mean music teacher you had (probably not) when you were 12. It has my vote for most mind-blowing production design of a Hollywood film: red ladders leading to nowhere, a hell with trumpet-faced jazz men. Theodor Geisel was disillusioned after his vision was made more pop than he wanted, so he stuck to TV specials forever after; even so, the auteur is more Dr. Seuss than Stanley Kramer (who I'm still shocked actually produced this). That means that there are multiple scenes of children being chased by wild animals such as wolves, cougars, and bears. There are also scenes where the family dog does battle with a cougar and a bear that aren't embellished with any cinematic magic. These scenes are interesting simply because logistically handling all these animals must have been an extremely difficult task. I am sure that the film employed many animal trainers, and I guarantee watching a making of documentary on this film would be a hundred times more interesting than the film itself.…

And then the rest of the movie is basically about the family interacting with the local wildlife, who are sometimes friendly and sometimes antagonistic. There are a few truly wild scenes of the family (including the two young kids) galavanting with bears, including one scene where they have a picnic with a full-grown bear who has a napkin tied around his neck. The young boy also picks up a raccoon on multiple occasions. But the movie itself is deadly dull otherwise

Adapted from C.S. THE ASSAULT is most and foremost a procedural which only gives one character (member of the squad time) a background for emotional involvement which is fine as many of these type of movies suffer from stretching out their running time as they try to cover too much ground in that regard. This is a very tight film which really builds up the tension and avoids any stylistic shenanigans (coming back to Mann again). So having now seen three of Leclercq's films which are all really good to great, he's definitely a director I'll continue to follow. Highly recommended.

reviews.text: It takes almost half the movie for the dude to actually go ahead and commit the murder, up until which point the movie is pretty rote, but after that Griffith empties out his bag of tricks to concoct a remarkable hallucinatory thriller. The best Griffith films use crosscutting to establish some sort of metaphysical connection between people or ideas; in The Avenging Conscience, Griffith merges sanity and madness, the imagined and the real, the sins of the past and the guilt of the present.

reviews.author: Matteo
reviews.text: The terrifying consciousness that haunts our coherent reality is distorted in the most visionary technicalities of experimental filmmaking, a subtle beginning to the capacity and great effect that D.W. reviews.text: The Avenging Conscience é uma obra relativamente modesta se comparada às grandes produções que D. W. Griffith realizaria posteriormente. Inspirado no conto de terror The Tell-Tale Heart e no poema Annabel Lee, ambos de Edgar Allan Poe, o filme explora de forma intensa os efeitos da culpa, da obsessão e do tormento da consciência após a prática de um crime. O protagonista, consumido por seu ato, mergulha em um estado de sofrimento psicológico que revela como a mente pode se tornar o maior carrasco do culpado.

Griffith does manage to deliver a story that impresses and taps into the madness and inescapable other-worldly retribution found in the gothic works of Edgar Allan Poe. Earlier that same year, Griffith would release JUDITH OF BETHULIA noted as the first American feature film, and THE AVENGING CONSCIENCE is also…

reviews.text: Griffith constrói um cinema que transita entre a experimentação formal e a intensidade emocional, articulando símbolos visuais, gestos e atmosferas como se fossem extensões do inconsciente. Seu uso da montagem não apenas organiza os acontecimentos, mas materializa conflitos internos, dando ao espectador a sensação de que o espaço fílmico é atravessado por forças invisíveis. Cada corte, cada sobreposição e cada detalhe de composição parece nascer da tentativa de traduzir em imagens o turbilhão da mente, como se o próprio cinema fosse o único meio capaz de acessar tais dimensões. O resultado é uma obra em que técnica e emoção não se separam: o artifício da encenação se transforma em linguagem pura, capaz de tornar visível aquilo que, na literatura ou…

This type of narrative structure isn’t necessarily bad, but Ava’s character is one that interests me a great deal, so it’s a bit frustrating not being able to grasp at the crux of her characterization without the male voiceover interruptions. There are some great moments that give us just a peak at her free soul, her drive, her desires, but much of the film is…

reviews.text: I live for that scene where Bravano tells off Kirk. He openly admits to being a parasite, and his honesty rips off the American-dream-mask Kirk wears. It's not the full excoriation of the bourgeoisie it could be, but it comes so close in such an unexpected place that I thrill to experience it. My preview review speaks of how this film is Maria's story told through the views of the men around her, and that remains a quality that has its cons. It serves as an interesting way to critique Hollywood, but it underserves Maria as a character. Still, the film shows her power undeniably, and that is something that few films manage when tackling this kind of story.

reviews.text: Hands down one of the most ruthlessly cruel and violent feeling noirs I've seen. Lang conceives the world of crime and corruption as a shadowy infection of pain and mutilation; even the faint glimmers of affection and hope here are severely undermined by the visual spaces they occupy and the larger system we know exists outside the frame. Marvin's mutilation of Grahame's face with a coffee pot is still one of the more shocking pieces of violence for the genre imo.

reviews.author: Todd Gaines
reviews.text: While watching Fritz Lang's The Big Heat, I realized a lot of cool aspects about what makes it such a special film-noir. Glenn Ford is insane as a cop out for revenge. Gloria Grahame is in most ways a femme fatale, yet she's not poison to Glenn Ford. Lee Marvin is running around throwing coffee on dames. Marlon Brando's sister, Jocelyn Brando is the type of girl you marry and wish you could live happily ever after with. Chris Alcaide is a bodyguard / possible boy toy for Alexander Scourby's Lasagna or is it Lagana, and I'm still wondering why he's wearing PJ's and sleeping so close to Lagana? There's these loco WWII vets who are ready to throw down.…

reviews.author: noen
reviews.text: It’s clear that Fritz Lang didn’t want to limit his noir only by exploring an act of common revenge; he aimed to expose the moral erosion that occurs when justice becomes very personal. Dave Bannion, the protagonist, begins as a beacon of righteousness, a policeman whose mission for justice feels almost archetypal in its purity. But after tragedy strikes, Bannion’s impulse becomes something darker, and his search for those responsible turns into a unique revenge that detaches from the juxtaposition of a hero or antihero.

reviews.author: Sethsreviews
reviews.text: I'm going to go out on a limb and say that this is easily one of the best noir films I've ever seen. The script is completely flawless. It's brutal, frequently displaying scenes of violence that many filmmakers would have avoided at the time, and it's not hesitant to confront death truthfully and examine its implications. Furthermore, it's loaded with clear politically cynical commentary, reminiscent of De Palma's Blow Out, for example. But, most importantly, it's a lot of fun. Fast-paced, with a number of scenes that had me on my feet. This is just outstanding.

reviews.author: Criterion
reviews.text: Noir doesn’t get any more hard-boiled than this scorching tale of vice and retribution, a film that finds director Fritz Lang working at the peak of his Hollywood style—stripped to the bone, simmering with outrage, and fatalistic to the core. A tightly wound Glenn Ford stars as a homicide detective whose investigation into a sprawling crime syndicate becomes a shockingly personal, hate-fueled quest for revenge. Costarring an iconic Gloria Grahame as the mink-coated gangster’s moll with her own axe to grind, and featuring a supporting cast led by a sensationally sleazy Lee Marvin, The Big Heat hits with raw, unstoppable force.

Chuck’s wife Marion (Ida Lupino) is about to divorce him over various infidelities. She’s looking to maintain the appearance of decorum but the potential scandal sets studio executives negotiating Castle’s new contract into a tailspin. Rod Steiger is especially notable as studio boss Stanley Hoff. His huge performance is reminiscent of young Brando. Meanwhile Jack Palance is very watchable in the lead role and rises to the challenge in…

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: This one seems to get lumped in with film noir - but it isn't. Instead it is a melodrama based on a stageplay. The film is very stagey, reptitive and slow. The Big Knife focuses on Hollywood and moral decay; Jack Palance plays an actor forced into signing a new contract against the wishes of his wife, who wants him to leave the lifestyle behind. The script is packed full of overwrought dialogue and while the cast is great, everyone overacts (some more than others, I'm looking at you Rod Steiger). Almost the full film takes place in one house. The drama is very slow moving and generally not all that interesting, which is shame really as I'm sure there's a cutting Hollywood story in here somewhere! Honestly I don't think this one has dated well at all. Outside of a few moments of interest, I did not enjoy it.

reviews.text: A mixed bag of a post-war military flick. The first act starts extremely slow as the air-trip to Berlin from the States at the end of the war makes several lay-overs creating a kind of compilation-film feel. Then act two settles into this wandering post-war Berlin romance that thought was almost as entrancing as Before Sunrise. There are a few other really remarkable dialogues including one with a laid-back Russian spy counting airplanes, one where a jerk US colonel is asked over dinner by a German date what Democracy is, and when the lies the characters tell each other all come out. This one doesn't have stellar ratings, but I found it found it to be entertaining once act one was over.

reviews.text: A high-strung insurance agent assumes fraud after a woman inquires about collections from suicide. Her husband then draws suspicion appearing passive as their young son is found hung. Authorities clearing his guilt make way for a pay-out, but the claims worker still feels the situation fishy. Especially after more close deaths...Slow burns usually strengthen revelations, but only to a point, especially after this Japanese thriller paints an hour with little intrigue. We're left clinging to touches seeming out-of-place; like the fidgety nature of the protagonist, quietly quirky tone, and a girlfriend pondering life like this is some indie drama. Looking at his filmography, maybe Yoshimitsu Morita wasn't the best choice to adapt this award-winning horror novel?

reviews.author: Peter Labuza
reviews.text: One of four Von Sternberg/Dietrich films discussed ever too briefly on this week's podcast. Seen in the rarer English version (does language play an issue into the German version in the difference between High German and Low German?). Seems like the obvious starting point for the collaboration where the Dietrich character is probably given the least complexity as much as the folly for Jannings at the protagonist. More revelatory than Dietrich's beauty, however, is Von Sternberg's use of sound. Like in Fritz Lang's M, it is a case where the advent of sound thus finally created silence in cinema, and the director uses the separated corridors to create an interesting dichotomy between private and public spaces. The one time sound finally travels beyond a wall - the trap door - is when Jannings's private desires become public knowledge, leading to his downfall.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: Josef von Sternberg's The Blue Angel is a perverse tale of a man ruining his reputation for the shallowest love. Emil Jannings plays a professor, someone important, dignified, and strict with his students. But all it can take to destroy a man is one woman. Marlene Dietrich plays his lover, a cabaret performer who is confident, audacious, and sexy. The Blue Angel is a harsh, humiliating film, showcasing a path of desperation and providing no respite. The professor humiliates himself, becoming dependent on his new wife, and eventually even playing a clown. Across the film, sexual infatuation turns into jealous rage. Theoretically he could be happy with this new, free life he has started, but instead lust and bitterness take…

Then Dan Aykroyd, that wonderful weirdo, writes this whole bible of mythology for their joke music personas and they make a blockbuster movie featuring Aretha Franklin, Ray Charles, and Carrie Fisher with a bazooka, and it’s both total nonsense and genuinely amazing. The To Be Or Not To Be players were the cast of Orson Welles' Macbeth compared to these louses: camera hogs with bulging eyes, arms like arthritic branches, a vaudeville "Take my wife, please" schtick that gets old, fast. The sick joke is on the unsuspecting viewer and fan of Sandy Wilson's 1953 original musical who rightfully expects no shenanigans; instead, what Russell serves up is a gnat-like backstage musical with no Jimmy Cagney in sight. reviews.author: Tasha Robinson
reviews.text: This would probably look like a pretty standard real-life inspirational story turned fictional movie, except that it's so rich and well-realized. The performances are terrific, and there's a lot of passion and emotion to the story. But what impressed me more was how thoroughly this film sinks into a local culture, capturing everything from the shifting tides of politics in a newly democratic environment to the unspoken presence of a cult that appears at transitional rituals like funerals. This is a very lived-in film, a convincing portrait of a society rather than the kind of glossy abstraction that comes out of so many based-on-a-true-story situations, and as a first feature, it's just stunning.

reviews.author: cutandsplce
reviews.text: This low budget "Quickie Western" of just 60 mins was a strategy from Robert L Lippert - his company API made these for 20th C Fox and was common back then as B movies for the intro of a double feature. They gave newer hopefuls like Jack Nicholson a chance to shine and established players like Kent Taylor busy as they neared their career end. Apacheland Movie Ranch was a sort of Disney like film Studio conception which eventually went bust and was sold ironically by a Sheriff's Auction in 1965. Restored in 1990 it became a tourist attraction but then sadly destroyed - burned down in 2004.

reviews.text: In a recent chapter in these chronicles, I expressed disappointment in Nightfall, adapted from a David Goodis novel. So I watched it again and was shocked by how good it is, a nearly perfect existential noir, demonstrating why the French have been so fond of the genre.

One of his gang is Jayne Mansfield! Obviously, this being a noir, complications ensue, which I won't spoil.

reviews.author: Channing Pomeroy
reviews.text: David Goodis is one of the Minor Prophets of Noir. Paul Wendkos’ adaptation does Goodis justice with a mixture Actor’s Studio Stanley Kowalksi-style acting and Noir camera moves, musical cues and casting. Shadowy burglars, great heist scenes, a gritty lair. Shabbily clever camerawork and editing. Kinetic, jarring quick cuts, exaggerated to the point of stylization. A workingman’s Third Man. Two expressionistic and thrilling set pieces bracket an existential middle. The a nice Atlantic City time-capsule that reminded me of the Coney Island we see in Harold Llodyd’s Speedy (1928).

reviews.author: mumblecorgi
reviews.text: Director Paul Wendkos gets his career off to an auspicious start with his feature-length debut The Burglar (1957). This late-in-the-cycle film noir stars noir stalwart Dan Duryea as Nat, a burglar with a small crew, including the daughter of his mentor, Gladden, played by Jayne Mansfield (who understandably gets all the poster love for this movie but is only in about 10% of it). The most notable thing about the movie is the on-location shooting, most of which takes place in Philadelphia, a city that didn't get much (brotherly) love during the film noir years, as well as Atlantic City. Wendkos uses lots of camera movement and some crafty editing to make this film more appear more exciting than it…

reviews.author: RetroHound
reviews.text: A nice little noir written by David Goodis (Dark Passage. Shoot the Piano Player). A thief (Dan Duryea) and his crew (including Jayne Mansfield) steal a necklace in Philadelphia. Duryea wants them all to stay holed up for a while till it cools off. Problem is, the others don't think so and with Jayne Mansfield cooped up with them, things heat up. Duryea sends her off to Atlantic City, but there are some others, besides the cops, looking for them and the necklace. The movie is a little too long perhaps, but a really neat show with Duryea turning in a solid performance.

reviews.text: Bless Tubi for making this film available. I first heard about it must be like twenty years ago and I'm glad I finally got to watch it. Farrah Fawcett gives an astounding performance in this as a woman who marries at 16 only to be abused over and over by her husband (even after they divorce!) with absolutely know help from the police or her in-laws. The non-linear structure is incredibly effective. It starts with her burning their home down, with him in it, then as she tells her lawyer their story we see what she's been put through over the years and the various ways the system has let and her kids down. It's chilling. And still so relevant today. A must-watch.

reviews.text: James Franciscus is the nominal star, but The Cat o'Nine Tails is pitched at the rhythms of Karl Madden's blind journalist. Argento is obviously pleased at having a recognized "good" American actor co-starring for him, and the amount of downtime between the leads gives this a far more classical and controlled shape than his thrillers usually have. Madden, for his part, might be slumming, but he does so in a far more lived in performance than usual for an Argento film, and it is worth pointing out that the other Argento film that The Cat o'Nine Tails suggests the most is Sleepless, with Max Von Sydow in a similar role. One of the consequences is that while The Cat o'Nine…

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Argento had a big hit on his hands with the release of his debut film; and so this second feature quickly followed. The Cat o Nine Tails is a more straight thriller than Argento's later work - it lacks the grandeur of Deep Red and wild confidence of films such as Tenebre and Inferno - but this is still an engrossing thriller in its own right. The plot focuses on a journalist and a blind former journalist who find themselves on the trail of a killer after a break in at a research institute. The film sees Argento developing his style - the action is littered with creepy POV shots and the idea of the observer features heavily in the…

reviews.author: Michael M.
reviews.text: Shūichi Okita is probably one of the most underrated directors in Japan. Only two of his movies have been released in the west, nobody really talks about him or his work (even the Netflix show "Hibana", where he directed some episode and which is maybe the best Netflix show I know, is basically non-existent) and everything I have seen so far, was just wonderful. This movie, too. Feels like a strange take on Japanese family movies (but the family consists of eight men) with a lot of loneliness (there are not even cute animals around). And while there is always a lot of sadness in his movies, they're basically just brilliant feel good films.

reviews.text: A crew of eight Japanese men working at an isolated research station at the South Pole...No, this is not THE THING or even A COLD NIGHT'S DEATH but another entry in the laid-back Japanese cuisine cinema. There isn't much going on here. You simply observe the crew bantering, working and eating. The movie somehow focuses on the chef (hence the title) and him preparing meals for his colleagues. There are also hints at how this kind of work effects the men's family lives leading to a neat ending.It's far from being as great as Naoko Ogigami's films but still a pleasant watch and the very definition of a hanging-out-movie.

reviews.author: Miguel Marías
reviews.text: Mi recuerdo (infantil) de "Little Boy Lost" es execrable, o casi, como lo son gran parte de las películas de Seaton, desde "The Big Lift" a "The Country Girl", y especialmente la "trascendente" escrita por Vahé Katcha en 1963 o "The Proud and the Profane" en los 50. Pero antes, casi sólo en los 40, hizo algunas discretas, deudoras o emuladoras de Capra. "The Counterfeit Traitor" es de lejísimos la mejor, quizá por ser una historia real, no inventada por Seaton; a mí me parece magistral, y no le veo McGuffin, ni se me hace pesada un solo instante, y eso que desde su estreno la he visto un montón de veces, sin que jamás decaiga mi interés.(Comentario en "un blog comme les autres", 14 de marzo de 2012)

It's the kind of film that makes you wonder at its very existence -- like, people actually put money into this? But as for entertainment value, it's pretty high. But it could have been higher if not for the nasty streak of racism that is a plot point, with two characters using the N-word, and several characters actively trying to get rid of the one black character.…

reviews.author: Diogo Serafim
reviews.text: A transient shade, a gesture bedecked of powerless charms, of someone who dies as he lives. There are those who clap their hands in the face of beauty, those who smile, those who cry, and those who turn their heads and close their eyes. Drenched in a sort of cold nostalgia, but one that inhabits the present with an ever so true immanence, of a delicacy almost ineffable, intangible, inexorable. A work full of singing and dancing and talking and remembering and living and dying that sweeps it all into a state of stillness, a ghostly aura of immediacy, of beauty, of tears, of laughter, of life, of holism, of nothingness. Faintly falling, the snow is falling faintly.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Impressively sustained and acted. The entire party is beautifully choreographed, almost musical in how it moves around the guests. As far as adaptation goes, it is very faithful but focused on the way the material resonates with Huston. At times, he can’t resist pushing the elegiac tone too hard. Huston has never been a subtle filmmaker, after all, it is certainly among his movies that the better ones use a certain homogeneity of tone he can easily fall for. A minor quibble to what is otherwise a very moving final film. That it is a final film, that 81-year-old Huston passed a week before The Dead got its first public screening at Venice, seems inseparable from its effects; even the unevenness of Huston’s career does hang over the movie.

Set off the coast of West Africa, shit goes awry as usual. Some military place crashes at the start of a zombie outbreak, but leaves only one survivor action hero rather than an entire group. It's kinda like Cast Away but with flesh eaters and nasty gore gags. Solid performance by Rob Freeman, a road horror that brings about real bleak metaphors and outlook to the table. I'm interested to see what the sequel is all about.

reviews.text: Shot in grainy 35mm and featuring slow-moving undead, the Ford brothers are clearly familiar with the classics of the zombie genre and have created a terrific throwback to them. An African soldier and an American Air Force engineer try to survive as the former looks for his son. While there are regular encounters with the undead, it's a bit of a slow-burner. This may be a turn-off for those who prefer their romps with the infected to be more action-packed and spectacular, but for purists The Dead is a real treat as it genuinely feels like something that could have come from Romero or the Italians.

reviews.author: Jayson Kennedy
reviews.text: A rogue cast and crew shooting a cheesy horror flick in a shuddered hospital discover a mysterious sarcophagus containing a deceased Rob Zombie and decide to use the corpse for their movie. The ill-advised decision awaken the look-alike along with his army of undead minions and so begins a scramble for survival.Like Rolfe Kanefsky's Corpses (2004), this Full Moon production is goodhearted fluff that gives off an inconsequential adolescent vibe. Exaggerated make-up, muddy gore, and spooky color filters made especially impressive by a ten day schedule. Tailor-made for the countless bargain DVD sets it's been featured in the years since.

reviews.author: Scumbalina
reviews.text: The movie doesn't just wear it's references on it's sleeve, it wears the t-shirt, the hat, the hoodie, the sweatband and the promotional koozie. This movie is so obsessed with it's references that it forgot to be a movie. Every other word out the characters' mouth is a reference to Evil Dead, The Hills Have Eyes, Romero, Savini, Lenzi and Fulci. Like a hundred fucking times with Fulci. Not subtle references, I was literally and physically assaulted by Fangoria fanmail. Fulci is mentioned by name at least three times, and then not by name at least three more. The bad guy actually says to his zombie minions "make them die...slowly". . .

reviews.author: KevVanDam
reviews.text: A late very 90's very low budget full moon zombie jam before Full Moon really doubled down on the cgi and were still kind of trying. A sort of fun but mostly run of the mill effort with its heart in the right place. Made by horror fans clearly but waaaaay too many cutesy on the nose references. Yes you love and want to be Lucio Fulci. Young filmmakers break into an abandoned hospital to film a zombie movie, find a dead body, open a portal to a dead dimension naturally, more zombies show up, the filmmakers have to fight to survive and try to escape and make as many The Beyond references as humanly possible.

reviews.author: Joe Wawrzyniak
reviews.text: A cleverly done low-budget zombie horror movie that has a lot of wicked fun with basic zombie horror genre tropes, this fright film further benefits from the fact that it's clearly done by folks with an obvious enthusiasm and affection for the genre and hence boasts lots of neat nods to classic horror fare (I especially dug the Evil Dead II chainsaw reference). Writer/director David Parker not only ably crafts a spot-on creepy ooga-booga gloom-doom atmosphere, but also takes excellent advantage of the rundown abandoned hospital main setting. In addition, Parker certainly doesn't skimp on the blood-spurting, gut-spilling, head-smashing gore. Alas, Parker doesn't toss any gratuitously bared boobies into the mix, but as the Rolling Stones so aptly put it,…

reviews.text: Late-90s Full Moon is pretty much what you’d expect. It’s kind of like 2000s Full Moon but with a smidgen less CGI...well until that unfortunate ending anyway. There’s a ripoff Rob Zombie leading a zombie cult of like three or four zombies, and only two of them even look cool. Actually, the cover zombie looks fantastic, and Matthew McGrory has one of his few acting roles here. Clearly lots of Fulci inspiration (if the Fulci Lives! bumper sticker doesn’t give that away 5 minutes in), but the execution leaves a lot to be desired.

reviews.text: the art of memory. what a beautiful thing it is to be remembered. can’t even speak about this yet, overwhelmed by how much it made me feel. Dolan will forever speak to me, the young formerly closeted kid with issues with his mother and trauma that overwhelms him, his movies will always feel like they exist for my solace, my catharsis. to me, it is impossible to be anything approaching objective, as it always has been for me in my discussions on movies here. but right now, to me, this is one of the best films ever made. and I am so grateful that it is in my life. I hope I live long enough to be remembered, even if it’s not as I dreamed.

reviews.text: Already a radically different sort of biopic than the straightforward Elgar, Ken Russell's Debussy Film uses the French composer Claude Debussy's writhing, melodramatic life as the starting point for an ambitious exploration of ideas of reality and fiction in film, Symbolism, historiography (who tells our stories? and for what means?), and the glories and pitfalls of artistic expression. This passionate 82-minute TV film is less of a biographical, fact-grounded account of Debussy's life than it is a free-form, Werner Herzogian attempt to literalize Debussy's music in cinematic form. The Debussy Film tries to understand what drove the mind of Debussy, who wanted his music to match the precise emotions of the painters (Casper David Friedrich, the impressionists) and writers (Flaubert,…

reviews.text: Until Ken Russell's work for the BBC is more widely available, I'm afraid he'll never be given his due. The first filmmaker to have considered the biopic a genre worthy of reinvention. Structurally provocative, at times visually astonishing, Russell attempts to convey a feeling for Debussy (and for artists in general) rather than laying out a chronology of life events. THE DEBUSSY FILM is one of a number of feature length works Russell made for the BBC during the 1960s.

The Joseph Zucchero (BAMBOO GODS AND IRON MEN) screenplay, directed by Cirio H. Santiago, relies on the tried-and-true “outsider investigates a mystery in a small town with secrets” plot to deliver chases, shootouts, fist fights, exploding miniatures, and other low-budget action tropes. When Santiago runs out of extras to shoot at or cars to crash, he pads the 78-minute (!) movie with stock footage meant to portray Hill’s ‘Nam flashbacks.

reviews.author: teamgal
reviews.text: This Best Picture nominee from 1959 is a middle-school homework assignment, mired in good intentions. The fact that its director, George Stevens, had previously documented the liberation of Dachau haunts every frame of this punishingly long film, and most probably accounts for his inability to detect the self-indulgence he allowed to run rampant here. Its righteousness makes it extremely difficult to criticize, but for every grace note, such as William Mellor's exquisite wide-screen cinematography, there's something unpardonable, like Millie Perkin's relentlessly monotonous turn in the lead. She's a black hole.

I was pleasantly surprised though I shouldn’t have been with George Stevens at the helm.

reviews.text: Beautifully bizarre, The Elm Chanted Forest is an ideological acid trip dressed as a children's cartoon. Disney has nothing on this international co-production that combines the cocaine-fueled golden age of the United States of Capitalism with the quiet-before-the-storm of post-communist, pre-genocidal Yugoslavia. I wouldn't say that the movie is well-made, per se, but there is a certain magic to its particular brand of nonsense. The story imagines the animal world as a confused (and confusing) playground of political messages that its target audience couldn't decipher, even if they cared to. reviews.text: My critical thinking skills are dead. This film has broken and ruined my perception of all that is good and bad. It’s a fever dream of wild colors and bizarre concepts hidden under the guise of a foreign visual imitation of a Don Bluth feature. It’s a film I absolutely adore, but cannot decide if it’s actually good or only ironically incredible. I was constantly awake and alert while watching, ready to witness the next idea that would cause me to exclaim “what the hell?” I don’t think I’ll be forgetting this experience anytime soon, and I’ll be recommending this to society for a long time now.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Sometimes you just cry your fucking eyes out for the last ten minutes of a mediocre movie, okay. Reunions, deaths, loves, renewals, inevitabilities all have their impact. The implications of the last film's ending seem erased here, though, in some ways, and the struggle feels at times like a rehash, redirected from lovers to family in the end. It's a weak facsimile of the original, itself a flawed by emotionally powerful movie. Shirley MacLaine reigns here, and her relationships with Rosie and Patsy especially feel worth exploring. But we don't see enough of Rosie (despite this, that arc is what made me cry the most), and Patsy is less a character than a recurring gag up til the end. This should have been left alone, she says as she wipes the stain of salt and water from her face.

reviews.author: Connor Carey
reviews.text: I bet most people didn't even know "Terms of Endearment" had a sequel let alone have even heard of this before. "The Evening Star" is one of the most unnecessary and pointless sequels ever made that's inferior to it's predecessor in every way. It ruins the ending of the first film and takes it's characters in directions that just didn't feel like natural progressions for them. This feels and is shot like a made for TV program and some of the storylines feel like they were pulled right out of a melodramatic lifetime movie. It even rehashes elements of the first film that don't work at all and the emotion feels so forced and manipulative this time around.

reviews.author: willmoviefan97
reviews.text: "The Evening Star" has to be one of the most unnecessary sequels I've ever seen. Its heart is certainly in the right place, and there's plenty of nice little moments sprinkled throughout, but unlike the fabulous original film, a lot of the emotions of this film honestly feel rather contrived, as good as the performers are. The first film told such a well accomplished, completed story, and not only does this sequel even undo some of that film's beautiful ending, there's nothing really here that is compelling enough to justify this film's existence. Shirley MacLaine is by no surprise still pretty great here and while I do not at all like what they do with his character, Nicholson's few scenes with her are again a highlight. The cast all work well together here, it's just unfortunately not a sequel story worth telling.

reviews.author: Krommedijk
reviews.text: The Evening Star is a flawed but entertaining sequel to Terms of Endearment. It's little more than an overly long drama-sitcom. Juliette Lewis plays Aurora's granddaughter who wants to make things as difficult for her grandmother as her late mother. In the meantime, control freak Aurora (MacLaine) still can't find love, so we have to wait for Jack Nicholson, who eventually appears, delivers some powerful lines and disappears again, after which the film continues for a long time. It has good scenes, but it could have been shorter - with less storylines. Good to see Marion Ross, tough.

reviews.text: The Experiment based on the chilling real-life event of the 1971 Stanford Prison Experiment, is a disturbing watch. The premise alone is deeply compelling, and i expected a bit more from the movie given its strong foundation. While it didn’t fully deliver on that potential and felt somewhat sloppy in parts, it never lost my attention. The prison setting was visually striking, the dark tones really stood out and gave the space an unsettling atmosphere. What stayed with me the most were the consequences faced once everything unraveled. Despite its flaws, the movie leaves an impact.

reviews.author: Tasha Robinson
reviews.text: My favorite Luis Bunuel film, and an all-time favorite in general, sees a group of upper-class elitists affected by a force they can't understand, which keeps them from leaving a fancy dinner party. Over the course of days, they head in a Lord of the Flies direction, sniping and tearing at each other while simultaneously critiquing each other's etiquette and bearing. Bunuel is, as usual, scathing about the pretensions and self-satisfaction of the bourgeoisie, but there's also a sense of humor to the fantasy, and I love the symbolism of the rich being stuck with each other in this unsatisfactory, cloistered life they've created for themselves.

reviews.author: noen
reviews.text: A confusing film. Good, but confusing. It’s pure surrealism, without unnecessary excess. The story is simple, a group of high-society individuals gathers for a dinner and, for some inexplicable reason, can no longer leave the salon. But there’s something in this concept that unfolds into several layers, and the most fun part is trying to understand, because the film refuses to be reduced to a simple allegory. It’s as if the film itself had an independent mind, sabotaging our logic scene after scene.

reviews.author: Ben Sheetz
reviews.text: The Exterminating Angel was a Kafka-esque movie about a group of bourgeoisies who meet up for a dinner party and find themselve psychologically trapped in one of the large house’s room. Quickly as they realize their entrapment, the refined patrons quickly disseminate shifting into their rude, violent, selfish, primal selves. Bunuel uses this strange concept to explore existentialist themes of the bourgeoisie, the nature of entrapment and the dichotomy of the presented self and the true self.

reviews.author: Drew Edelstein
reviews.text: Sometimes I like to imagine a world where the ideals of silent cinema weren't so crudely and quickly rejected. This world would see film embrace oddity and artifice, seeking to delight and entertain above all else. The lo-fi charm of toying with the physical medium of film would be present, and whether the filmmaker would have to tint the stock, draw on the frame, blend live action with animation, or do any other number of tricks to create the worlds they envision, there would be a sense of earnestness that feels all too absent in modern cinema. That the unique grammar of silent film was so easily abandoned is the greatest travesty I can see in the history of film…

reviews.text: I'm not going to question why a documentarian might want to imitate Errol Morris - he's opened up documentary form and content as surely as Welles or Godard opened up narrative cinema. And when you're dealing with one continuous monologue, perhaps it's inevitable that you'll recall Morris in some way (though I think Blind Spot: Hitler's Secretary managed it without too much of a debt). But David Sington's film is a bit too much Morris, I think: slo-mo shots of coffee cups breaking that recall the percolator in Mr. Death and the dropped milkshake in The Thin Blue Line simultaneously, and a "revealing but apparently irrelevant anecdote, then back to unravel the story" structure borrowed from several First Person episodes…

reviews.text: This really should have been better as it has a killer premise - a loner Dirty Harry-esque cop (Gary Hudson) is murdered while doing an investigation. His spirit then enters the body of a by-the-book rookie cop (Jason Gedrick) when he is shot. The cop/rookie (cookie?) then teams up with the cop's wife (Kim Delaney) to solve his murder. Sadly, the proceedings are as bland as the cover art. Producer Pierre David was transitioning this year from SCANNERS sequel overload to the type of thrillers he would mass produce over the next 25 years. Director Mark Rosman had done THE HOUSE ON SORORITY ROW (1983), but he stages everything here so blandly. And the script's mystery is the kind of thing you figure out right about 20 minutes in. The leads are all good though and it is never boring. Just could have been much better.

reviews.text: Jack Nicholson mugging and Warren Beatty blustery in a slapstick farce set in the 1920’s; these two con men trick Stockard Channing into marriage for the sake of bilking her. Directed by Mike Nichols, The Fortune has a sometimes delirious, sometimes labored delirium to it; at worse, the visuals are somewhat arid, lacking vibrance. You might want to throw on this movie because it happens to be a favorite of the Coen Brothers, but those guys direct with an artist’s sense of sheen. Takes me awhile to get used to the dumb schtick of Nicholson and Beatty, but I admit, fair enough, this flick has got some quack amusement to it.

reviews.text: Spillane longing for the good-old Joe McCarthy HUAC days, and trying to compete with the burgeoning Bond franchise. Like Spillane's fiction, it's brutal, ugly, reactionary, paranoid, misogynist, and ineptly rambling. Apparently Spillane had undergone a religious conversion and had put the violent and sexual pulp fantasies on hold for a few years, and somehow felt that The Girl Hunters could be reconciled with his new found piousness. Spillane's turn as Mike Hammer is surprisingly effective for a non-actor, which may say more about Spillane's cartoonish Hammer character than any innate acting abilities.

reviews.author: Marquis de Suave
reviews.text: The novelty of this film is that Micky Spillane plays his own creation Mike Hammer. This gives him a chance to exert his toughness while struggling through his own dialog. Mike Hammer here is a bonehead going crazy about communism while on the search for his long gone secretary Velda. He gets back to detective work after a seven year bender. An FBI agent named Cole has been shot. On his deathbed, Cole tells Hammer that he was shot infiltrating a commie network and Velda is still alive. Along the way, he meets up with a sexy bikini clad Shirley Eaton as the wife of a deceased senator. Throughout this entire film, from its awkward star turn to Roy Rowland’s uninspired direction, I kept fantasizing about watching Kiss Me Deadly (which apparently Spillane hated). Spillane is no Ralph Meeker but this interesting curio zips by at just over ninety minutes.

reviews.text: Looking in retrospect, the film's depiction of the persecution of Jews is quite shocking. It becomes rather disturbing and also ironic when you consider that it was made in Germany in the early 20s. For that reason alone, I do consider this film to be one of the most significant achievements of German Expressionism.

reviews.author: Travis Lytle
reviews.text: Whether it be clay figures or cadavers, the idea of imbuing inanimate objects with life has long been a staple of the horror story. From European folk tales and gothic literature, to pulpy American potboilers, horror has long been marked by stories of human beings granting life to things that have no business living. "The Golem: How He Came into the World" is such a tale. Based on Jewish folklore, the film is an expressionistic and engrossing look at humankind's desire to play God.

reviews.author: Edgar Cochran ✝️🍋
reviews.text: Spellbinding testament of obsession and paranoia, breathtaking in its scope and unprecedented special effects that enhanced the sensation of demonic dementia. Magically, Wegener, behind and in front of the camera, also managed to create a fantasy perspective of heartwarming appeal and insightful topics through an iconic image. Pure genius.

reviews.author: Channing Pomeroy
reviews.text: This is evolutionarily halfway between Georges Méliès and James Whale. It has the feel of Kafka’s Prague and Disney’s Grimm. While it’s a cornerstone of German Expressionism, it seems older than the genre or even the medium of cinema itself. It recalls legends from Prometheus and Samson. Its Mitteleuropa DNA flowed into Jerry Segal & Joe Shuster and Bob Kane & Bill Finger and into every superhero movie since. Despite its happy ending and Star of David fade-out, watching this today, I sense the falling barometric pressure and the storm of National Socialism on the horizon only a few years later.

reviews.author: Ben Neild
reviews.text: The first mention of the golem can be found in the Sefer Yetzirah: a medieval work of Jewish mysticism that explores the creation myth through the lens of mathematical and linguistic theory, which many scholars believe served as a manual for theurgic magic used to obtain spiritual power. A forerunner to Frankenstein’s Monster, this Hebrew homunculus was a clay figure brought to life though Kabbalistic rituals to act as a protector for the Jewish people in times of existential danger, the most popular version of the story concerning a Talmudic scholar named Rabbi Loew who raised this promethean entity to battle antisemitism in sixteenth century Europe.

reviews.text: I just now got it. I guess I always subconsciously realized it was there, but I never really processed it. Murnau’s films have a subtle, but unmistakable rhythm. I don’t mean in the editing. I mean the way the actors move. They have a deliberate, but graceful way of moving; slowly but smoothly, punctuated by a usually curved motion (such as a wave of a hand, a turn of a head, a roll of an eye) at a faster pace at the end of a point, similar to the swing of a pendulum. This is especially true in his mysterious or villainous characters. How Murnau managed to get so many different actors to adopt this specific way of moving is…

reviews.author: sirvived
reviews.text: This was a lot better than expected. I went into this expecting a brutal, violent, action-packed horror but what I got is a slow survival/revenge tale instead. But I'm incredibly impressed by how compelling this film actually is. There's a lot to admire in this low-budget effort. The story while minimal works incredibly well and what it lacks in action makes up for overbearing sense of dread and alluring atmosphere of the period it is set in. It does feel like a short film that is stretched out to fit a feature length, but for me its 72-minute runtime is still tolerable. This obviously won’t work for everyone but I highly recommend this to anyone who's looking for a slow-burn revenge story.

As Corbucci was one of the most prominent directors within the Spaghetti subgenre of westerns, most are familiar with his film "Django" (1966). Sequentially directed between those two titles (along with a couple other features as it seems that Corbucci was able to turn out a lot of productions) is this featured film, "The Hellbenders". The film is set in the days directly after the United States Civil War with Joesph Cotton's character of Colonel Jonas still holding steadfast that the Confederacy will rise again. reviews.author: Ben Hibburd
reviews.text: "Bonnie and Clyde" (1967) was one of the most important films to come out of Hollywood in the 1960s. Alongside "Midnight Cowboy" and "Easy Rider," it sparked a cultural revolution in how we consume media. Gone were the days of your typical clean-cut good guys and bad guys, and in their place came characters that were complex, nihilistic, and flawed, whilst having a tangible sense of realism. So, going back to that well was always going to be a challenge. Thankfully, "The Highwaymen" is a Bonnie and Clyde film without Bonnie and Clyde. Rather than getting a regurgitated remake of the 1967 masterpiece, this time around, the focus is on the two officers who stopped their crime spree.

reviews.author: tobe_whooper
reviews.text: In case it escaped your notice, this movie is about selling out. The characters in the first film were a group of friends who enjoyed each other's company, who were brought together by a mutual love of haunted attractions and were having some humble fun exploring them together on their own terms and with their own resources. A year passes, the second movie happens, and suddenly there's fame, money and sponsorships. Friendships are strained (and eventually shattered), the crew is being given platforms and meeting celebrities, drones are purchased, secret deals are struck, lies are told. The woman of the group is the recognizable face; her image is commodified and exploited; she holds the most power but is somehow also…

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: I'm standing by this as more notorious than actually any good. Nevertheless the careful balance here between empty sleaze and absurdist humor is pretty uncanny, one part John Waters/Herschell Gordon-Lewis tacky splatter, one part Andy Milligan cheap misanthropic bloodletting, all played with a heavy dose of self awareness, violence as transgressive performance. Whether you buy that enough to keep you from wincing at some of its simple nasty misogyny (the brain-sucking scene is both ridiculously stupid and downright horrifying), well, I dunno, but this is a bizarrely fascinating relic and quite the nodal point on the trash cinema axis.

It is very entertaining, don't get me wrong, and Evans narrates with a vigour that makes some of his claims here sound almost plausible, but I smelt bullshit, a lot of it.

reviews.author: Will Steele
reviews.text: How I had never heard of Robert Evens is beyond me! This autobiographical documentary certainly highlights the heights and skims over the lows as you’d expect. Mr Evans doesn’t exactly come out on top, but he certainly lived one hell of a life. The presentation is like a moving picture book. It’s stylisation is so rapid and flashy that it feels like a parody of itself. However, it does encapsulate a time of excess and glamour with a heady mix of affection and disillusion. Evans reveals a hollow beauty to Hollywood which he perhaps didn’t intend to, and that’s what makes this worth watching.

reviews.author: noir1946
reviews.text: After watching The Offer and reading Mark Seal’s Leave the Gun, Take the Cannoli: The Epic Story of the Making of The Godfather, a revisit to The Kid Stays in the Picture seems like the next natural step. This time we get Bob Evans’ side of the story in his own words. What’s most interesting about The Kid Stays in the Picture is that the film is narrated by Evans, with some of the narration coming from his reading of the audio version of his 1994 memoir, the first of two, and directors Nanette Burstein and Brett Morgen choosing film clips and photographs to match his words. What emerges is a charismatic, clever, but undisciplined person and an unreliable witness…

reviews.author: Chris Hughes
reviews.text: From a technical standpoint Paul Leni’s final film The Last Warning is one of those superbly made late period silents. The shots are gorgeous, the lighting is subtle, the special effects are handled well, the camera is fluid and insistent and the flow of shots and scenes is good. The cast, led by Laura La Plante, is consistently solid in their grasp and performance of advanced pantomime. The issue for me with The Last Warning is the lackluster backstage murder plot. This was Leni’s follow up to The Cat and the Canary (1927) and it just isn’t as good. The story lacks edge and sparkle. So ignore the blasé plot and just bask in Leni’s masterful technique.

reviews.author: Avirup
reviews.text: Murder, a potentially haunted theatre, group of people where everyone's a suspect. Dusty backstage areas, thick cobwebs, twisted staircase, hidden passages, dark hallways. The atmosphere is nicely creepy with also some moments of campy humour. Leni's direction is terrific, there's some really good stylistic flourishes with fine use of odd camera angles and precise camera movements. Overall the plot is stupid but with its moments of spookiness and character centric gags , it moves along at a great rhythm. It's entertaining and equally creative. Another Leni gem. Shame he died so young, this was his final picture.

reviews.author: Tim Brayton
reviews.text: The cobbled-together print that Universal restored in 2016, from what presumably must have been the best available elements, looks like it was used to line a litter box, which is a crying shame. What a movie! The last film Paul Leni made before his untimely death is a tremendous mixture of creepy-crawlies (the film has a world-class spiderweb game) and effective broad comedy; maybe not quite as good at the former as The Cat and the Canary, but I think I laughed more. And this perfect blend of tones is floating atop a wild ride of visual storytelling, with skewed angles making the inside of an abandoned theater feel like it's looming over us and ready to topple at any…

reviews.author: David W
reviews.text: Like Sybil a year later, this made-for-TV film packs a powerfully unnerving punch, especially in its final half hour, despite a preponderance of otherwise timeworn courtroom proceedings. The film opens after the murders of Borden’s father and stepmother have occurred, then moves chronologically through accusations leveled against Borden to an inquest and then to her actual trial, culminating in a verdict. Across this linear timeline, flashbacks to recent events leading up to the murder as well as to more distant events from Borden’s childhood intersperse and become more and more clearly coded as Borden’s own reflections and memories, prompted by the courtroom proceedings.

reviews.text: This was pretty out there for a made-for-television movie. It concerns the real life hatchet murder of Lizzie Borden's father and step-mother in Massachusetts in the early 1890s and her arrest, trial, and acquittal. The director Paul Wendkos was good at making scenes with dark undertones beneath the surface. The domestic scenes of her life with her father and step-mother are full of disturbing vibes suggesting all kinds of twisted family relations. The weirdest thing is when her father demands the maid serve some mutton broth that had gone bad from the August heat. It's awesomely disgusting watching and hearing him and the missus slurp down the putrid broth. Anyway Elizabeth Montgomery as Lizzie Borden is pretty hypnotizing, especially if you ever saw her in Bewitched. Wendkos really exploits all of her qualities, saving the twist for the end, not necessarily terrifying but pretty mindblowing.

The movie has some of the most dynamic, inventive, experimental editing that mixes time frames and points of view, it's style adds significant substance to character & plot. In 1967 he emigrated to Australia with his family and began producing the long-running Dot series as well as other films (like this one,) which became staples for a generation of Australian children.The Magic Riddle was heavily criticized upon release for its cheap-looking animation, schmaltzy soundtrack and moments which critics claimed were swiped directly from Disney films. reviews.author: Michael Shawn
reviews.text: A nearly unwatchable mess of shitty animation, overly frenetic characters, incoherent plotting, and awful songs. The animators seemed to work under the assumption that in order to get kids' attention you have to have something chaotic going on every single second, and it gets overpowering and exhausting very quickly. Plus, some of the characters are really inappropriate for children, like Cinderella's stepmother, whose saggy boobs flop around constantly and who shows off her underpants, among other idiotic choices. It's actually difficult to focus in on what exactly is wrong with the film because every single choice made is stunningly wrongheaded. It isn't necessarily a bad idea to mix together all of the fairy tales into one story, but these creators didn't have the first clue how to make it appealing. It's bottom-of-the-barrel stuff.

In the second half, characters often have their back turned to the camera so the animators don’t have to draw mouth movements and facial expressions. I am aghast!!

reviews.author: Chris Hughes
reviews.text: The Man From Yesterday is an average WWI centered melodrama. A woman (Claudette Colbert) gets pregnant with her new husband (Clive Brook) who promptly goes off to the front and gets killed. She eventually gets involved with a new man (Charles Boyer) but surprise! Her husband isn’t actually dead but badly wounded and in the process of recovery. It’s a well made film with a serviceable plot, but as others have noted it ends very abruptly with a development that isn’t fully justified. To that extent it fails. But it’s still worth while to watch Colbert and Boyer do their thing in excellent clothes courtesy of costume designer Travis Banton. Karl Struss’ cinematography is solid as well.

The main draw for me was that it was the only non-Western Sergio Corbucci directed during the run of films he’s best-known for: Django, The Great Silence, The Mercenary, etc. I gather that Corbucci and his screenwriters depart from the novel in significant ways, especially in its setting and ending. I also get the feeling that Corbucci was more interested in the novel’s Gothic elements than in its melodrama. But Hugo was a good storyteller, and the bones of…

reviews.author: Stephen M
reviews.text: It's hard to unfavorably compare this Corbucci adaptation with the classic 1928 silent film by Paul Leni of Victor Hugo's novel. For one thing, it's moved back in time to Renaissance Italy, throws in the Borgias, and is turned into a swashbuckler adventure film. In fact, Victor Hugo's not even mentioned in the credits. But in spite of all the swordfights, torture scenes and steamy sex, it's rather stodgy and boring.

reviews.author: Scott Kelly
reviews.text: Franco-Italian Saturday afternoon matinee swashbuckler in the fun for the whole family vein. Spaghetti Western maestro Sergio Corbucci in the same year of Django helms (though he really touched on many genres) a flick that riffs, rather loosely, on the Victor Hugo source and it stars, in a dual role (Prisoner of Zenda vibes), pretty boy Alain Delon-lite Jean Sorel. Commentators on this one are surprisingly harsh (IMDb - 4.5!) largely resenting the fact that it’s not a patch on Paul Leni’s 1928 stone cold classic silent film version of the Hugo tale featuring Conrad Veidt. “It’s not that bad” is hardly an unqualified recommendation, but it’s a passable time waster and you won’t sprain any brain muscles.

reviews.text: Tonal shift is not uncommon to films that dare to give something else to their audiences. But what happens if the film's tone drastically change not because it wants to provide with something the audience is not expecting but to stray away from the themes it started? It's as if "The Man with the Iron Heart" suddenly does not want anything to do with its premise so it can be on the side of righteousness. And while you're at it, throw a romance, no make it two, one depicting the love between a man and a woman and the other depicting the platonic love between two friends who are trying to survive the horros of one of mankind's worst times. It started so well and it was going on a great path, surprising me a lot. The end result is not as good as the first half.

My low rating is mainly due to the fact that I didn't want to continue the film due to its redundancy, however, while I normally enjoy and am fascinated by films that depict Nazi history, the parts I saw did nothing for me. The way Heydrich's life was documented had no real consistency or a good narrative flow. The cinematography was fantastic though.

reviews.author: Scott Tobias
reviews.text: Just ignore the rating. It's not important. The Manitou is not what you'd call a "good" film. It is, however, some kind of batshit wonderful. In a way, the premise compels it to be crazy: How can you make a movie about a 400-year-old Native American shaman who appears in the form of a tumor-fetus on someone's neck and have it turn out any other way? But still, it didn't have to have Tony Curtis as a sham psychic who reads tarot cards in a wizard's robe or Burgess Meredith as a hirsute anthropologist or a 20-minute climax in a star field that looks strikingly inexpensive. So hats off to you, The Manitou.

reviews.text: Basically riddled with spoilers so read on with that in mind. Similar to the story in Rosemary's Baby, a husband (Alan Alda) with a beautiful wife (Jacqueline Bisset) gets involved with a satanic cult, this time led by a dying concert pianist (Curt Jurgens) who sees the young man's body as the right "vehicle" in which to transplant his doomed soul. Barbara Parkins is pretty impressive as Jurgen's daughter. Her body is possessed by the soul of his dead wife. The old man now gets to be the husband of Alda's beautiful wife played by Bisset, but in a merely temporary arrangement, as she's more of an obstacle, though Alda's sex drive has been supercharged and Bisset falls in love with the new incarnation, setting up a nasty showdown with Parkins. This almost equals Rosemary's Baby under the skillful direction of the underrated Paul Wendkos.

reviews.text: There’s an old film-critic proverb—maybe Manny Farber said it first?—Never waste your time writing breathlessly about the latest record-shattering numbers at the Chinese box office, because your sentence might be outdated by the time you put a period on it. Way back in late January—in this very magazine—I wrote about a film called Monster Hunt, which had just become the highest-grossing blockbuster in China’s history. And while a month ago it was hard to imagine that anything could ever top that fantasy adventure about a small-town mayor who gives birth to a vampiric radish creature, I simply didn’t know that Kung Fu Hustle director Stephen Chow had a 3-D mermaid message movie waiting in the wings.

reviews.author: Sean Gilman
reviews.text: With an engaging mix of goofy comedy, charming romance and a heartfelt, if somewhat trite, message of ecological sanity, Stephen Chow’s The Mermaid has achieved massive financial success. After less than two weeks in release, it has become the highest-grossing Chinese language film in history, soaring past last summer’s Monster Hunt. The story of a mermaid sent by her people to assassinate the real estate developer who has been trashing their home waters, but who instead falls in love with the guy and leads him to a new ecological awareness, the film lacks much of the anarchic edge or verbal dexterity of Chow’s early mo lei tau comedies, or the transcendent martial arts climaxes of his Shaolin Soccer and Kung…

Wes escapes and then sets out to track down the miscreants. Then he returns home to his loving ma (Myra Marsh) and bankteller brother, Tom (William Ching), after being away for five years doing stuff. His sweetie, Rela (Barbara Stanwyck) has been waiting patiently, though Tom longs for her big time. Then Wes’s old pal…

reviews.text: A thrilling Z-grade pulp adventure, and the ultimate Women-in-Prison film, transforming from quasi-feminist exploitation into full-on anti-patriarchal rebellion. These are tough, resourceful, violent women. They're all Black, there's no sexy white heroine and no junkie character. Most importantly they haven't been railroaded by a rigged system; they're deliberately risking themselves to blow up the institution from the inside. No victims. No kinky lesbian warden. About halfway through they burn the place to the ground and take off into the jungle and it becomes an action revenge picture. The girls bust out of the joint and never look back.

It shows us that although Stephen Chow doesn't film in Cantonese anymore because he wants to recruit new talents in the industry and because of funding issues, he's still essentially a Hong Konger, making films in Mandarin with his Hong Kong heart. I give you some examples - there're plenty of sarcasms in the film, from mainlanders' obsession with plastic surgery, selfie, to skin-deep beauty. And you seldom find a mainland Chinese film…

reviews.text: Canadian animated film of the Nutcracker directed by Paul Schibli (The Christmas Racoons) is fairly faithful to the E.T.A. Hoffmann novella while keeping the music cues and minimal set pieces of the ballet. An all star voice cast includes Megan Follows, Kiefer Sutherland, Peter O'Toole and Phyllis Diller. The main animation style looks similar to Disney efforts of the 80s as they were transitioning into their more modern style. There is a drastic departure for a lengthy flashback that makes up the second act, crudely sketched in a way that reminded me of Rocky and Bullwinkle history routines. Where the film falters is its theatrical structure, which feels insubstantial and uncinematic. This a shame, given the rest of the picture's polish.

There’s very little of the original Felix and Oscar here, they’re both playing it like John Gustafson and Max Goldman, only this time Matthau softens a bit and Lemmon has an angrier edge. The “fourfecta” rant is nothing less than virtuosic. It takes some peculiar turns once supporting characters begin shuffling in, but I can’t bring myself to care. reviews.text: Director Roy Rowland's The Outsiders is another of Joel McCrea's forgotten Westerns. Starring alongside the likes of James Whitmore and Barry Sullivan as three escaped Confederate prisoners near the end of the Civil War, McCrea and his buddies manage to evade a Union posse on their trail and are found by a Confederate militia leader with ties to Quantrill. He sets them a task to travel South to Mexico, where a wagon train of gold is being smuggled into the country by Don Chaves (Ramon Novarro). Jeff Corey's Keeley, wants McCrea and his men to avail themselves to Chaves as outriders, offering help in leading the wagon train to New Orleans. Chaves however, is suspicious of McCrea's Will Owen and…

Joel McCrea's lead performance is burnished with a dusty integrity and a fun James Whitmore (whose witty-beyond-his-years grandson I once taught in high school) is bedraggled and salty, but we're meant to basically root for a bunch of ex-Confederates and the casual mowing down of indigenous warriors. reviews.author: NoNameNoMercy
reviews.text: The Outriders doesn’t bother with legend or ceremony, it’s all about the ride, the choices, and tension that keeps building with every mile. Joel McCrea carries it clean, moving through a story that’s tight and direct, trusting momentum over flash and never asking for patience. It grabs you quick, and doesn’t slow down until it’s done. The wagon train from Santa Fe to St. Louis becomes the spine of the movie, a long exposed march of families and Union gold, with McCrea and the other riders earning trust by fighting off danger while quietly guiding everyone toward something much darker.
