Digo isso não só porque gostei do filme, mas porque senti algo diferente, que só acontece com alguns diretores: a sensação de que ele criou um mundo próprio, com suas próprias regras, com um ritmo diferente e com uma forma única de enxergar a vida. Antonioni não parece estar tão preocupado em contar uma história com começo, meio e fim. Ele parece mais interessado em fazer o espectador sentir uma certa emoção, algo mais difícil de explicar. A história do filme é bem simples. Um jornalista que está cansado da própria vida decide virar outra pessoa e assume a identidade…

reviews.text: A fascinating film, slashed through with weighty expressionistic techniques by Austrian director Berthold Viertel in what would be his penultimate film. Conrad Veidt plays a mysterious stranger who fetches up at a London boarding-house one summer evening, shouldering symbolism, and gradually performs micro-miracles in the behaviour of the mostly unpleasant, certainly unhappy, lot that inhabit the building. His counterpart, the Lucifer to his Gabriel, is a conniving property magnate played by Frank Cellier, who recognises Veidt's inspiring aura and morale-building methods and predicts their failure with some relish.

reviews.text: Lon Chaney's legless villain Blizzard is so good that I was rooting for him and his army of Reds to terrorize San Francisco through most of the film. All the 'good guys' are dorks who are smartly given short shrift in both story and camera time by director Wallace Worsley; it's all about Lon. Chaney went against the advice of doctors and caused himself a great deal of pain in order to play this role, which meant strapping his legs to his back with a series of belts and walking around on his knees. His agility makes his performance utterly convincing.The ending is a wet blanket to the fun and the movie knows it. Once Lon has his transformation, it's time to say goodbye as quickly as possible.

reviews.text: This reminded me a lot like It’s a Wonderful Life, except it’s much more sinister and depressing. Everything has a nice modern feel to it; in particular, the performances and the score haven’t aged one bit. I’m not quite sure if it has intentional jump scares, but one scene made me jump out of my seat as it suddenly shifted its tone without any clear warning. That being said, the score may give you trust issues — but it’s one of the best scores I’ve heard from the 1920s, so the anxiety is worth it. All in all, The Phantom Carriage is a somber silent film that is full of sorrow and despair, but ultimately it fulfills this emotional journey to be worthwhile in the end.

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: The Phantom Carriage is a Swedish silent film from 1921, and it's an absolute classic. Directed by Victor Sjöström, it's steeped in atmosphere, masterfully utilising its chiaroscuro lighting to create a dreamlike world that's brimming with emotion. The story follows a deathbed promise made to help free a man of his sins, and is filled with both pathos and hope. This spiritual journey speaks deeply to the human condition, and the sentimentality that accompanies death. Despite being made nearly a century ago, The Phantom Carriage still holds up today and is an absolute must-see. The visuals are stunning and the acting range is impressive, especially considering the lack of dialogue. This film is not only a masterpiece of the silent film era, but of film overall. Highly recommended.

reviews.author: Evan “Raymond Gun-Virus” Pincus
reviews.text: The perfect movie for our 21st-century 5G-addled brains. You’ve gotta be really all-in on 60’s anarcho-comic modernist kitsch for this to work, so I’m probably lucky I saw this super young. Revisiting for the first time since I was 15 (and I first saw it a few years before then) - still holds up, in its own ridiculous way. This time around (benefitted by having seen actual 60’s paranoid thrillers instead of this being my first exposure) I really appreciated the new-wavey editing and camerawork, a more than credible pastiche of the formal tics of the genre, only here geared towards silliness instead of oblique nerviness. Every performance here is pure gold, but Coburn is a live wire - certainly wouldn’t say it’s his best performance, but it might be his most dynamic; he moves like Schifrin’s (great) score is being beamed directly into his skull.

reviews.text: a miniature and embellished version of d.h. lawrence's novel that ken russell obviously understands the spirit of, but the breadth of the book's multi-generational vision of a diminished way of life is crammed into ursula's personal journey, so it feels a tad unwieldy. yet all of russell's valorous theatricality and brashness is a perfect exterior reflection of lawrence's volcanic prose, and the second half where ursula is schooled in the hard knocks of repressive british authority is a good sketch in anger and bad faith. no one would mistake this for being better than his women in love adaptation, which is possessed of a everlasting flame, but the rainbow is handsome and sweet in a way that russell doesn't get the proper credit for. amanda donohoe is the standout player as a bisexual lawrentian who serves as ursula's gateway into the wider world.

reviews.author: Ford H
reviews.text: I recently watched The Devils and have been quite eager to dig into the rest of Ken Russell's filmography, which I hope to spread out over the course of the next few months. The Rainbow has a very wondrous opening sequence that sets the tone very well, and I love how we come back full circle with the titular visual element, which is beautifully aligned with the film's themes and character motivations about finding one's own path in life, even if it means leaving home. Overall, the film is decent, but I did find that it was an exhausting experience due to an overstuffed plot, and some of the transitions didn't work for me in terms of how the narrative conveys the passage of time.

reviews.author: Amy Hensarling
reviews.text: The Rainbow, unlike Harry Potter and the ___________, emphasizes the absence of cosmic orchestration. What I like so much about HP is never having to worry whether he’ll get out of a dire scrape when things go south ‘cause when things go south, they are always moving him toward victory. Not so with dear Ursula here. She must FORCE her direction, fight for it, insist upon it, DEMAND it. So when her lover leaves, the students revolt, the coworker threatens, and the boyfriend condemns, we don’t sit back and say, never fear, Ursula. This is but the universe’s way of leading you to great purpose. No. Consequences do not equal life lessons.

reviews.author: Fredrik Fyhr
reviews.text: Early biopic about Edgar Allan Poe (played by the dead ringer Henry B. Walthall) that should be more curious than it is. Goes through the central parts of Poe's life with a lot of spleen and drang, also stages the title story. It's a relatively interesting film of its time – on the one hand it's a rather stilted display done in that detrimental 1910's style (sort of like a living waxwork exhibition), on the other hand it does have a few nice moments, like some inventive image composition and some early special effects - hardly new or groundbreaking, but on point for the story it's trying to tell. In great need of a new restoration, though; it's quite possible that a restored, more complete version would reveal new things.

reviews.author: Michael
reviews.text: This movie, made late in 1915, includes many of the technical advances that became common in that year. We’ve got tracking shots, and other camera movements (even re-framing when new actors enter a shot was radical the year before!), a good number of close-ups, and cutting within scenes to punch up dramatic moments. Walthall makes a good Poe, as many critics commented at the time, and he handles the tragic moments well, showing agony without overdoing it in close-up. Unfortunately, the surviving print is very washed out, making faces frequently hard to discern, and background details almost completely obscured. I was warned about this, by The Silent Era among others, so I have no one but myself to blame, but…

It shouldn't matter because a film should be alive to both possibilities (or, like Festen, use its plot as a springboard for general insanity) - but this one badly lacks that extra nuance, making its heroine too (self-)righteously victimised, which is a problem when she's being played by the film's director (playing 'herself'). She is a farm girl whom sticks to the daily rituals like everybody else in her village, a time when women had their particular duties and men had theirs.

reviews.text: The Road Home, a simple, old-fashioned love story from Hero director Zhang Yimou. For every single second that Zhang Ziyi appeared onscreen, I couldn't help but be enchanted by her presence. There was something so extraordinarily pure and wholly intriguing about her that I couldn't quite put my finger on. But whatever it is, she's got it and it works. However, even though Zhang is unquestionably talented, I suspect that her magnetic performance in The Road Home is not simply the product of fortuitous casting. No, director extraordinary Zhang Yimou knows what he's doing, and one can see a master storyteller at work from the film's very first frame.

The harsh yet beautiful winter landscapes add a powerful atmosphere to the film; the snow covered scenery creates a feeling that is both peaceful and slightly melancholic.

reviews.author: Quiller
reviews.text: The plot turns out to be no better than “b” western hokum: renegades exploit lingering North-South tensions in post-Civil War border state Missouri by burning barns in order to pick up land dirt cheap. But there’s a depth of feeling to this film that always wins me over — though, to be fair, I always remember it being better than it actually is. I suspect its emotion results partly from its post-WWII context. The anxiety of the MacBean family (father Thomas Mitchell, mother Selena Royle, sister Janet Leigh, and brother Dean Stockwell) for son Marshall Thompson, who has yet to return from the war, likely speaks to the sense of loss many Americans felt for loved ones in 1947.

I found it very irksome. In 1952, the film was released in Britain in English dub, with Julie Andrews voicing the singing princess, her first ever film role.

reviews.text: Switching between the East German and West German sides of the Berlin wall, as well as a listening post, multiple stories are told in parallel and are interconnected. If you're familiar with the circumstances of that time, it's pretty clear which side is shown at any time. Thematically, the storylines cover what you might expect when thinking of the DDR: spying, surveillance, and family dramas, some caused by the former country's politics and people's dedication to them. Given that it's set in 1974, politics and sports are also part of some. Unfortunately, the ending is rather open.The spoken language is predominantly German, understandably, but there are also English parts on account of characters being from the US or UK.There are some spoilers for the novel Tale of Two Cities and the film Don’t Look Now.

reviews.text: The Servant is oozing with displace gay desire. In the sharing of a female lover (Vera, played by Sarah Miles), for example, or the discussion about how both Barrett (Dirk Bogarde) and Tony (James Fox) have felt what they feel for one another once before, in the military, or the way that Barrett regularly inserts himself into the sexual space between Tony and Susan (Wendy Craig). All of it shouts of the existence of a desire that dare not speak its name, a legal and social requirement of silence that crosses class lines, unlike much of what is being explored by Harold Pinter and Joseph Losey.

reviews.text: "The Shooting" is a 1960's western that very much resonates within the organic ethos of the 70's. This is because as the New Hollywood movement predominately resided within the realm of the decadal 70's in most apparent recognition, much it expands to a proportional part of the 60's before and the ensuing bit of 80's after. Within the realization of this, "The Shooting" is easily on of the early examples of the waves inception as its tone and feel simply feel different that the other western efforts that were currently in circulation, in studio or not.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: The symbology of the western reduced to minimalist images (a typo-laden grave marker awkwardly shoved into the dry soil, a figure in black appearing at the top of a mesa on the horizon) and reflective of a modernist approach in which the inherent beauty of valleys and rolling hills is replaced with deliberately awkward framings that render vistas as grotesque and alienating, not a symbol of God's majestic architecture but evidence of His absence. Like a New Hollywood Red River, this is also something of a showcase of various emerging methods of acting, from Oates' character-actor-as-leading-man naturalism to Perkins' almost Brechtian strangeness to Nicholson as a new kind of movie star. And in the end Hellman and Eastman render the conflict of Man vs. Nature as so stripped down that it betrays that such a conflict is always in the end about man confronting himself.

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: Fritz Lang's third film and the first that has survived long enough to allow us to watch it, The Spiders: Golden Sea (IDK why LB and TMDB call it a lake when no one else does) is a shot of pulpy goodness, one which hints at Lang's gift for kinetic narratives as it hurtles from San Francisco society to a roadhouse shootout; from a parachute jump from a hot air balloon to the heroic murder of a young-lady-menacing python. Even at this early point in his career, Lang largely embodied Elmore Leonard's sage edict to cut out all of the stuff the audience would skip if it was left in.

reviews.text: very silly pulp, lang's obvious rip-off of feuillade, featuring cowboys, pirates, spies, lost civilizations, conspiracies, adventure archeology, pagan armies, ritual sacrifices, female villains, cursed relics -- my kinda jam! it's endlessly amusing to me that basically all the great masters of early 20th century cinema like fritz lang got their start with things like adventure serials, which have never had any real critical reception outside of auteurist apologia, but i think the spiders still very much feels fresh and exciting; it's safe to say that spielberg, lucas and hitchcock would not exist at all without this film.

reviews.author: Silversaxophone
reviews.text: A pure, exhilarating pulp template for the majority of Fritz Lang’s future German films, this early Fritz Lang work (It was his third film.) is largely devoid of the heavy social/political subtext of his subsequent adventure/sci-fi/fantasy epics such as Dr Mabuse and Metropolis. Instead, it’s a celebration of dashing heroes, damsels-in-distress, exotic locales, mysterious and oddball villains (including a particularly nasty femme fatale) of the kind spilling out of pages of popular magazines of the period. The emphasis on espionage, secret societies and underground cities points to the influence of Louis Feuillade, which Lang was later able to fashion into symbols for social corruption and evil, but here are merely conjured as colourful incidents and bizarre, unexpected twists, as a…

reviews.author: Lencho of the Apes
reviews.text: Pulp for pulp's sake, more Sax Rohmer than H Rider Haggard. There are a few distinctively Langian touches, and a couple of places where he disavows himself of the genre's imperialist tendencies (highlighting - for example - the way "great industrialist" Paul Terry's fortune has its origins in a 16th century pirate's career was pretty clever) ... but really, it's pretty anonymous. Staging and pacing are the whole story here, and Lang's deft use of all the toolbox to create a charged, dynamic narrative is more impressive here than it was in some of his movies of the 20s.

He accidentally gets sent back to 1976 and must adapt to society in the funkiest of decades. Spirit of 76’ is a zany fun spoof and homage to 70’s culture and the earliest example of a zany decade spoof movie I can think of. Der vorliegende bebilderte Geschichtsunterricht macht auf alle Fälle auch nichts falsch.Schon fast im Doku-Stil, mit Erzählstimme (zum Glück nicht zu strapaziös), die Daten und Fakten zum Besten gibt, mit einer immensen Anzahl von Stars und solchen die es noch werden, wird die Geschichte um das titelgebende Massaker erstaunlich ruppig und rau erzählt.Zur Aufheiterung gibt es einen schon fast genialen kurzen Fight zwischen Capone und seiner Frau/Geliebten(?), in dem eine Suite in ihre Einzelteile zerlegt wird. Und überhaupt ist Jason Robards als cholerischer Al Capone allein den Eintritt hier wert.Keine Figuren zum mitfiebern, keine verzwickte Geschichte, keine romantische Verklärung, aber ein erstaunlich kurzweiliger, sehr üppig ausgestatteter Gangsterfilm mit einem tollen Look.Und irgendwo gab es ein Cameo von Jack Nicholson, welchen ich aber nicht entdecken konnte.

reviews.author: Wilson
reviews.text: Roger Corman's The St. Valentine's Day Massacre is a really entertaining gangster film. It plays like an American version of Battles Without Honour or Humanity, with less honour and less humanity. It is a tally of death, voiced like a documentary, like a 1967 version of Call Northside 777. The voice-over is probably the most interesting aspect of the film. It announces everyone's name, their crimes, their death's. It does it pompously and interestingly. A bold twist on Corman's otherwise pulp thriller.

The acting was very strong across the board. It’s another single-location film, and there’s a lot of interrogation, which keeps the tension high and the atmosphere brooding. At times, it was hard to hear, though—I’m not sure if the audio was low or if it was just the mumbling, but it made parts difficult to follow. The film is well shot, with great use of lighting to make the most of a dim setting. I had a lot of questions about the plot, and the ending, while decent, felt a bit too convenient after all the build-up. Despite that, it was still a good watch.

reviews.text: The story of The Student of Prague is interesting, because losing his reflection bedevils the title character (producer Paul Wegener in his screen debut as Balduin) not because, as we might expect, it deprives him of a crucial part of his being (his soul; his goodness; his empathy), but rather because the doppelgänger interferes with Balduin's plans. We have no sense that, when whole, he wouldn't have chased a married woman, or gambled, or debauched himself in myriad ways — the issue is only that, now that he finally has the money to do everything of which he's dreamed, he also has a double who, for reasons which are left murky, won't let him alone, sitting in apparent judgement upon…

reviews.author: mykola
reviews.text: A haunting fable about the danger of desiring more than your soul can afford. The Student of Prague explores what happens when ambition, class longing, and romantic idealization sever a man from himself — literally. Balduin's downfall isn’t just about a doppelgänger — it’s about how easily we trade our identity for illusions. Love, status, even self-worth become hollow when they’re driven by ego. In the end, it’s not the mirror that breaks — it’s the man who looked too long into it.

reviews.author: Ian West
reviews.text: Be forwarned about the nature of this being a traditional giallo, if you’re expecting another intensely-titled giallo... be prepared for so much more... polizio comedy gialli? I can’t really explain Suspicious Death of a Minor, but it’s hella fun and throws so much of what was popular in Italy at the time at the table with its genre elements... sleaze, Street chases, the same pair of glasses getting broken about 25 times, a stellar soundtrack, and a rollercoaster shootout that’s pretty damn amazing.Regardless, Martino’s poliziotteschi/euro comedy/giallo thriller mashup is still entertaining as it weaves its way in and out of sub genres (with success... most of the time) and is definitely worth a watch if you ask me.

reviews.author: WraithApe
reviews.text: Also known as Too Young To Die, Sergio Martino's genre mash-up is confused, and oftentimes confusing. There are elements of gialli, poliziotteschi and most bizarrely, screwball comedy, all competing for your attention but never fully meshing. What should be tense chase scenes - the excellent POV rollercoaster shootout especially - are undercut by goofy carny ditties when what's really required is something propulsive; some angular jazz maybe, or spangly 70s funk rock. You do get the latter, repetitiously in fact, though Luciano Michelini's score is a far cry from the best of the era.

reviews.text: An actual, considerable improvement upon an already delightful premise. For one thing, Winterbottom's vistas of Italy are far more loving and epic than his more pastoral depiction of the English countryside. For another, the focus shifts away from Coogan, who starts to attain a sense of contentment in life (ironically from losing a job, a set of circumstances that nonetheless allows him to move back home to be with his son), while Brydon now has to deal with the temptations and miseries of fame and attention. It shakes up the dynamic without doing anything to radical, and watching Brydon deal with the nervousness of attraction to a guide, or of getting a potential big-break part, loads his chirpy impressions now…

reviews.author: Sam Van Hallgren
reviews.text: Expert sequel-ing. Self aware, and yet avoids trying to top the pleasures of the original. And if not funnier than the first at least as funny, while also digging a little deeper into Brydon and Coogan's anxieties. A day later, I'm still laughing about kumquat. And Brydon's Man in the Box making an appearance in Pompeii was not only hilarious, its borderline inappropriateness - along with Coogan's response to it - actually made the thousands year-old tragedy of the place hit home in a way that surprised me. And the look on Brydon's face after he books the big movie gig told me more about the melancholy of the movie business than anything this side of (the oft mentioned) Fellini.

reviews.author: Justin Decloux
reviews.text: Back in my video store days, THE VIOLENT PROFESSIONALS was the film that started my love for Eurocrime, so I was surprised on this re-watch to discover it's only a solid example of the subgenre. It's got the Dirty Harry Cop (Luc Merenda) killing bad guys without mercy and some solid directorial gymnastics by workhorse Director Sergio Martino, but beyond that, it’s a pretty bog-standard undercover story that skimps on the action beyond a few brief fistfights and a solid car chase. It’s head and shoulders above the output of hacks like Stelvio Massi but it doesn’t hold a candle to Enzo G. Castellari on a good day. I guess it explains why Martino’s other Eurocrime films, like GAMBLING CITY and THE SUSPICIOUS DEATH OF A MINOR, are more genre stews than straight-ahead action pictures.

reviews.text: I know that the majority of this film is "fictional," but the fact that it's a government funded film which essentially demonstrates the horrific course of action that the government would take in the event of nuclear warfare makes it incredibly haunting. Some of the scenes and imagery in this film are unforgettably bleak; at only 48 minutes, it's much, much heavier than most films three times its length and makes perfectly good use of every second of its runtime. Imagine what people must have thought seeing this film back in 1965... it depicts anything and everything from firestorms to executions, martial law to the disintegration of an entire civilization - The War Game should be watched by all. It's possibly the best short film that I've seen since Night and Fog, and I can only hope that it isn't prophetic.

The grandiosity of 1970's live action victorian England (vests) combined with grimy cartoons and (inexplicably) a number of rousing musical acts with depictions of chimney sweeps in elegant bowlcuts and the desperation of girls bedrooms in 1970s period pieces. Water Babies poses the question of wearing a starched apron among furniture covered in white sheets, that thing where the same actor plays two different characters, and yes, an idiot villain sidekick. It sets out to solve the problem of animated lobsters. To define the place my memory overlaps with “Water Babies” would mean to poorly animate hundreds of partially clothed swimming babies, silver rimmed glasses and veiled praise of Charles Darwin’s On The Origins of Species.

reviews.author: DavidS60
reviews.text: The Window is a quiet little movie from Argentina. Set in the vast expanse of Patagonia, an elderly writer rests on his deathbed, waiting for the arrival of his estranged son in order to make amends before his demise. The film is slow and meditative as it details a day in the life of a man who knows that death is imminent. The camera follows him as he admires the beauty of a horse in a field, as he wanders through his garden, as he watches a boy with a dead rabbit returning home for dinner. Sound is equally important, whether it is the sound of a ticking clock or the striking of a piano key or the rustling of wind-blown grass. The Window is beautifully filmed, almost certain to be rewarding for anyone who’ll allow it to wash over them.

reviews.text: When I was a kid, my dad represented a man accused of multiple murders, and when he was acquitted of the crimes, as a show of gratitude, he took our family out to dinner at Bonanza Steakhouse. As we all sat there eating, I kept staring over at the man, wondering if he was capable of such atrocious acts. At one point, he busted me, looked up from his plate and met my gaze. He set his silverware down and adjusted himself in his chair so that he was staring directly at me. He didn’t nod or smile. He didn’t blink. And when I looked away, for a few moments after, I could still feel him watching me. No one else seemed to notice, and after a spell he turned back to his food.

The Women of Brewster Place is a stirring emotional drama that guts you with tragedy but also offers immense safety and space to let the tears fall. (For me, it was a much more digestible form of For Colored Girls.) We get to hear so many compelling conversations on marriage, death, womanhood, parenting, the pursuit of happiness, finding your peace. The accompanying dialogue was poignant and pure, almost flowing like a stage play. And although laughter healed some of the women, so did the power of community. This Is My Life never received the praise that your Seinfelds, your Apatows, and your other Masters of None did, but it’s one of the most heartfelt and least narcissistic…

reviews.author: Wesley Stenzel
reviews.text: Nora Ephron’s shockingly undervalued directorial debut follows a single mother in pursuit of stand-up comedy stardom, and her career’s impact on her two young daughters. Many of the filmmaker’s best movies are about the power of words, and This is My Life is the Ephron movie that best explores the relational consequences of her signature quick wit. Throughout her career, the filmmaker consistently creates charming, chattery characters who constantly deliver perfectly poetic dialogue, full of humor and poignance. Here, Ephron confronts the interpersonal strain of a sharp tongue — if every character can perfectly articulate their rage and fear and distress into brilliant one-liners, how can those characters tolerate one another, let alone build a loving relationship?

It’s a pretty watchable film, but ultimately a bit of a nothing burger, the kind that coasts more on its cast than its content. Zane does his usual slick, slightly unhinged thing, and Brook, well… let’s just say her screen presence is memorable for obvious reasons. There’s a pulpy charm to the setup, and for a while it’s not dull, but the final act really drags and deflates whatever fun the film had going for it. Still, if you’ve got a soft spot for trashy early-2000s island thrillers, you might find some fleeting entertainment here.

The man‘s backstory is revealed to us through flashback. reviews.author: Andy Summers 🤠
reviews.text: Dana Andrews has slowly grown on me during my Western odyssey, popping up in 8 half decent Westerns, both in starring and supporting roles which have lingered. Funnily enough it has been his later films that have endeared him to me most, when he was a little chunkier, a little craggier, and far from the handsome twenty-something he was in Otto Preminger's Laura, or as the tragic Donald Martin in William A Wellman's The Ox-Bow Incident. Andrews was a fine actor, although the description of him being 5"10" did come across as somewhat generous given the films that I've seen him in, but a diminutive stature never did Audie Murphy or Alan Ladd any harm either?

reviews.author: ScreeningNotes
reviews.text: Neat little premise and award-worthy pun title: a man is nearly lynched and returns for revenge, and the merciful sheriff gives him 3 hours to figure out who was behind his almost-death before the marshal arrives to arrest him. It's one part Western Murder Mystery and one part 3:10 to Yuma-style Time-Bound Thriller, so it's a bit perplexing that it doesn't manage to wring more dramatic tension out of such a great formula. Ultimately it's probably hamstrung by its short run time, leaving not enough time to develop the various suspected characters, but even if it's a bit unexceptional it's still a solid little flick and deserving of more than the few views it's got on here

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: The 19th century was the century of Britain. The 20th century was the century of America. The 21st century seems likely to be the century of China. In which case, Tie Xi Qu: West of the Tracks may be the most important film of the century, the one most about how we got here, on a human level.

reviews.author: Marcissus
reviews.text: Tie Xi Qu is 551 minutes of tragedy and desolation and uncertainty and solitude and imminent extinction. And sometimes it's real cosy, and sometimes it's real fun, and sometimes I wished I was there, and doesn't that "this is the way our family used to be" just slice you right in half? This flip-flopping meandering of humanity is hard to even quantify, filmed from 1991-2001 but doesn't feel like it's from either century. I watched Remnants (Part II) twice just for the hell of it. Sometimes you just want to drift into another world. It feels like time-travelling.

reviews.author: comrade_yui
reviews.text: the full and final realization of total cinema: labor, life, passage. filmmaking proper began with workers leaving the lumière factory; now the factory's closing, the workers are laid off, and the night grows cold, only wang bing's camera capturing the fleeting embers of cigarettes amidst burst water pipes and molten slag spilled over across the industrial plains of modern china. andre bazin speculated that the ideal of 'total cinema' would liberate the image from division and allow the viewer to experience the immensity of virtual space rendered in fearful clarity to the eyes and ears -- wang bing's vision does not flinch. he seeks out every nook and cranny of tiexi's labyrinth, a silent cartographer of stories and complaints and…

reviews.author: evilbjork
reviews.text: Unquestionably the best documentary I have ever seen. Wang Bing's masterful eye for where to point the camera and how to move it perfectly lets you enter the world he is showing. You are just another factory worker playing cards after a shift. This voyeuristic way of filmmaking completely justifies the 9 hours run time. If this film was made like the average documentary there would be informational voice-overs and quick cuts showing events which for me at least would get pretty exhausting after a few hours. Here instead of that, the entire time you feel as if you're in the room, experiencing and figuring out things for yourself. The time went by surprisingly fast and affected me much more…

reviews.text: One action can condemn you. One action can save you. Time, feelings, things left unsaid, circumstances, much can provide for an excuse, for a glimpse of redemption, but, in the end, it comes down to actions. One action. That action. It will haunt you forever, the knowledge that your action is responsible for life, responsible for death. Gambling away your house. Waking up your son. Performing puppets show. Giving a bun to a starving man. Actions, so meaningless when compared to the consequences they causes, so small you almost don't even notice them, until it's too late, until the mechanism they operate is brought to its conclusion. Actions. Fate's tangible presence.

I did not expect To Live to be as nuanced as it was towards communist China, with a lot of criticism and also some glimpses into positive idealism. Having said that, To Live only uses history as a backdrop, it's mostly just the story of family. The characters may make a point of trying to appease the political situation around them so as to not appear politically backwards but it's still a story about people above all else.

reviews.text: China allowed Zhang Yimou to film To Live because it highlighted the resilience of the Chinese people who faced a very tough road from the Great Leap Forward through the Proletariat Revolution. China banned To Live and didn't allow its citizens to see it because it critiqued the Great Leap Forward and the Proletariat Revolution. To Live is a great successs because it is both of these things, a portrait of resilience and a biting critique, Zhang doesn't tip the scales in one direction of a narrative. When bad things happen to this family it feels equal strength of character and equal critique of government. It's a delicate balance. What's astounding is that the critiques involve dark humor. This one even gets near the idea that Woody and the gang's relative stability is a privileged experience, that the life of your average toy is probably a sad, lonely one, that their self-actualization is rare. The adventure this time is slight but the egalitarian streak is ramped up, I really related to the new character who only wants to go in the trash, and I'd gladly sit through another story if it's going to be this stealthily thoughtful.

I still am but I feel like it is crucial to point out those interests have been with me for most of my life – I sought out and still enjoy twisted tales with bizarre setups, surreal imagery and grisly outcomes that leave room for some dark humor. Imagine my surprise when “Trapped Ashes” managed to make me think, “well, I’ve never seen -THAT- before” on two separate occasions. When a horror anthology manages to do that, you know you’re dealing with something special.

reviews.author: Michael Shawn
reviews.text: Just based on the enormously high quality and pedigree of most of the films they release on Blu-ray, it can't help but feel like Deaf Crocodile is slumming it with this horror-anthology by an almost all-star slate of directors. Joe Dante, Ken Russell, Sean S. Cunningham, Monte Hellman, and... John Gaeta(??) working together on one film? But even if the final product is a little uneven, I felt like it was still better than a good 75% of anthologies. At least it holds together thematically, unlike most of them. And though some of the stories are a bit underbaked, it features some satisfying gore, lots of nudity, and at least three recognizable stars. Also, for once, the wraparound story is…

reviews.text: Ulysses & Mona opens with a shot of a tennis machine spewing out balls for an unseen tennis aficionado, while a twee synth-based score by Minizza bounces its own rhythm in your ears. It feels like an apt summation of Sébastien Betbeder’s film: the score foreshadows its largely precocious tone, while the machine is representative of Betbeder himself, lobbing out his ideas to us and hoping we serve back appreciatively. The trouble is, the machine is set on the easiest mode possible, so we serve back diligently but unenthusiastically. If the reward is in the challenge, then there’s no help in being disappointed.

reviews.text: A millennial fairy tale that’s very confused about who actually belongs to that demographic cohort (aren’t we all), Brie Larson’s “Unicorn Store” is too adult for kids, too childlike for adults, and too muddled for the motley lot of misfits and dreamers who just want to think different. It’s a movie that sustains its strained plot with a huge heart — a movie that redeems its empty characters with a terrific cast. Most of all, it’s a movie that reminds you why “Mr. Magorium’s Wonder Emporium” opted not to have a subplot about sexual harassment.

reviews.author: Not Andrew Sarris
reviews.text: Up the Down Staircase can be considered a failure for asking questions it is afraid to answer. Why should ghetto children receive an education modeled after middle-class values outside the ghetto? How do educators break the vicious circle of hopeless home environments causing hopeless classroom situations that will perpetuate hopelessness into the next generation? With updated lesson plans on Silas Marner and A Tale of Two Cities? With tea and sympathy, or faith, hope, and charity? Or by pretending that problems do not exist except in the minds of bigots, and that all children are created equal and treated fairly?

reviews.author: Cinema_Strikes
reviews.text: The Ken Russell version of Babylon is still not all that great, but certainly far less obnoxious. As an actor, Rudolf Nureyev is a great dancer, but he definitely keeps up the male end when it comes to nudity. Carol Kane is fun in a limited role, and we get scabrous portraits of period figures like Alla Nazimova and Fatty Arbuckle (Nazimova in particular gets an all time great entrance). Michelle Phillips (of the Mamas and the Papas) at least brings a bizarre energy to her portrayal of Valentino’s paramour, operating on the same arch and mannered level as the film.

reviews.author: SwedishLlama
reviews.text: A criminally underseen film that, to me, is superior in every single way to Damien Chazelle’s Babylon. The story of a film star in 1920s Hollywood, women are reported to have attempted suicide due to Valentino’s death. The first Hollywood sex symbol, setting a precedent for an entire century of American media, yet he’s mostly forgotten in the 21st century. Ken Russell’s biopic has his usual over the top, flamboyant and campy style with a very charming craziness and stunning visuals. The restoration of this just looks perfect. The colours, set and costume design are some of the best in any film ever, really. Just look at any scene and the style shines through, with Russell’s appreciation for this era of…

reviews.author: Onno
reviews.text: Odin, Thor, Loki, Asgard, Walhalla – alles Namen, die mittlerweile aus der Popkultur nicht mehr wegzudenken sind. Es gab bis dato zahlreiche Verfilmungen der nordischen Mythologie, doch besonders Marvel hat diese mit den THOR-Filmen und –Comics massentauglich gemacht. Aber schon Jahrzehnte davor, machte sich eine dänische Zeichentrickproduktion auf, diese massentauglich zu machen und zerbrach an diesem. Die Firma ging Pleite, aber zumindest Quark, der kleinste Riese der Welt, hatte es sich in zahlreichen Kindheitserinnerungen gemütlich gemacht. Nun kommen er und die Geschichte von WALHALLA wieder, als eine skandinavische Co-Produktion in Realfilmgestalt.

Cena antológica: a protagonista Roskva e o amigo gigante Quark em uma viagem psicodélica lisérgica no meio do filme após ingerirem cogumelos. Vale ressaltar a arma de lançar talco do Odin. reviews.author: Karl Janssen
reviews.text: Even for a lover of peplum films, this adventure of the Greek Gods holds little charm. It's chock full of all the qualities the genre is chided for—a story full of holes, bad acting, cheap sets and costumes, and relentlessly amateurish direction by Emimmo Salvi. Venus, using her seductive wiles, stirs up a conflict between Mars and Vulcan. Perennial peplum favorite Gordon Mitchell has a supporting role as Pluto, but he isn't given much to do. For special effects, a thunderbolt from Zeus is rendered by scratching a jagged white line in the film. The film's one saving grace is Cuban-born beauty Bella Cortez, whose sexy dance number is the highlight of the film.

reviews.author: John Charles
reviews.text: Tired of typical sword and sandal fare? Here you go: this is one of the strangest pictures in the genre. Made with tongue in cheek, its laugh quota is even higher, thanks to inept staging and bad English dubbing. Iranian muscleman Rod Flash has the title role and is accompanied on his adventures by an annoying comic relief dwarf sidekick. The various gods on Mount Olympus (including Gordon Mitchell and Roger Browne) take an active role in the plot, which features the usual genre battles staged with decidedly less flare than usual (lots of people getting bashed with rubber clubs). Peplum completists will find some fun here; others should look elsewhere.

reviews.author: Silversaxophone
reviews.text: Pleasingly calm anti-Red thriller done in the semi-documentary mode established by Henry Hathaway's House on 92nd Street, also produced by Louis de Rochemont who, not surprisingly, co-created the March of Time series. The spies, sleeper agents and local treasonous villains are mostly presented as cloying and snivelling, but they are also varied and have their own reasons, and their dynamic as a group, which gets agitated by the arrival of a senior agent from Moscow Central, is the most interesting thing about the picture. Plus there is a least one Red who hates the smugness of Capitalism and wants to see it brought down, which is nice. There is the usual technical detail of the FBI investigation, including all the latest gadgets and techniques, but it is director Alfred Werker's eye for composition and suspense which keeps the plot engaging. Not exactly The Americans but worth a look.

reviews.text: Considering how Wash lacks in terms of any clarity, it totally accounts for with the atmosphere and ambiguity that spin that into its benefit. This is director Kristofer Kiggs Carlsson’s second outing as a short filmmaker, and like his previous effort Spiritus Lepus (2017), there’s a slightly bizarre fascination with rabbits. Maybe that should be obvious given his production company ‘Atomic Rabbit Productions’ - perhaps suggesting some kind of Atomic Rabbit shared Universe - it is however not to be rendered as ‘silly’. Wash channels the ‘not so imaginary’ best friend dynamic with great subtlety and finesse. Nothing is explicitly explained, we are instead guided into the world of Wash. In many ways it feels like the beginning of a terrifying third act.

reviews.text: In the rare event when a major Hollywood studio advertises one of its films as “the most original movie of the year” — as Universal has done in the trailer for “Welcome to Marwen” — it tends to be code for: “We spent a ton of money on something that we have absolutely no idea how to sell.” And while that was certainly the case here, it’s hard not to sympathize with the poor souls in the marketing department, who were tasked with promoting a story that director Robert Zemeckis had no idea how to tell. In hindsight, it seems they did the best they could. As disconcerting as it was when the previews for “Welcome to Marwen” reduced the complicated and ineffably human saga of Mark Hogancamp into a glossy inspirational fable about the power of friendship, it’s even more disconcerting to find that the film itself does much the same thing.

Corbucci's direction is swift but too unfocused, however, his ability to stage elaborate, well-filmed action sequences remains unphased and when combined with a decently melancholy Ennio Morricone score, it does give the film a bit…

Both tackle the same conceit of throwing a comedic duo into a serious wartime scenario. In this situation, a pious preacher finds himself tethered by fate to a playboy actor and together experience the entirety of the Mexican Revolution - even becoming central figures to the movement! You could say it's The Odd Couple mixed with Duck, You Sucker!, with the two frequently going through that moment in The Good, The Bad and The Ugly where Blondie and Tuco feign allegiance with who they believe to be Confederate soldiers again and again.

reviews.author: Nick Langdon
reviews.text: Director Sergio Corbucci is most well known for his spaghetti westerners, with Django (1966) being his most famous and enduring work. However he was a jobbing filmmaker who dabbled in almost all the genres popular in Italy across the decades. He started makings dramas in the 1950s, then moved into peplum/sword & sandal epics in the early 60s, followed by Eurospy in the late 1960s, then finally to Bud Spencer & Terence Hill comedies in the 1970s. Really the only things missing were giallo and poliziotteschi. Again, while mostly remembered for his blood-soaked sagas of the American west, in the 70s he developed a taste for comedy, and that leads us to the dismal and dismally unfunny, What Am I Doing in…

reviews.author: Will Sloan
reviews.text: This documentary about Pauline Kael hits all the expected beats: Limelight, Hiroshima Mon Amour, The Sound of Music, Bonnie and Clyde, Last Tango in Paris, "Raising Kane," Woody Allen, Warren Beatty, Shoah, and Casualties of War. Her disgraceful review of Shoah is quoted at length, and the film's defense boils down to: "No movie is sacrosanct, and hey, at least she was honest, right?" The many lapses in "Raising Kane" - her only work as a film historian - are glossed over, and the film pathetically attempts to make the case that, actually, this essay helped revive interest in Welles!

reviews.author: Chris Cabin
reviews.text: As absent of anything like intellectual rigor or historical curiosity or visual buoyancy or insight or simple joy as any documentary that I've seen, centered on a subject that should rouse all of those at once. Limp yet overbearing direction; music that holds your hand to make sure you're feeling the right things; interviews with colleagues, admirers, and friends boiled down to sound bites, scrubbed almost entirely of intimacy. Among all these issues, it's worth underlining the fact that Kael would have absolutely hated this movie. A complete waste of time and good footage.

Begeistert von der deutschen Filmlandschaft, feierte er ausgiebig die Indizierung samt Folgeindizierung 2011 seines harmlosen Poesie Werkes in vollen Zügen, obwohl er 3 Jahre zuvor das Zeitliche segnete. Ist eben ein Könner dieser Cirio H. Santiago. Was er natürlich auch in seinem philosophisch angehauchten Meisterwerk "Die Solo-Kampfmaschine" zeigte. Während Mel Gibson ihm zu billig war, setzte er auf Laiendarsteller ohne Perspektive. Dort strahlte der Protagonist noch weniger aus, als ein Stein am Waldweg mitten in der Nacht umringt…

John McPhails been a director I’ve admired since Anna and the Apocalypse, and he shares something in common with my other favorite filmmakers James Gunn and Edgar Wright. He wears his sincerity like a badge of honor. And damn it he should. It’s on Freevie and it’s a little more than 80 minutes (barely 90). Check this baby out. A city slicker woman is wooed out west, but even the wide rural expanse is complicated somewhat by the fact that her husband and the film's serial killer daylights by installing wildly elaborate, bespoke hi-fi systems into homes as sleek and modern as anything in prime Antonioni or Argento. But when the blood-letting starts, it unfurls in lysergic splashes of psychosexual release, punctuated by flashbacks that brim with primal, prehistoric savagery and a transition blend of dissolves, irises and frequent "pillow shots" of…

reviews.text: White of the Eye feels like a desert bleach sun rot death spiral into a nightmare in a damaged brain. Sure, the investigatory exposition dumps drag and the acting comes across frightened and amateurish and jittery in spots. But those slow swooping camera movements and out-of-place closeups on eyeballs and dripping meat and broken bloodstained glass looked like an abstract expressionist painting spawned from the brush of John Wayne Gacy, Jr. though! This feel bad, art damaged movie got on my weird wavelength and held tight once the final act coagulated into a putrid too real heap of screaming and giant blades and family trauma.

The DIY production, the gleeful violence, the feverish "Video Joker" emcee narration, they all mark this (at least to my questionable mind) as pure, completely guileless exploitation cinema. This is the work of people excited to see themselves on screen, an unmediated product of their own self-image. Outsiders and smarter people than myself can dissect it as ethnography, and they should, but above all it just wants to be "Uganda's First Action Movie", and it's great.

reviews.author: kat🕷
reviews.text: A surprisingly captivating movie, nothing like what you might dread based on the title. On the contrary, it's perhaps the finest version of what you could hope for with a name like this. It stands as the ideal counter-program to "Pretty Woman", demolishing every sugary cliché about this profession."Whore" lays bare the dark realities: abusive clients, ruthless pimps and a complete absence of genuine love or affection. It's not a voyeuristic experience or porn; rather, it sheds light on the dehumanizing plight of streetwalkers. It also delves into their fragility, dependence, and the near-impossibility of escaping to a "normal life". A criminally underrated dramedy by Ken Russell.

Although its spokesperson is female, Ken Russell's WHORE is a film about men and what it is that they think about sex. There's nothing subtle about it, it's even abrasive in its post-modernism, but one has to give it credit for at least tackling a thorny subject head on. Not as successful as his earlier CRIMES OF PASSION, most probably because Theresa Russell is too edgy an actress, lacking the kind of warmth that Kathleen Turner brought to that earlier LA-set sex flick.

While it doesn't quite have that punchline structure of most shorts, this one instead excels at giving you a perfect slice out of a feature length pie. No drawn out runway hoping the wheels will eventually get off the tarmac, this starts up in the sky and stays there with a firm hold on powerful dark cinematography, thick retro synths, and a plot that feels both original and familiar in just the right ways. Love how it's hinting at so much doom and destruction, steeped in the 80's horror charm we all eat up, but ready to take a bold step forward.

Centering on a young woman being pursued by a masked stranger through the snow. She takes refuge in a random home, decorated to the nines with yuletide spirit, and unknowingly awakens an ancient evil. Available to watch via YouTube and Vimeo, this dark dash of holiday horror is a great way to get through the season.

reviews.author: Joe Wawrzyniak
reviews.text: A really solid and effective 4-minute horror short that checks all the right boxes. Psycho freak in an illuminati mask? Yep. Funky pulsating retro 1980's-style synth score? Oh boy, do we ever get that! Does it take excellent eerily unsettling advantage of a bleak wintry landscape? Once again, we get that too. Some kind of weird creepy demon thing with antlers? Yeah, it pops up briefly at the end. Spooky ooga-booga atmosphere? Yes, this short radiates these seriously shuddery vibes throughout. Bright giallo-inspired lighting? Man, talk about some cool striking use of red in one specific scene. And how about this short taking place at Christmastime? Well, this short even covers that particular base quite nicely. To sum up, this short certainly hits the pleasingly shivery spot and then some.

reviews.text: In The Punk Singer, a powerful documentary about singer, feminist, and artist Kathleen Hanna, there's a scene in which Hanna casually mentions that "There is always suspicion about a woman's truth." It's a comment about which I frequently think, and one that came to mind again and again as I watched Witness to Murder, a film released just a few weeks before Rear Window in 1954, and one which also depicts its main character seeing something through the window that makes them sure a neighbor has committed murder. And the comparisons to Real Window are instructive, because they throw into stark relief the different levels of authority carried by the voices of men and women.

reviews.text: An artful fable that examines what it really means to save the world, Benedikt Erlingsson’s “Woman at War” is the rarest of things: A crowd-pleaser about climate change. Combining Paul Schrader’s dire urgency with Roy Andersson’s droll brand of despair — to cite two other filmmakers whose work has wrestled with the maddening, quixotic idea of a single person trying to redeem an entire planet — Erlingsson has created a winsome knickknack of a movie that manages to reframe the 21st century’s signature crisis in a way that makes room for real heroism.

reviews.author: Cinematic Underdogs
reviews.text: Benedikt Erlingsson’s Woman at War is a vital, genre-bending parable about the perils of human complacency in the face of planetary collapse. A superb eco-conscious thriller, the film follows a radical guerrilla-activist—the middle-aged Halla (played by the tenacious Halldóra Geirharðsdóttir)—who has realized that passively protesting environmental catastrophe is no longer sufficient. Halla is a quirky, well-adjusted, headstrong woman. She meditates, rides her bike around town, disseminates political pamphlets, and eagerly anticipates the opportunity to adopt a Ukrainian child. She also would be defined—absurd as it is, when viewed holistically—as a ’terrorist’: given that she is a solo, renegade crusader (the news coverage nicknames her “Mountain Woman”) hellbent on disrupting the power lines feeding energy to a remote aluminum plant.

reviews.text: fritz lang made many famous films in america but i'll always prefer the fantastical silent epics he made in pre-war germany with his then-wife (and future national socialist) thea von harbou as screenwriter. lang's last silent, 'frau im mond,' is often heralded as the first scientifically plausible sci-fi film. unfairly overshadowed by the flashier 'metropolis,' it's an eminently enjoyable melodrama clearly inspired by comics and pulp fiction adventure tales, which lang collected. the outsized characters include an entrepreneur and his assistant, both in love with the female scientist who insists on accompanying them on their trip, a half-mad professor whose theories about moongold inspired the project, the devious henchman for a gang of international capitalists out to hijack the mission,…

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: Fritz Lang's Woman in the Moon is best known for its attention to the technical aspects of space traveling, including the employment of an actual rocket scientist as an advisor, the depiction of a multistage rocket, and what is widely considered the first use of a countdown to launch. In addition, as with Lang's Metropolis the use of miniatures for the rocket and its launch is breathtakingly clever and completely effective.

reviews.author: Flávia
reviews.text: Fritz Lang, em minha opinião, ocupa um patamar de criatividade, ousadia e genialidade como raramente se vê no cinema. Em filmes como Woman in the Moon e Metropolis, conseguiu antecipar o futuro como se o observasse por um telescópio. É certo que muitos dos aparatos científicos mostrados nessas obras hoje parecem fruto da imaginação inocente de uma criança, mas grande parte do que ali se apresenta ainda impressiona pela riqueza de detalhes e pela antecipação quase exata de uma realidade que só se concretizaria muitas décadas depois.

reviews.text: Fritz Lang´s final silent film “Woman in the Moon” is another visionary sci fi epic that was far ahead of its time. To be exact, the film follows a space journey to the moon 40 years before the real-life moon landing. And if you think “what´s the big deal, Georges Méliès has done that already in 1902” then you´re correct but the difference is that “Woman in the Moon” takes space travel and the science behind it seriously. Rocket scientist Herrmann Oberth worked as an advisor on the movie and his influence is clear to see. The launching sequence, which is the centerpiece of the film, has been widely praised for its accuracy and prescience in its portrayal of technical…

reviews.author: Colin the dude
reviews.text: The first time you watch 'Xanadu' you're a sponge absorbing the madness. You take it in, ridicule it, spit it out. The second time, if a second time doesn't sound like suicide, the experience is much kinder and the unapologetic sincerity behind it spreads like a contagion. Most are immune, but some get infected. Consider me infected. If you're an ELO fan, the film is wondrous background noise. And when you're watching the screen, there's magical colors, tap dancing, roller boogieing, laser beams, coked up dancers and it's cheez wiz heaven. 'Xanadu' is a beautiful bridge between the old (the Gene Kelly generation) and the new (the Olivia Newtown-John generation). Or more like a rainbow of 70s decadence and the pot of gold at the end is the 80s. The 60s closed with Altamont and the 70s had 'Xanadu'. The end of an era.

Unfortunately, the judge makes an example of Dillinger and sentences him to a long prison term. reviews.author: chas
reviews.text: See the birth of the legend in YOUNG DILLINGER, starring Nick Adams as the titular criminal. This film traces his early career, from Cagney-inspired romantic to psychopathic gang leader. Unforgiving and brutal in its’ depiction, the film prefigured Bonnie and Clyde’s nihilistic violence. The kind of thrilling, amoral crime picture Dillinger himself would’ve enjoyed, this film was originally produced for, and then banned from, TV. A rare film, unavailable on DVD, it also features Victor Buono as the memorably droll criminal consultant Professor Hofman.

It's all here.

reviews.author: Cliff
reviews.text: I'm not entirely convinced that it's a wise idea for a movie documentary to be longer than the actual film it's about, but at least you can't accuse this 146-minute look back at Tom Holland's 106-minute directorial debut, Fright Night, of not being comprehensive. (This is actually a shorter version of the doc, which unedited runs for an extra hour and eleven minutes, covering the 1988 sequel and 2011 remake.) It would have been nice to have lost all of actor Simon Bamford's appearances though: not part of the original cast, here he plays Roddy McDowall's ham horror star character Peter Vincent in a highly irritating and unfunny way. But pretty much everyone else who turns up is good value,…

reviews.author: James
reviews.text: Smog enveloped skyscrapers, government enforced population control and oppressed, subservient citizens—no, not present day China, but a bizarre relic of seventies sci-fi cinema. Z.P.G. has an interesting premise that's incredibly prescient when viewed today—the idea that mass overpopulation and reckless use of resources will plummet humanity into a totalitarian dystopia doesn't seem so farfetched these days.
